note: Consolidated top-level descriptions: everything the catalogue establishes about the castle, each area and each place, gathered in one place. Paraphrase only. Every fact cites catalogue records and carries an evidence label. Estimates are modelling minimums, not figures from the books.

castle.summary: Hogwarts is a vast stone castle on a cliff above a lake. Its main body has eight storeys, a ground floor and seven numbered floors in British numbering, with a dungeon level below the ground floor. No floor above the seventh is ever numbered: everything higher stands inside a tower. Five towers are named. The Astronomy Tower is the tallest. Ravenclaw and Gryffindor are the next highest. West Tower, with the Owlery, and North Tower, with the Divination classroom, are lower but still rise above the seventh floor. Gryffindor Tower starts on the seventh floor with dormitories stacked above its common room, so the best modelling figure for its top is the fourteenth floor, 15 storeys up. The castle has 142 staircases, about 20 between each pair of floors. It houses hundreds of pupils, and its shared rooms are built to match: a Great Hall that took about 1,200 seats at one ball, kitchens of the same size beneath it, and a library of hundreds of rows. The books give no overall dimensions, so its size has to be built up from these counts. It should read as far larger than an ordinary school or an ordinary castle.

conventions.title: Floors are British
conventions.text: The ground floor comes first, and the first floor is one flight above it. The seventh floor is therefore the eighth storey. The books agree: from the seventh floor it is six floors down and then the marble staircase, seven staircases link the ground and seventh floors, and the dungeons are eight floors below the seventh.

conventions.title: Floor numbers and storeys differ
conventions.text: A floor number leaves out the ground floor and a storey count includes it, so the fourteenth floor is the fifteenth storey.

conventions.title: Evidence labels
conventions.text: Explicit: narrated as fact. Reported: a character says or believes it. Inference: deduced from the text, with the reasoning shown. Estimate: a modelling minimum resting on an assumption the books do not give, with the arithmetic shown.

conventions.title: Estimates are not canon
conventions.text: Estimates exist to stop a model being made far too small. Treat them as lower limits to design above, and never present them as facts from the books.

conventions.title: Only the novels count
conventions.text: Films, games, wikis and companion material are not evidence here. Anything known only from them is left out, including their castle plans.

conventions.title: Dated states
conventions.text: Keep the permanent building separate from dated states such as decorations, tournament set-ups, classroom changes under each teacher and battle damage.

facts.text: The main body has eight storeys: the ground floor and seven numbered floors.
facts.because: From the seventh floor it is six floors down and then the marble staircase; seven staircases link the ground and seventh floors; no higher floor is numbered.

facts.text: A dungeon level lies below the ground floor: the dungeons are eight floors below the seventh.
It is described from the first as vast, with many turrets and towers, and later as a towering mass of turrets.
Durmstrang, by one of its own pupils, is not as big and has only four floors.
There are 142 staircases, of many forms: wide and sweeping, narrow and rickety, some with a vanishing step, some going elsewhere on a Friday.

That is about 20 staircases per gap between floors, or about 16 after setting aside 30 for towers and shortcuts. These are separate flights spread across a wide plan, not a stair stack counted floor by floor.
facts.because: 142 / 7 gaps = 20. (142 - 30) / 7 = 16. Any one climb from ground to seventh uses seven of them.

facts.text: Five towers are named. Astronomy is the tallest; Ravenclaw, Astronomy and Gryffindor are the three highest; West and North are lower.

Gryffindor Tower's best modelling height is a top floor of 14, 15 storeys counting the ground floor: seven dormitory levels above the seventh-floor common room. The strict minimum from the text is top floor 9.
facts.because: Seven year groups, one room per year on its own level: 7 + 7 = 14. The text proves at least two doors below the top room: 7 + 2 = 9.

facts.text: At 4.5 to 5 m per storey the seventh floor stands 32 to 35 m above the ground floor. Gryffindor's top room is then about 56 to 60 m up, and the Astronomy Tower must clear it.
facts.because: 7 x 4.5 to 5 m = 31.5 to 35 m. Adding 7 dormitory levels at 3.5 m gives 56 to 59.5 m. All storey heights are assumptions.

facts.text: Seen from outside, the main body should show at least eight rows of windows, with far more up the towers.
facts.because: Eight storeys of rooms, with windows recorded up to the seventh floor, where at least thirteen run along from West Tower.

facts.text: Plan a main block at least about 200 m long.
facts.because: A 50 by 24 m Great Hall, a library of 1,500 m² and eight storeys with about 20 staircases per gap will not fit in much less, and Ron's ten minutes to the top of North Tower implies several hundred metres of corridor. Rough, and not a stated figure.

facts.text: Pupils are always counted in hundreds, never given as a number. Plan on about 300 to 800.
facts.because: About a hundred coaches at three to five pupils each gives 300 to 500. One five-bed room per year and twenty-place classes point to about 280; more than a hundred exam tables point higher. Size shared rooms for the top of the range.

facts.text: Great Hall: about a hundred tables of about a dozen people each at the 1994 ball, more than a hundred exam tables on another occasion, and hundreds of sleeping bags across its floor.
The Great Hall needs at least 1,200 m² of floor, about 50 by 24 m, and at least 12 m to the ceiling.
facts.because: About 1,200 seats at about 1 m² a seat. All spacing is assumed.

facts.text: The kitchens directly under the Great Hall are as large as it is, with at least a hundred elves at work.
The Entrance Hall could take a whole four-bedroom house, and its ceiling is too high to see.
The library has hundreds of narrow rows, thousands of shelves and tens of thousands of books.
The library needs at least 300 m of row spacing and about 1,500 m² of floor, as one hall or a suite of rooms.
facts.because: 200 rows at an assumed 1.5 m per row = 300 m. Rows about 4 m long plus aisles give about 1,500 m².

facts.text: The Room of Hidden Things is the size of a large cathedral, with walls of objects up to fifty feet high.
The Owlery holds hundreds upon hundreds of owls, on perches rising to the top of the tower.
The Prefects' bathroom has a bath like a swimming pool with about a hundred golden taps around it.
The Quidditch hoops are fifty feet high, and the whole school fits in the stands.
Ron allows ten minutes from the Great Hall to the top of North Tower.
The seventh floor is a full storey: it carries the Gryffindor entrance, the Room of Requirement's wall, the Headmaster's gargoyle, Flitwick's office and the foot of the North Tower stair.
facts.because: Each is placed on the seventh floor separately, and the gargoyle is said to be on the far side of the castle from the Room of Requirement.

facts.text: Rooms are not sorted by type. Teachers’ offices, classrooms and bathrooms are scattered through every floor.
facts.because: Offices are placed on the first, third and seventh floors and in the dungeons.

facts.text: The largest states of the Room of Requirement cannot fit behind a seventh-floor wall, so treat them as a separate volume reached by the door.
facts.because: A cathedral-sized room would not fit on one upper floor of the castle.

conflicts.text: Hospital wing: never numbered. The only journey that counts floors gives the third; other journeys read as the first, and one as the seventh or higher.
Defence teacher's office: second floor in Book 2, third in Book 5, and fourth on one Book 4 route.
Moaning Myrtle's bathroom: first floor by Hermione in Book 2, second floor by the narrated climb and in Book 4.
Trophy room: third floor by the one walked route, sixth by a reading of the Marauder’s Map.
Headmaster's gargoyle: seventh floor in Book 6, while routes in Books 2 and 4 read much lower.

open: The overall plan and footprint: wings, courtyards and how the towers join the main body.
The height of the cliff and of every tower, and the width of each tower.
The floor of the library, and of the Transfiguration and History of Magic classrooms.

levels.note: No floor up here is numbered. Everything stands inside a tower.

castle-and-terrain.summary: The castle, its cliff and the surrounding country, taken from the horizon inwards. Mountains surround the site and one overshadows Hogsmeade; caves up there have hidden Sirius, Hagrid and Grawp. Boundary walls enclose wide grounds of sloping lawns, with the lake below the castle and the Forest to one side. The castle stands on a cliff above part of the shore, a vast stone mass of towers and turrets, with at least eight storeys in its main body and tower storeys above the seventh floor. Astronomy is the tallest tower, with Ravenclaw and Gryffindor next, then West and North towers. Inside are courtyards, an east and a west wing, 142 staircases, and a pupil body of about 300 to 800 by estimate. Layers of ancient and dated protection cover the whole site, stopping Apparition at the boundary. No dimension of the castle or grounds appears in the text, so scale has to be built up from storeys, window counts, crowds and walking times.

facts.text: Minimum level stack: dungeons, ground floor, seven numbered floors, then tower storeys. That is at least eight storeys in the main body, on top of a cliff, and about twelve at the highest towers.
facts.because: The floors and dungeons follow from B04-106 and B05-110, the storeys above the seventh from B03-111. The figure of about twelve is the estimate given under castle-exterior.

facts.text: Astronomy is the tallest tower; Ravenclaw, Astronomy and Gryffindor are the three highest; West and North towers are lower but above the seventh floor.
School roll: about 300 to 800 pupils, with the clues splitting into two clusters. Size whole-school spaces for 800. Not canon.
facts.because: Class and dormitory clues give about 280; coaches, desks and crowds give 350 to 800. The arithmetic is under castle-interior-general.

facts.text: 142 staircases, and a Headmaster who says he does not assume he knows all the secrets.
The grounds fall away from the castle on the narrated sides, and every return is uphill. The lake lies below, and the greenhouses are behind.
Nobody but house-elves can Apparate within the boundary, which leaves the gates, flight, Portkeys, secret passages and the Vanishing Cabinet as ways in.
The site is harshly seasonal: frost by November, snow of several feet and a frozen lake by December, mud in February, hot Junes.

conflicts.text: Pupil numbers: class and dormitory clues and crowd clues differ by nearly three times.

open: The height of the cliff and towers and the plan of the main block: the text gives no measurements.

arrival-and-gates.summary: The approach to the school, in the order you would travel it. From London, a barrier between platforms nine and ten leads to the platform for the Hogwarts Express, which leaves at eleven and runs north all day to Hogsmeade station on the far side of the lake. There the school divides. First-years go down a pine-lined path to the shore and cross in small boats, four to a boat, to an ivy-hidden opening in the cliff, a tunnel and an underground harbour, then climb through rock to grass by the front steps. Everyone else takes one of about a hundred coaches, drawn by Thestrals, along a long uphill lane to the winged-boar gates, up the long sweeping drive, and stops at the same stone steps below the great oak front doors. Both routes end at those steps. Every stage climbs towards the castle, and it is far longer than a coach ride suggests. The Knight Bus is a rare alternative that stops outside the gates.

facts.text: About a hundred coaches run in convoy, three to five pupils in each, while first-years cross four to a boat in an uncounted fleet.
Train: at least seven carriages. Road: far longer on foot than Harry expected. Drive: long enough that the castle's foot looks distant from the gates. Only estimates give lengths.
Order for most pupils: station, road and lane, gates, drive, steps, doors. The village lies off the same lane, left of the gates as you leave.
The two routes part at the station, one crossing the lake and the other going by road, and meet again at the steps.
facts.because: The boat route ends on grass below the steps (B01-009), and the coaches stop beside the same steps (B05-015).

facts.text: Every stage rises: the lane climbs to the gates, the drive climbs to the steps, and the steps climb to the doors. Only the first-years' path drops, to the lake.
Gates and walls are jinxed, and Apparition stops at this boundary.
Dated changes: Dementors at the gates from 1993 to 1994, Secrecy Sensors at the doors from 1996, and breaches of the wall in 1998.

open: Lengths of the road and drive, and the line of the boundary wall.

entrance-hall.summary: Walking in from the stone front steps, the oak front doors open straight into the Entrance Hall, a vast torch-lit stone room on the ground floor. It could take the whole of a four-bedroom suburban house, and its ceiling is too high to see from the floor. The marble staircase stands directly ahead and climbs to the first floor. On the right are the Great Hall’s double doors, and to the right of the staircase a door leads down to the kitchens and the Hufflepuff basement. On the staircase’s other side a door leads down to the dungeons and Slytherin, and a corridor on that side runs to classroom eleven. Small rooms open off the hall: the chamber where first-years wait before the Sorting, another empty chamber, and a broom cupboard. Giant house-point hourglasses stand in wall niches in one corner.

facts.text: The Entrance Hall is the castle’s main junction: the grounds, upper floors, Great Hall, kitchens and dungeons all connect here.
facts.because: The front doors, marble staircase, Great Hall doors, kitchen door and dungeon steps all open off this one room, and ordinary routes between them cross it.

facts.text: Doors on the Great Hall side lead to the rooms under the Great Hall; those on the other side lead to the dungeons.
facts.because: The kitchen door is to the right of the stairs, on the Great Hall’s side, and the kitchens lie under the Great Hall. The door to Slytherin is on the other side of the stairs.

facts.text: Modelling minimum, not canon: about 250 m² of open floor in the hall, plus the staircase and side rooms.
facts.because: From the Entrance Hall overview: about 400 people at an assumed 2.5 per m² in a band round a clear middle, 16 m by 16 m = 256 m².

great-hall.summary: The Great Hall is the castle's main dining and assembly room, on the ground floor, with the kitchens directly beneath it and matching it in size. Thousands of floating candles light four long house tables, which run up the room from the double doors to a staff table on a raised platform. It has to hold everyone at once: about a hundred tables of about a dozen people each stood here at the 1994 ball, more than a hundred exam tables in another year, and the whole school has slept on its floor. Behind the staff table, at the end where Hagrid sits, a door leads to a smaller room with paintings, a fire and a low chandelier; other small chambers beside the Hall are mentioned, but the text does not say they are that room. As a modelling minimum rather than a figure from the books, the Hall needs at least 1,200 m² of floor.

facts.text: Modelling minimum, not canon: at least 1,200 m² for the Great Hall, plus its side chambers.
facts.because: From the Great Hall overview: about 100 tables × about 12 seats × an assumed 1 m² per seat, checked against a span of fifty yards (46 m).

facts.text: The Hall and the kitchens form a two-level block of matching plan, the kitchens’ four tables lying exactly under the four house tables.
facts.because: The kitchens are stated to be as large as the Hall above them, and their tables are placed exactly beneath the house tables, so the two plans have to line up.

facts.text: The side chamber door is behind the staff table at Hagrid’s end, opposite the Hall’s main doors at the back of the room.
facts.because: The main doors open at the back of the Hall on the Slytherin side, while the side door is at the top, at the end nearest Gryffindor, so the two lie at opposite corners.

circulation.summary: The castle's connecting fabric: 142 staircases, stone corridors on every floor, and concealed shortcuts between them. Walking down from the top, the seventh floor holds the Fat Lady's corridor, Sir Cadogan's landing at the start of the North Tower stair, and the Barnabas tapestry. The fifth floor holds the Prefects' bathroom corridor and the east-wing corridor of the 1996 swamp. The fourth has a large vase halfway along one corridor, a blocked mirror passage and the head of a two-floor tapestry stair. The third holds the forbidden corridor, the one-eyed witch and, by inference, the Charms corridor. The second holds the disputed attack corridor outside Myrtle's bathroom and a tapestry shortcut towards Gryffindor. The first floor is the head of the marble staircase, and the ground floor is the Entrance Hall. With seven gaps between the ground and seventh floors, the staircases average about 20 per gap, so each floor is crossed at many separate points and no single stair stack will do. Routes are long: Ron allows ten minutes from the Great Hall to the top of North Tower. Windows along them look over the grounds.

facts.text: 142 staircases serve eight main levels, about 20 per gap, or about 16 after allowing for tower spirals and shortcuts.
facts.because: 142 ÷ 7 gaps = 20.3. With an assumed 30 set aside: 112 ÷ 7 = 16.

facts.text: Floors count in British style along the main route: six floors down from the seventh, then the marble staircase to the Entrance Hall.
The dungeons lie eight floors below the seventh floor.
Each floor needs at least about 400 m of corridor, and one long route covers about 450 m on the level.
facts.because: 16 staircases at an assumed 25 m apart: 400 m. Ron's ten minutes less about 4 minutes on stairs, at an assumed 1.25 m/s: 450 m.

facts.text: Concealed shortcuts behind tapestries, panels and false walls link floors, and the Marauder's Map shows many of them.

conflicts.text: The second-floor attack corridor's floor is disputed within Book 2: see that place.

gryffindor.summary: Gryffindor Tower is a round tower holding one House's common room and dormitories. You reach it on the seventh floor, the highest floor the books number, along a dead-end corridor closed by a large portrait of the Fat Lady. Given the password, the painting swings out like a door over a round hole set above floor level, and you climb through into the common room: a cosy, shabby, round room with a fireplace, sagging armchairs, rickety tables and noticeboards, big enough for the whole House. Across the room two doors open on separate stone spiral stairs, boys' and girls'. Dormitory doors open along the stairs. At the head of the boys' stair, at the top of the Tower, is a circular room with five four-poster beds and high narrow windows. Its boys kept it from 1991 to at least 1996 while the year sign on the door changed, so rooms stay with a year group. Only this room is described. A round room cannot hold both stairs, so they rise outside the rooms, and the rooms need two stacks or alternating levels. No book gives the Tower's height. With one room for each of seven years on its own level the top floor is the fourteenth, 15 storeys counting the ground floor. That is the best modelling figure, not a stated one. Only the Astronomy Tower is known to stand higher.

facts.text: The Tower is entered on the seventh floor, the eighth storey counted from the ground: six floors above the head of the marble staircase, seven staircases up in all.
No floor above the seventh is named in any book, so all dormitories lie inside the tower, above the numbered floors of the castle.
facts.because: A search of all seven books finds no eighth floor or higher. The North Tower and Headmaster's stairs also start from the seventh floor.

facts.text: A corridor ends at a large portrait of the Fat Lady. On the password it swings out like a door over a round hole in the wall.
The hole is a climb, not a doorway: its lower edge sits above the floor and it passes one person at a time.
facts.because: Everyone climbs or scrambles through, a short first-year needed a leg up, and pupils queue at it.

facts.text: Beyond the hole is the common room, a round tower room with a brick fireplace, worn armchairs, rickety tables, noticeboards, and glazed windows that open.
The whole House can crowd into it at once. About fifty at one 1997 party is not its limit.
It should be at least 13 m across, and about 17 m if two dormitory stacks stand on it.
facts.because: Assumes 0.75 m2 a person among furniture and a House of 175: 131 m2 is a circle 13 m across. Two 8.5 m stacks need 17 m.

facts.text: Across the room from the portrait hole, two separate doors open on two separate stairs, so neither stair rises inside the room.
facts.because: Boys and girls are sent through different doors and divide after crossing the room. Each stair starts behind its door.

facts.text: Both stairs are stone spirals. The boys' has walls close enough for a running boy to hit. The girls' turns into a long smooth slide when a boy reaches its sixth step.
Dormitory doors open off the boys' stair, and other dormitories lie below the top room. Boys of all years use the one stair.
The top boys' room stands at the head of the stair and at the top of the Tower.
It is circular, with five four-poster beds with deep red velvet hangings, a trunk at each foot, bedside cabinets, and high narrow windows.
Rooms stay with a year group: the five boys of 1991 took the top room as first-years and still held it in 1996, with only the door sign changing.
facts.because: It is the same room at the stair's head in 1991, 1992 and 1994, with dormitories below it in 1996.

facts.text: The Tower is circular in plan, though no outside view of it exists.
facts.because: Round common room, circular dormitory and spiral stairs. New pupils deduce a tower from the spiral.

facts.text: Its windows overlook the lawn, the Whomping Willow, the lakeside beech, Hagrid's cabin and the Forest edge.
No book states the Tower's height. The strict minimum from the text is top floor 9, which is 10 storeys counting the ground floor.
facts.because: The text proves two or more doors below the top room. If they share a level, that is 7 + 2 = 9.

facts.text: Read as a top floor, 10 to 12 means 3 to 5 dormitory levels and 11 to 13 storeys. It is a sound lower limit, but needs rooms sharing levels.
facts.because: Seven rooms stacked 3+3+1 give 10, 2+2+2+1 give 11, 2+2+1+1+1 give 12. Read as storeys from the ground, the top floor would be 9 to 11.

facts.text: One room per year group on its own level gives floors 8 to 14: top floor 14, which is 15 storeys counting the ground floor. This is the best single figure.
facts.because: 7 + 7 = 14; adding the ground floor gives 15. Assumes every year has one room per stair and each fills a level. Only Harry's year is shown.

facts.text: A round room cannot hold both spiral stairs side by side, so the stairs must rise outside the room circles.
facts.because: Assuming rooms at least 7 m across and stairs 2.5 m across, two shafts would fill most of the width at every level.

facts.text: Two round stacks side by side stay at top floor 14 but need a plan 17 m wide or two turrets. One stack with boys and girls alternating reaches top floor 21, 22 storeys.
facts.because: 2 x 8.5 m per stack = 17 m. 7 + 14 = 21. Top floor 21 looks too high, as the Astronomy Tower would have to clear it.

facts.text: At a modest 3.5 m per storey, the top room's floor is about 49 m above the ground floor and the climb from the common room about 120 steps.
facts.because: 14 x 3.5 = 49 m; 7 x 3.5 = 24.5 m; at 0.2 m per step about 120 steps. Both heights are assumptions.

facts.text: The Astronomy Tower must overtop it: at about floor 15 level or more if its top floor is 14.
facts.because: Astronomy is the tallest tower, and the top room's ceiling is at about floor 15 level.

facts.text: Gryffindor and Ravenclaw share the second rank, neither stated as taller, and both must overtop the West and North Towers, which themselves rise above the seventh floor.
facts.because: A 1998 plan names Ravenclaw, Astronomy and Gryffindor as the three highest. That order is no ranking, since Astronomy comes second.

conflicts.text: One five-bed room per year on each stair gives 70 beds, but 200 people in Slytherin green at the 1994 final and over 100 exam desks for one year in 1976 imply Houses of about 175 or more. If so, some years need several rooms, which can add rooms per level without adding levels.
Common room and top dormitory are called round or circular, yet both are given corners.

open: How the boys' and girls' rooms are stacked: two turrets, one stack with alternating levels, or half-round rooms round a shared stair core. Only the top boys' room is known to be a full circle.
Whether the round shaft reaches the ground or springs from the main block near the seventh floor.
What caps the Tower. No roof is described.
How many rooms each year has, and the plan of every room but the top boys' room.

slytherin.summary: Slytherin's rooms are underground. Coming down the marble staircase, a door on the right leads to steps and a passage, then to a bare, damp length of stone wall where a concealed stone door slides open to a password. Inside is a long, low common room of undressed stone, with round greenish lamps on chains, a fire under a carved mantelpiece and carved chairs. Harry later says it lies under the lake with green light, though no window is described. The dormitories are also in the dungeons, close by, and have never been seen.

facts.text: Common room and dormitories both lie in the dungeons, below the Entrance Hall.
The way runs through a door on the right as you come down the marble staircase, down steps, along a passage, to a concealed stone door that obeys a password.
The common room is long and low, of undressed stone, lit by round greenish lamps on chains and a fire under a carved mantelpiece.
Harry says it is under the lake, which turns the light green. This is his unconfirmed account.

open: Whether lake windows exist, and how the dormitories connect to the common room.

ravenclaw.summary: Ravenclaw's rooms are in a tower in the west of the castle, one of the three highest, and not the West Tower. A spiral stair climbs in tight, dizzying circles to a handleless old door with a bronze eagle knocker, which asks a question and opens to a reasoned answer. Inside is a wide, circular, airy common room with arched windows and silk hangings of blue and bronze, a domed star-painted ceiling and midnight-blue carpet, with tables, chairs and glass-fronted bookcases. Opposite the door a niche holds a tall marble statue of Rowena Ravenclaw. A door beside it leads up a stair to the dormitories above.

facts.text: Ravenclaw Tower stands in the west of the castle and is one of the three highest towers.
A tight spiral stair ends at a door with no handle or keyhole. Its bronze eagle knocker asks a question, and a reasoned answer opens it.
The common room is wide, circular and airy, with arched windows, silk hangings, a domed star-painted ceiling and a view of mountains by day.
A door beside the statue opposite the entrance leads to a stair and the dormitories above.
With dormitories above its common room, the tower must rise well past its entrance door, and as far as Gryffindor's if it mirrors that stack.
facts.because: It holds a House's dormitories over the common room and ranks with Gryffindor among the three highest. No floor is stated.

open: The floors of the stair foot, door and common room.

classrooms.summary: Teaching rooms run through the whole height of the castle. Below ground is the Potions dungeon, one storey under the Entrance Hall. On the ground floor, classroom eleven and other little-used rooms open off the corridor opposite the Great Hall. The first floor has several ordinary classrooms near the head of the marble staircase. The third floor holds the Defence classroom, four floors below the Gryffindor common room, probably the Charms classroom, and an empty room beside the one-eyed witch. History of Magic and Transfiguration lie on unstated upper floors. The disused Mirror of Erised room is around the fourth floor, and more classrooms lie on the east wing's fifth floor. North Tower's round Divination room tops the sequence, above the seventh floor. A normal class is two houses of one year, about twenty pupils, and only the Divination room has a table count. Rooms are numbered to at least eleven, and many stand empty.

facts.text: A normal joint-house class is about twenty pupils.
facts.because: Twenty brooms are laid out for Gryffindor and Slytherin first-years, twenty cauldrons for the same pair in 1992, and about twenty pairs of earmuffs for a Herbology class.

facts.text: Counts the text gives: twenty cauldrons in Potions, at least twenty tables in Divination, twelve pupils at three tables in N.E.W.T. Potions. No other room has a seat count.
Allow at least 50 sq m for an ordinary classroom.
facts.because: Twenty desks at an assumed 1.5 sq m each is 30 sq m; aisles, the teacher's end and a blackboard add about 20 sq m.

facts.text: Allow for at least a dozen teaching rooms in use at the same time.
facts.because: Seven year groups, each split into two joint-house classes, gives up to fourteen classes at once. Assumes greenhouses and lawns take only a few of them.

facts.text: Floors stated or implied: Potions below ground; classroom eleven ground; Defence and probably Charms third; Mirror room about fourth; classrooms on the fifth, east wing; Divination above seventh.
facts.because: Each is worked through in its own overview. Transfiguration and History of Magic have no stated floor.

facts.text: Rooms are numbered in series: classroom eleven and dungeon five imply at least eleven classrooms and five dungeons.
facts.because: A numbered name implies lower numbers exist, though none of the others is ever listed.

open: Transfiguration and History of Magic have no stated floor and need a modelling decision.
The Defence and Charms classrooms may share the third floor, close to the Defence office, but the text never relates the two classrooms.

offices.summary: Staff offices are scattered through the castle, not grouped, and a teacher's office is often far from the classroom. From the bottom up: Snape's office is in the dungeons, close to Potions. Filch's windowless office is probably on the ground floor, as is the long panelled staff room. McGonagall's small office is on the first floor. Slughorn's oversized room lies between the marble staircase and the hospital wing. The Defence teacher's office is on the third floor, though Book 2 once says the second and a Book 4 route reads as the fourth. Flitwick's office is on the seventh floor, and the Headmaster's round office stands in a tower above a seventh-floor corridor. Trelawney lives at the top of North Tower. Madam Hooch's office is unplaced. The seventh floor alone carries Flitwick's and the Headmaster's rooms, the Gryffindor entrance, the Room of Requirement and the foot of the North Tower stair, so it must be a full, long storey.

facts.text: The text puts on the seventh floor: Fat Lady's portrait, Room of Requirement wall and Barnabas tapestry, Cadogan's landing, North Tower stair, Flitwick's office, Head's gargoyle, Lachlan statue and a boys' bathroom.
One level meets four towers: Gryffindor's above its entrance, North Tower, the Head's tower and West Tower, whose flank is counted window by window on this floor.
facts.because: Each connection is on or read from the seventh floor. They need not be close together, and Harry places two of the entrances on far sides of the castle.

facts.text: The seventh floor must be a full storey running round the castle, not a small top gallery.
facts.because: The Room and the gargoyle are round opposite sides of the castle yet linked on foot on this level, and Flitwick's window is thirteen bays from the West Tower.

facts.text: Teachers' offices need not adjoin their classrooms: Flitwick's is on the seventh floor while Charms is lower, and from 1996 Snape teaches floors above his dungeon office.
Capacity shown: Defence office fourteen people, Headmaster's nine, McGonagall's eight, Snape's five.
facts.because: Head counts from named people present in single scenes. Each is a minimum, not a maximum.

conflicts.text: The hospital wing is the hinge of several floor problems. Book 5 puts it on the third floor. Yet Pomfrey is asked to come down from it to the Defence office, also on the third, and the Headmaster's office, above a seventh-floor corridor, is one flight above it.

open: Decide the hospital wing's floor before fixing the Defence office and the gargoyle, because their stated routes all run through it.

library.summary: The school library and its Restricted Section. The books give its size in three counts: hundreds of narrow rows, thousands of shelves and tens of thousands of books. It is reached up the marble staircase and on through corridors, with no stated floor, though the best clue points to about the fourth. One door opens from a corridor. Inside, reading tables and lamps stand by mullioned windows and among the shelves, and the rows run back to the Restricted Section, behind a rope at the very end. At an assumed narrow 1.5 m per row, even 200 rows need 300 m of row spacing and at least about 1,500 m² of floor, as one great hall or a suite of rooms. This is far larger than an ordinary room. Read literally, the counts also keep the collection under 100,000 books, which suits rows about 3 to 4 m long.

facts.text: Books run to the tens of thousands, shelves to the thousands, narrow rows to the hundreds.
At least 300 m of row spacing and at least about 1,500 m² of floor, as one hall or a suite of rooms.
facts.because: 200 rows × an assumed 1.5 m = 300 m. 300 m × 3 to 4 m rows = 900 to 1,200 m², plus cross-aisles, tables and the Restricted Section.

facts.text: The Restricted Section lies at the very back, behind a rope.

open: The library's floor is never stated.

washrooms.summary: Bathrooms and toilets on many floors, listed from the top. The seventh floor has a boys' bathroom near the Room of Requirement. The sixth has a tiled boys' bathroom, wrecked in a 1997 duel. The fifth has the Prefects' bathroom, a white marble room with a sunken bath the size of a swimming pool and about a hundred golden taps. The fourth has a toilet where Montague was found. The second has several bathrooms, including, by most evidence, Moaning Myrtle's out-of-order toilet with the hidden entrance to the Chamber of Secrets, though one character puts that on the first floor. The girls' toilets of the 1991 troll are upstairs on an unstated floor. Elsewhere there are a girls' bathroom one floor below Transfiguration and other unlocated toilets. Myrtle moves between them by the pipes.

facts.text: Bathrooms are spread over at least five floors, from the second to the seventh.
facts.because: Named examples on the second (B05-239), fourth (B05-209), fifth (B04-131), sixth (B06-152) and seventh (B05-199) floors.

facts.text: They range from a cubicle that barely fits three pupils to a bath the size of a swimming pool.

conflicts.text: Myrtle's bathroom is on the first floor by Hermione's word and on the second by narration and Book 4: see that place.

room-of-requirement.summary: The Room of Requirement is a room on the seventh floor that appears on need, behind a stretch of blank stone wall in a corridor with an enormous tapestry of Barnabas the Barmy and his ballet-dancing trolls. Walk past the wall three times thinking hard of what you need, turning at the window at one end and the man-sized vase at the other, and a door appears. Behind it the Room becomes what you need, at any size, and its door turns back to stone afterwards. Three states matter. From 1995 it was a spacious torch-lit practice room seating 28 on cushions, with bookcases and Dark detectors. In 1997 and 1998 it was a cathedral-sized store of hidden objects, a city of heaps with one wall fifty feet high, until cursed fire swept it. In spring 1998 it was an enormous panelled refuge with balcony and hammocks, with a passage to the Hog's Head and a stair whose exit moved daily. The largest states cannot physically fit on the seventh floor, so treat the interior as a separate volume.

facts.text: The entrance is on the seventh floor, in the blank wall facing the Barnabas tapestry.
Walking past three times while concentrating makes a door appear. It turns back to stone when the room is left.
Size follows need: a broom cupboard, a room for 28, a cathedral-sized store, and an enormous refuge that grew from one hammock.
The practice room seats 28 on cushions and takes 14 duelling pairs, but is too tight for all to practise Stunning at once.
The store of hidden things is as big as a large cathedral, with thousands and thousands of books and a heap fifty feet high.
The refuge took hundreds passing through on the night of the battle, with more than twenty living there before it.
facts.because: Harry hears hundreds marching towards it and Aberforth reports hundreds through his pub at the far end.

facts.text: The largest states cannot fit behind a seventh-floor wall, so treat the interior as separate from the castle's plan.
facts.because: The same wall opens on a cupboard or on a space over 15 m high, more than four storeys, and no floor above the seventh is named.

conflicts.text: The door is on the seventh floor, yet the 1998 refuge stair runs up to a fifth-floor corridor.

open: Whether the Room survived the 1998 fire. Ron asks and the books do not answer.

stone-defences.summary: The Stone defences begin on the third floor and end far below it. From the locked door closing off the Charms corridor the way leads past Fluffy to a trapdoor in the corridor floor, then straight down: a drop past the second, first and ground floors to the level of the dungeons or lower, into a chamber of Devil’s Snare. A stone passage slopes down to the high key chamber; a door opens into the huge chess chamber; a passage climbs to the troll chamber; doors lead on to the potion room; and black fire bars the last chamber and the Mirror of Erised. The vertical drop is the feature to plan first. The shaft is a sealed column through or beside every lower floor and the dungeons, and the chambers need a large block of deep space that no other scene shows. The text gives no dimensions. Hermione’s miles under the school is a guess and Dumbledore’s dungeons a passing phrase. Everything here is dated to 1991–92.

facts.text: Top to bottom: third-floor corridor, shaft past three lower floors, dungeon level (four floors under the third), the plant chamber there or lower, then a downward slope to the key chamber.
facts.because: Floor numbering and the dungeons’ position come from the eight-floors-below note; the chamber order and slopes are narrated. No scene fixes a chamber to a named level.

facts.text: Modelling minimum: 15–20 m from trapdoor to plant chamber, then lower again down the sloping passage, so the deepest rooms are well over 20 m below the third-floor corridor.
facts.because: Stamp arithmetic gives 12–24 m; four storeys at an assumed 4 m give 16 m. The passage’s fall is not stated, so any further depth is open.

facts.text: The shaft cannot sit over an ordinary room: whatever is drawn under the trapdoor on the lower floors must leave a closed vertical column, wide enough for a rider on a broom.
facts.because: A shaft from a third-floor floor must displace what is below it, and Harry assumes brooms can use it. No lower-floor scene shows it, so it has no doors or windows.

facts.text: Under the castle the chain needs a tall void for the key chamber and a wide one for the chess room, clear of the dungeon rooms or below them.
facts.because: Both rooms are too big to fit unnoticed among named dungeon rooms, and no scene shows a connection to them.

facts.text: The route is one-way in practice: nothing lets anyone climb the shaft, so the only way back up that the text names is by flying.
facts.because: There is no ladder or steps at the trapdoor, and Harry’s escape plan depends on brooms.

facts.text: Set up for the 1991–92 year. After June 1992 no text says what became of any stage.
facts.because: The ban was announced for that year only, the Stone was destroyed, and no later book returns.

chamber-of-secrets.summary: The route to the Chamber of Secrets descends from Moaning Myrtle’s bathroom, on the second floor by most evidence, to below the dungeons. A sink that opens only to Parseltongue exposes the largest pipe of a branching system, which slants and twists down past the first and ground floors and the dungeon level, then levels out into a wet stone tunnel high enough to stand in. That tunnel bends repeatedly past small bones, a shed skin and a rockfall to a solid wall carved with two serpents. Behind it is the Chamber: one very long pillared hall ending at a statue of Slytherin as tall as the room, with a dark cavity behind its mouth that housed the basilisk. Nothing here has a stated dimension except the snake, at twenty feet or more. Harry’s miles under the school and Ron’s under the lake are guesses; the narrated fact is only that the way goes deeper than the dungeons.

facts.text: The one narrated depth: the pipe descends further below the school than the dungeons.
Harry’s miles under the school and Ron’s under the lake are characters’ guesses at the foot of the pipe, not surveyed depths.
Top to bottom: second-floor sink, pipe past the first and ground floors and dungeon level, tunnels at the bottom, then the Chamber at the far end.
facts.because: Floor numbering places the dungeons one level under the ground floor, and the narrated order of pipe, tunnel and door gives the rest.

facts.text: Modelling minimum: if the hall lies below the dungeons its floor is about 30 m under the bathroom, since its 15 m height must fit beneath them.
facts.because: Three storeys to the dungeon floor at an assumed 4 m, the estimated 15 m hall and some rock over it. If the hall lies clear of the castle, under the grounds or lake, it could be shallower.

facts.text: Modelling minimum: the walk from the foot of the pipe to the back wall of the Chamber is about 250 m, most of it tunnel.
facts.because: Adds about 200 m of tunnel and about 45 m of hall, both assumed minimums.

facts.text: The route was used about fifty years before 1993 by report, again in 1992–93, and once more in 1998, when the rockfall was evidently passable.

dungeons.summary: The dungeons occupy the level directly below the ground floor, reached by stone steps from the Entrance Hall. They are a maze of dim, cold stone passages lit by torches. From the foot of the steps the passages lead to Snape’s office door, the Potions classroom with its queueing space, numbered dungeon rooms, at least five of them, and the roomier dungeon used for the 1992 Deathday party. They run on deeper under the school to the blank wall hiding the Slytherin common room. Only one level is ever counted. The kitchens and Hufflepuff basement lie at the same depth, but are reached by a separate door and are broad and brightly lit.

facts.text: The dungeon level lies exactly one storey below the ground floor: eight floors below the seventh floor in British numbering.
facts.because: Seven floors down from the seventh is the ground floor, so the eighth is the first level under it.

facts.text: The kitchens and Hufflepuff basement lie at the same depth but on the other side of the marble staircase, bright where the dungeons are gloomy.
facts.because: Both are one run of stone steps below the Entrance Hall, reached by doors on opposite sides of the staircase. The text contrasts the kitchen corridor with the gloomy passage to Snape’s dungeon, and Book 6 lists the dungeons and the basement separately.

facts.text: Two dungeon rooms are singled out for size: Potions is held in one of the large ones, and the 1992 party in one of the roomier ones.

conflicts.text: Harry says the Slytherin common room is under the lake, yet the castle stands on a high cliff over the lake and the dungeons are one storey below ground. Both hold only if the passages descend a long way.

owlery.summary: West Tower is the tower that carries the Owlery. It rises above the seventh floor, though it is not one of the three highest towers, and seventh-floor windows are counted from it. Climb its spiral stair and the steps beyond to a door with a handle, and you enter the Owlery at the top: a circular stone room with unglazed windows, straw and droppings underfoot, and hundreds upon hundreds of owls on perches and rafters rising to a vaulted ceiling. Windows look over the Forest and Hagrid's cabin. The tower's top also has battlements, reached by a doorway from a tightly spiralling stone stair.

facts.text: The Owlery is at the top of West Tower, which rises above the seventh floor.
facts.because: The top is named outright. A Hippogriff carrying a passenger from a seventh-floor window has to climb to reach West Tower's top.

facts.text: Hundreds upon hundreds of owls roost on perches climbing all the way to the tower's top.
A spiral stair and steps reach a hinged door. A tightly spiralling stone stair also links the battlements to a corridor.
The Owlery is circular and of stone with unglazed windows. The top of the tower has battlements.
West Tower is lower than Gryffindor, Ravenclaw and Astronomy Towers.
facts.because: A 1998 plan names those three as the highest, leaving it out.

conflicts.text: A rising route from the seventh-floor portrait passes the fourth-floor corridor on the way to the Owlery.
Vaulted ceiling and rafters at the tower's top sit with walkable battlements at the same top.

open: Which floor the Owlery stair starts from, and how battlements and vault fit together.

hagrid.summary: Walking down the sloping lawns from the castle for about five minutes brings you to Hagrid’s cabin, a one-room wooden house on the Forest edge, built for a man twice normal height. Before it lies open lawn used for lessons and, in spring 1995, a dug plot. Behind it, through the back door, is the fenced garden and pumpkin patch, ending only yards from the first trees, with Aragog’s grave mound beyond the patch from 1997. Two hundred yards from the front door, from October 1994 to June 1995, stood the house-sized Beauxbatons carriage with its paddock for twelve elephant-sized horses, and trees begin a short way past that paddock. Care of Magical Creatures uses all this ground and more: crates by the cabin, trestle tables ten yards from the door and behind the walls, the Forest-edge lawn, and a separate fenced paddock five minutes’ walk round the trees. No stable, barn or classroom building is ever described here.

facts.text: Order from the castle: sloping lawn, cabin front, cabin, back garden, first trees.
facts.because: Every approach descends the lawn to the front door, the garden lies behind, and the rescue of Buckbeak runs from the patch straight to the trees.

facts.text: About five minutes on foot from the front doors to the cabin, and about five more round the trees to the 1993 paddock.
facts.because: The paddock walk is timed in the text; the castle walk rests on Harry leaving at five to three for tea at about three.

facts.text: The carriage stood about half as far from the cabin as the cabin stands from the castle front doors.
facts.because: Two hundred yards is about 180 m, against 330 to 420 m for a five-minute walk.

facts.text: Everything here runs oversized against pupils, so ordinary cottage and garden proportions will read far too small.
facts.because: The householder is twice normal height, the visiting carriage is house-sized with elephant-sized horses, and the pumpkins reached garden-shed size.

facts.text: Lawn links the area to the stadium; the school vegetable patch is a detour from the direct way down and leads on to the greenhouses.
Animals here are tethered, crated or fenced in the open; no stable or barn is described.
facts.because: Hippogriffs, Skrewts, horses and Buckbeak are all kept on chains, in crates, in paddocks or at tethers outdoors.

open: Hagrid’s hen-coop exists (B02-080) but has no stated position.

lake.summary: Walking down from the front doors, the lawns reach the lake at muddy banks and shallows that deepen from knee to waist height. The Durmstrang ship lay anchored here from October 1994 until the end of that school year. The shore can be walked right round. Going one way, a large beech stands on the water's edge, in direct view of a Gryffindor dormitory; across the water from it lie the funeral bank and the white marble tomb, by the bank the judges used in 1995. Hagrid's side and the site of the 1994 Dementor attack face each other across what is probably a few hundred yards of water. A steep path from the station meets the shore opposite the castle, whose cliff rises from the water. Out from the shallows the bottom drops from sight into a dim country of weed and mud with ten-foot visibility, and over twenty minutes' swim from the far bank lies the merpeople village, a quarter of a mile from the castle. No size is stated. Model at least half a mile on the long line and at least 100 feet of water in the deep.

facts.text: Allow the lake at least half a mile on the line from far bank to castle, narrowing to a few hundred yards at crossings.
facts.because: A swim of over twenty minutes ends a quarter of a mile from the castle. At least 0.5 m/s gives 600 m, plus 400 m. Night sightlines show a much narrower crossing elsewhere. Minimum only.

facts.text: Three laps of the shore fit into one morning, so the shoreline is a few miles at most.
facts.because: At walking pace a long morning covers six to nine miles.

facts.text: Allow at least 100 feet of water over the deep basin, which is deep enough for a ship to rise from it.
facts.because: A masted ship came up whole at the middle, and the water stays dark until close to the surface on the way up. Assumed from real lakes.

facts.text: The castle stands on a cliff above one shore, the lawns run down to another, and Ron takes the lake to lie south of the castle.
From the top of the lawns the surface is open to view as far as its centre; from inside the castle only parts are seen.
The far-side bank is within a ten-minute sprint of the library.
Dated installations: the ship (1994 to 1995), second-task stands and judges' table (February 1995), funeral chairs and tomb (June 1997).

open: A shore plan placing the beech, Hagrid's side, the funeral bank and the second-task stands. The text gives only pairs of opposite banks.

forest.summary: The Forest area runs from the lawn’s edge inward. At the edge, near Hagrid’s cabin, a narrow earth track enters thick trees and forks a little way in. Along the outside, about five minutes round the trees, is the 1993 creature paddock, and far beyond the Beauxbatons paddock, out of sight of castle and lake, the 1994 dragon enclosure. Inside, about ten minutes’ walk brings a class to the dark, snow-free Thestral feeding place. About twenty minutes along the spider path the sky disappears; leaving the path, the hollow of the Acromantula colony lies at least another half-hour on, downhill, towards the heart of the Forest, ten rough minutes by car from the edge. Centaurs claim the whole wood; fifty were seen at once in a dim clearing far along that same old path. A long way past the Thestrals and off the path, through brambles and thorn, then fifteen more minutes past nettles, is the clearing where Grawp was tied in 1996. The dead unicorn of 1992 lay nearly half an hour beyond the regrouping point. Treat every walking time as real but no bearing as known: the books give no map, and the relative positions of these sites must not be invented.

facts.text: Round the outside from the cabin: about five minutes to the 1993 creature paddock; much further, past the horse paddock, to the dragon enclosure.
Inward from the edge: about ten minutes to the Thestral place, about twenty along the spider path before the sky disappears.
Deep sites: half an hour or more off the path to the hollow; fifteen minutes past a far off-path halt to Grawp; nearly half an hour past the regrouping point to the unicorn.
Coming out: ten rough minutes by car from the hollow, and ten on foot from where the Grawp route rejoins a path.
The Thestral place is shallow compared with the rest.
facts.because: Hagrid says that visit did not go in so far, and the Grawp walk runs a long way past it.

facts.text: The sites overlap ground the centaurs hold: the spider path passes one of their clearings, and the way back from Grawp’s clearing crosses their patrol.
facts.because: Hermione deliberately leads Umbridge along the old path to meet them, and Magorian’s group stops Hagrid in knotgrass on the return.

facts.text: Treat the deep sites as at least about 2 km inside a Forest at least 4 km across.
facts.because: Timed walking gives about 2 km at 4 km/h on path and 1.5 km/h off it, and the car’s ten minutes agrees. The hollow lies towards the heart.

facts.text: Routes thicken going in and thin coming out; on the spider path the sky was lost after about twenty minutes, and it returns shortly before the edge.

open: No bearing, map or route junction between any two sites is given; keep the times and sequence only.

quidditch.summary: Walking down the sloping lawns from the front steps, with the Forest on the right, the stadium comes up as a landmark seen from much of the castle. A tree marks about the halfway point. At the foot of the slope stand the changing rooms, at the pitch's edge, with a separate broom shed across the grass. A gap in the stands opens on to the pitch, a flat grass ground with three hoops at each end, fifty feet high. The banked stands around it take the whole school, so model at least 800 to 1,000 seats, the top of 'hundreds', probably in separate blocks. The pitch is at least about 200 yards long on one line, as the 1995 maze shows: twenty-foot hedges filled it, with fifty yards to the first fork and a hundred-yard run to the Cup at the centre. The first-task arena lay elsewhere, a long way round the Forest edge behind a clump of trees, out of sight of the castle and the lake and about ten hurried minutes from the front doors. Its conjured seats ringed a plank-fenced field that had held four dragons.

facts.text: Hoops are fifty feet high; the maze hedge that later filled the pitch was twenty feet high.
The pitch is at least about 200 yards long on one line.
facts.because: The Cup, at the centre, was seen a hundred yards away from inside a maze whose outer hedge followed the pitch's edge.

facts.text: Seat the stadium for at least 800 to 1,000, the whole school plus staff; this stays within the text's 'hundreds'.
facts.because: A crowd of about 800 follows from 200 people in green being the quarter not in scarlet. Over a hundred pupils in one exam year gives 700 or more over seven years. Assumes one seat each.

facts.text: The stadium lies downhill from the castle and is probably west or north-west of it.
facts.because: Maze compass: the centre lay north-west of the entrance facing arrivals. Castle windows glow red at sunset as seen from the shed.

facts.text: The first-task arena lay out of sight of castle and lake, about ten hurried minutes from the front doors.
Dated installations: conjured stands at the dragon enclosure (November 1994), the same seats by the lake (February 1995), and the maze on the pitch (May to June 1995).

open: Distance from the castle to the stadium. It is always distant, and the only time given is Wood's fifteen-minute allowance from the dormitory.

greenhouses.summary: From the foot of the front steps the forecourt lawn opens out, large enough for the whole school to line up. At Christmas 1994 part of it became the conjured rose garden of the Yule Ball. Sloping lawns then fall away towards the lake, the stadium and Hagrid's cabin, with the flying lawn on the far side of the grounds from the Forest. Turning aside from the direct line to Hagrid's, a walker reaches the vegetable patch, with its low stone wall, and beyond it the greenhouses, behind the castle. There are at least three, numbered, and Greenhouse Three alone holds a class of about twenty with trays, a central bench and hanging flowers the size of umbrellas. A compost heap lies near them, and the Whomping Willow is in view in the distance. Going on from there leads round the Willow to the Forest.

facts.text: At least three greenhouses are implied by the names One and Three; the total is not given.
facts.because: The numbering implies a Two, and pupils can take time to find the right one in mist.

facts.text: Greenhouse Three holds a class of about twenty; allow at least about 15 m by 8 m.
facts.because: Twenty pupils at about 3 square metres each, plus a bench, stored pots and dangerous plants. Assumed, not stated.

facts.text: The forecourt lawn takes the whole school in rows with a house-sized carriage landing beside it.
On foot the order from the castle is vegetable patch, then greenhouses; from the air it was greenhouses, patch, lawns, Willow.
The flying lawn lies on the far side of the grounds from the Forest.
Christmas 1994: the Yule Ball grotto stood on the forecourt lawn.

conflicts.text: Book 1 places the greenhouses behind the castle, while Book 4 has pupils leaving them within reach of the stone steps.

open: Size of the vegetable patch and number of greenhouses.

hogsmeade-and-tunnels.summary: Hogsmeade lies outside the Hogwarts gates, downhill from the castle at the foot of a mountain, and everything in this area joins the school to it. The ordinary way is the road: through the winged-boar gates, left, and down a twisting lane to the High Street with its shops, the Three Broomsticks, Honeydukes and, up a side street, the Hog’s Head. Past the Three Broomsticks a slope climbs to the Shrieking Shack. Hidden tunnels make the same journey underground. From the third floor, the one-eyed witch passage drops by stone chute, runs low and winding for what feels like over an hour, and climbs two hundred steps and more into Honeydukes’ cellar. From the middle of the grounds, under the Whomping Willow, a still lower tunnel of similar felt length reaches the ground floor of the Shack. Those two belong to the seven passages on the Marauder’s Map. From spring 1998 a lamplit passage joins the Room of Requirement to the Hog’s Head. Treat the two older tunnels as works a kilometre or more long. The village core, by contrast, is tiny, with a minute between its two pubs.

facts.text: The village lies downhill of the castle, and its High Street is reached from the gates by road or twisting lane.
Seven mapped passages lead out of the castle, and the Room-made Hog’s Head passage of 1998 makes an eighth.
Modelling minimum: Honeydukes tunnel about 2 km, Willow tunnel about 1 km, Hog’s Head passage over 400 m. None is stated; each comes from felt or narrated walking time.
facts.because: See each passage’s own estimate. Taken at face value, the Honeydukes walk gives 3.5 km.

facts.text: The tunnels start from three different levels: the third floor, ground level in mid-grounds, and an upper room of a village inn, ending at a cellar, a ground-floor room and the Room of Requirement.
Only one route carried a crowd: hundreds of pupils left by the Hog’s Head passage in 1998, while the Willow and Honeydukes tunnels are tight for one person.
facts.because: The older tunnels are narrow and low, while the 1998 passage is lamplit and walked upright.

facts.text: The links open and close: Dementors patrol the village in 1993–94, passages are guarded from 1996, sealed by 1997–98, and a new one appears in spring 1998.

open: The real distance from the castle to the village. All surface and tunnel lengths depend on it, and no figure is given.

other.summary: A mixed group of one room and several school-wide subjects. The trophy room is a display room with a door at each end, on the third floor by the walked journey and the sixth by a Map reading. The Marauder's Map is a parchment plan of every floor. Portraits line corridors and stairs, and their subjects move between frames. Armour and statues stand on plinths throughout the castle, with a long gallery of armour near the trophy room. Ghosts move through walls with no need of openings. Unnamed one-off rooms, including a laundry, cupboards and a vanishing room of chamberpots, complete the group.

facts.text: Portraits, armour and statues recur in corridors across many floors, so bare corridors would be wrong.
facts.because: Armour and statues are a general corridor fitting (B01-027, B07-063), and portrait-lined corridors recur from the first night on (B01-021).

facts.text: The Map shows a detailed plan of every floor, with its many shortcuts and secret passages.

conflicts.text: The trophy room's floor is disputed between the third and the sixth: see that place.

castle-exterior.summary: Hogwarts Castle is a vast stone castle on a high cliff above the lake, with mountains around it, reading from any distance as a dense mass of towers and turrets. Five towers are named: Astronomy, the tallest; Ravenclaw and Gryffindor, which with it make the three highest; then West Tower and North Tower. The minimum stack is dungeons below ground, a ground floor, seven numbered floors, then tower storeys above the seventh floor, so the main body stands at least eight storeys high before any tower begins, all on top of the cliff. A seventh-floor frontage runs at least thirteen windows along from West Tower. An east wing reaching at least a fifth floor and a west wing are named. The front has stone steps and oak doors with the Astronomy Tower rising directly above them; the greenhouses lie behind. Walls are thick stone, windows mullioned, tower tops crenellated. The text gives no height for the cliff or any tower and no count of towers, so every height below is an estimate.

facts.text: Called vast at first sight. Every distant view shows a crowded skyline of towers and turrets; no count of either is ever given.
The main body stands at least eight storeys above ground: the ground floor plus the first to seventh floors, British numbering, with dungeons below that.
facts.because: From the seventh floor it is six floors down and then the marble staircase to the Entrance Hall (B04-106); the dungeons are eight floors below the seventh floor (B05-110); the marble staircase route up to the seventh is walked in B03-111.

facts.text: Minimum stack to read on the exterior, bottom to top: cliff, at least one dungeon level, ground floor, first to seventh floors, then tower storeys. That is nine levels before any tower storey.
facts.because: One dungeon level, the ground floor and seven numbered floors make nine. The dungeons being eight floors below the seventh puts one level under the ground floor (B05-110). Whether that level shows on the cliff side is not stated.

facts.text: The sixth floor is never named in the books, though it must exist: all the other numbered floors appear, and the count from the seventh floor passes through it.
facts.because: A search of the full text finds no mention of a sixth floor, while six floors down from the seventh (B04-106) and eight floors from the seventh to the dungeons (B05-110) both require one.

facts.text: Five towers are named: Astronomy, Gryffindor, Ravenclaw, North (Divination) and West (Owlery). Hufflepuff and Slytherin have none; they live in a basement and the dungeons.
The seventh floor is a broad working level, not one tower top: Flitwick's office, the Fat Lady's corridor and the Room of Requirement wall all lie on it.
facts.because: Three separate locations are placed on that floor, and the office has twelve windows between it and West Tower, so more than a single tower must reach this height.

facts.text: Tower storeys continue above the seventh floor: North Tower's spiral starts there, Buckbeak climbs from a seventh-floor window to West Tower's top, and Gryffindor's dormitories rise above its entrance level.
facts.because: Pupils queue on the North Tower spiral at the seventh floor (B03-111) and climb on to a landing and ladder (B03-016); Buckbeak carries them upward from Flitwick's window (B03-155); the dormitory stair rises from the common room behind the seventh-floor portrait (B01-053, B02-016).

facts.text: Model the three highest towers at least about twelve storeys above the ground, roughly four storeys clear of the seventh floor. Not canon; the text gives no storey count for any tower.
facts.because: Gryffindor needs seven year rooms each for boys and girls, 14 in all (assumes one room per year and sex, B02-016). Even at four rooms per storey that is 4 storeys above the seventh-floor common room: ground plus eleven floors is 12 storeys. Harry's room is at the stair top with others below it (B04-021, B05-217), and Astronomy must exceed this.

facts.text: At an assumed 4 m per storey the main body rises at least 32 m above the lawns and the highest towers at least 50 m, before adding the cliff. Not canon.
facts.because: 8 storeys x 4 m = 32 m. 12 storeys x 4 m = 48 m, and Astronomy must stand higher than Gryffindor. The 4 m storey is an assumption; these are lower limits to stop an undersized model, not targets.

facts.text: The Astronomy Tower is the highest tower of the castle; the books call it the tallest wherever heights come up.
Kingsley names Ravenclaw, Astronomy and Gryffindor as the three highest towers in May 1998. The order of Ravenclaw and Gryffindor below Astronomy is not given.
West Tower and North Tower rank below those three, though both still rise above seventh-floor level.
facts.because: Kingsley's list of the three highest omits them; their height above the seventh floor rests on the North Tower spiral (B03-111) and the climb from Flitwick's window (B03-155).

facts.text: Flitwick's office is the thirteenth window along from West Tower on the seventh floor, so at least thirteen windows run along that frontage. Harry counts them to the tower's right.
At an assumed 3 m per window bay, that seventh-floor frontage runs at least 40 m from West Tower, and may continue past the office.
facts.because: 13 windows x 3 m = 39 m. The bay width is an assumption. The count stops at the office only because that is where the instruction stops.

facts.text: Krum says Durmstrang has just four floors and is a smaller castle than Hogwarts, the only direct comparison with another school building.
The one height figure near the site is the lake looking a mile below the flying car in 1992. That is flight altitude, not the height of the cliff.
It stands high on a cliff above the lake, first seen from the far shore and towering over the boats as they near the cliff face.
The cliff guards only part of the shore. Elsewhere people walk down sloping lawns to the water, so model a cliff on the boat side and open slopes on others.
facts.because: Boats meet a cliff (B01-006), yet the Durmstrang party walks up from the lake to the doors (B04-056), the lake is in view from the top of the lawns (B04-041), and Harry runs down the lawn to the shore (B04-158).

facts.text: The Astronomy Tower stands at the front: the front doors open directly beneath its parapet, and its foot meets the lawn at the castle front.
The greenhouses lie behind the castle; a car turning away from a castle wall flies over them, then a vegetable patch, then lawns.
Ravenclaw's tower stands on the west side of the castle.
An east wing and a west wing are named. The east wing reaches at least a fifth floor; the extent and junctions of both are unknown.
Compass hints: a high landing looks south to part of the lake; Ravenclaw and a wing lie west; from the front steps the evening sun drops over the Forest; dawn rises over mountains.
facts.because: Each is one observation from one spot. Ron's south is a schoolboy's reading of a view, and the Headmaster's window is not placed on any side. Together they suggest the lake to the south and the Forest towards the west, nothing firmer.

facts.text: Aberforth reports attackers with giants apparently breaching the North Battlements in May 1998. These are the only named battlements; whether they are on the castle or an outer wall is not said.
From the lake bank the West Tower frontage is near enough for Harry to count windows, and a Hippogriff reaches the seventh floor from there in one short flight.
Long sightlines: a lantern at the castle's foot shows from the gates, lit windows show from the drive, and the sky above the school shows from Hogsmeade High Street.
Walls are stone, dark by night, and thick enough to shelter the castle in winter gales, though it stays draughty.
Windows are mullioned in general views, in the Great Hall and in the library, and at night show as scattered bright patches high on the dark mass.
Flitwick's seventh-floor window is a tight fit: very thin Sirius has to brace on the frame and squeeze his head and shoulders through.
Named towers read as round: the rooms in Gryffindor, North, West and Ravenclaw towers are circular, and tower access is by spiral stairs.
facts.because: Circular rooms in four towers, spiral stairs in Gryffindor (B02-016), North Tower (B03-016) and Astronomy (B01-101). No tower is called round from outside.

facts.text: Tower tops are crenellated where described: the Astronomy Tower has ramparts with a door to a spiral stair, and West Tower has battlements a Hippogriff can land on.
Roof sculpture is hinted at once: in May 1998 Grawp swings what looks like a stone gargoyle torn from the roof.
facts.because: The narration offers it only as an appearance, so roof gargoyles are likely but not established.

facts.text: A school bell is heard overhead in the castle, but no bell tower is named.
Flyers land on tower tops or hover at windows. No ledge is mentioned at Flitwick's window, and Buckbeak stays on the wing there.
Binns says the four founders built the castle together more than a thousand years ago; the exact date is uncertain.
Muggles are said to see a decaying ruin with a danger sign. The real castle is intact.
Window lighting varies with the night: many lit on arrival evenings, none lit before dawn in March 1998, blazing with light in May 1998.
Battle damage, May 1998: part of an upper corridor's outer wall is blown out and giant spiders climb to the gap; windows lose their glass; a giant smashes an upper window.

conflicts.text: Book 1 once speaks of the tallest astronomy tower, which could imply more than one. Every other passage treats the Astronomy Tower as a single building.
West Tower's top holds both the Owlery, with perches rising nearly to the tower top, and battlements on which Buckbeak lands. The modeller must fit both on one summit.

open: Height of the cliff and of each tower: no figure exists anywhere in the text.
The plan of the main block: how wings, courtyards and towers join, and how much of it reaches the seventh floor.
How many towers and turrets stand beyond the five named towers.
Which compass direction the front faces.

courtyards.summary: Open-air courtyards in the castle where pupils spend breaks. The books never name one, count them or give a plan, so these scenes may be one yard or several. Between them the scenes show sheltered corners, a dripping balcony overhead, a stone step, a pillar, a side door and a corridor opening out from the staff-room area, with routes on down to the dungeons. A crowd from several year groups can stand there in separate huddles, so do not make it small.

facts.text: Large enough for many pupils at break: people stand about in separate huddles, the crowd from a corridor pours in, and groups on opposite sides ignore each other.
facts.because: Huddles around the yard (B05-033), a flood of students swept in from the corridor (B05-091), and the twins selling on the far side from the trio's corner (B05-184).

facts.text: Wide enough to cross in view of everyone: Hermione waits until Cho is halfway across before speaking, and Snape crosses the yard past a group at its fire.
It has corners used as regular spots, some sheltered from wind and one catching the sun, so walls enclose at least part of it.
One corner lies beneath a heavily dripping balcony, showing an upper level overlooking the yard.
There is a stone step to sit on, and voices echo around the space.
At least one pillar stands in the courtyard of the 1970s memory. No covered walk or cloister is described anywhere.
A corridor by the staff room leads straight out into a courtyard at break, and in 1992 a side door leads from one into a corridor and a staircase up to Lockhart's classroom.
From a courtyard pupils go down stone steps to the dungeons for Potions, or on to the Entrance Hall, so it is on or near ground level.
facts.because: The routes lead down to the dungeons and across to the Entrance Hall without any climb being mentioned.

facts.text: The lesson bell is heard overhead from the yard.
It is open to the sky: freezing in November, misty drizzle in September, ankle-deep snow in January 1997, sun in spring.

open: How many courtyards there are, and where they sit in the plan.
Whether the balcony and pillar belong to the same courtyard.

castle-interior-general.summary: School-wide conditions inside the castle, not one room, and the place to size everything else from. The interior is stone, lit by wall torches and candles, heated by fires and draughty in winter. It is very hard to learn: 142 staircases, trick doors and a layout that seems to move. An east wing and a west wing are named. Over a hundred house-elves clean at night. The pupil roll is never stated and the clues disagree. Class and dormitory clues (five beds, twenty cauldrons) point to about 280 pupils; crowd clues (a hundred coaches, a hundred-plus exam desks, two hundred in green at a match) point to 350 to 800. Plan on about 300 to 800, and size whole-school rooms for the top of that range. Everything seasonal or imposed, from Christmas trees to Umbridge's decrees, is listed under changes.

facts.text: School roll: plan on about 300 to 800 pupils, which is 75 to 200 per house and about 43 to 114 per year. Size whole-school spaces for 800. Not canon.
facts.because: The text gives no figure. Dormitories and classes give 224 to 280, rounded up to 300 as a floor. Coaches give 350 to 580, exam desks 350 to 700-plus, Hall benches about 530 to 640, the 1994 crowd about 800. 300/4 = 75 and 800/4 = 200; 300/7 = 43 and 800/7 = 114.

facts.text: Use narrated sizes for small rooms and the top of the range for shared ones: about twenty to a two-house class, five to a dormitory, 200 to a common room, 800 in the Hall.
facts.because: The class and dormitory evidence is direct for those rooms, and the crowd evidence is direct for shared spaces, so this avoids forcing the two sets of clues to agree. 800/4 houses = 200 in a common room.

facts.text: The books always count pupils in hundreds: hundreds of faces in the Hall, hundreds moving between lessons, hundreds to evacuate. The living school is never called a thousand.
Coaches: about 100 take everyone above first year, with three, four and five riders seen and coaches filling up. That suggests about 350 to 580 pupils.
facts.because: 100 x 3 to 5 = 300 to 500 riders, plus one year group in seven for first-years (50 to 83). Assumes all coaches load about the same.

facts.text: Boats: no more than four first-years to a boat, in a fleet that is never counted, so the crossing fixes no roll.
Match crowd: at the 1994 final two hundred wear green while three-quarters of the crowd wear scarlet, which implies a crowd of about 800.
facts.because: If the green block is the remaining quarter, 200 x 4 = 800. The whole school attends and staff are few. Both figures are Harry's impression, not a count.

facts.text: Exam desks: over a hundred single desks fill the Great Hall in Snape's O.W.L. memory. Seating one or two year groups, that suggests 350 to 700-plus pupils.
facts.because: In 1996 fifth- and seventh-years are both called into the same layout (B05-256), so 100 desks may be one year or two: 100/2 x 7 = 350, 100 x 7 = 700. Over a hundred makes both figures lower limits.

facts.text: Yule Ball: about a hundred small tables seating about a dozen each give about 1,200 places, for fourth-years upward, invited younger partners, staff and only about twenty visitors.
facts.because: 100 x 12 = 1,200. The tables are not said to be full, so this shows what the Hall can hold, not the size of the roll.

facts.text: Great Hall: four long benched tables seat the school at once. In a Hall at least fifty yards long that is about 530 to 640 seats.
facts.because: A duel about fifty yards apart (B07-129) makes the Hall at least 46 m long. Assume 40 m tables seated on both sides, 80 m of bench each: at 0.6 m a place 133, at 0.5 m 160, times four tables. Table length and seat width are assumptions.

facts.text: Sleeping bags: in October 1993 the whole school sleeps on the Great Hall floor in hundreds of sleeping bags, with the tables moved to the walls.
Dormitories: a Gryffindor year has five boys in one round room signed with the year, and at least three girls. At eight to ten per house-year that gives only 224 to 280 pupils.
facts.because: 8 to 10 per house per year x 4 houses x 7 years = 224 to 280. Assumes every house and year matches Harry's Gryffindor year.

facts.text: Classes: first-year flying has twenty brooms, second-year Potions twenty cauldrons, Greenhouse Three about twenty pairs of earmuffs. Each serves two houses, suggesting about forty per year and 280 in all.
facts.because: 20 per two-house class = 10 per house = 40 per year; 40 x 7 = 280. Assumes each class is a whole year of two houses and that all years match.

facts.text: Sorting: the 1991 roll implies at least 24 first-years; in 1971 a dozen remain at Snape, near the end of the alphabet; the 1994 and 1995 lines are both called long.
facts.because: 21 names are called in 1991, Crabbe and Goyle are already seated, and Dean Thomas is never called, making 24. The list skips names, so that is a lower limit.

facts.text: Only a dozen sixth-years, from all four houses, go on to N.E.W.T. Potions in 1996. That is an exam-filtered class, not a year group.
A house fits a common room: in 1992 what looks like all of Gryffindor packs into the round room, standing on the tables and chairs.
Post: about a hundred owls reach the Great Hall at breakfast in Book 1, hundreds by Book 5, and the Owlery holds hundreds.
Nearly Headless Nick says over a hundred house-elves work at Hogwarts, the largest number in any British dwelling. They keep to the kitchens by day and clean and tend fires at night.
The building is too large to learn quickly: 142 staircases, doors that need asking or tickling, false doors, and after two years the trio have still not seen all of it.
