Ron allows ten minutes to reach the top of North Tower from the Great Hall, and seven long staircases only bring the trio to the last stretch.
Dumbledore says he would not assume he knows all the castle's secrets, reporting a wrong turn into a room he had never seen.
The interior divides into wings: an east wing with a fifth-floor corridor, and a corridor leading off towards a west wing near the Owlery stairs. No north or south wing is named.
Walls are stone and lit by torches in brackets. Corridors are draughty and icy in winter while fires warm the common rooms and Great Hall.
Fixtures seen across the school: suits of armour, statues, vases, lanterns, candles, blackboards, noticeboards in every common room, and at least one crystal chandelier.
Giant hourglasses record house points. This record gives no location; a later scene places them in the Entrance Hall.
Standing rules: the Forest is out of bounds, magic is banned in corridors between lessons, and pupils may not be out of bed after hours.
Hogsmeade trips need signed permission and can be cancelled; notices appear on common-room boards. In 1997 Ginny was reported barred from visits.
Hallowe'en 1991: a thousand live bats on the walls and ceiling, another thousand over the tables, and pumpkin smell in the corridors.
Each Christmas: twelve Great Hall trees, holly and mistletoe along corridors, lights or candles in armour, and in 1994 everlasting icicles on the marble staircase and armour that sings when passed.
Weather reaches inside: rain drums on windows, winter blizzards darken the day, storms need extra torches, and classroom windows rattle in the wind.
Spring 1993 emergency: pupils back in common rooms by six, teacher escorts to lessons and bathrooms, paired night patrols of teachers, Prefects and ghosts.
1993 recovery: an all-night feast in pyjamas, exams cancelled, ordinary life restored.
1996 under Umbridge: decree notices on boards and in corridors and classrooms, a notice naming her Headmistress overnight, and observers in lessons.

Spring 1996 disorder: Weasley fireworks through classrooms, Dungbombs fouling corridors, and Peeves wrecking fittings, flooding the second floor and loosening a chandelier. Temporary, not a permanent ruin.
June 1997: Fawkes's lament carries through windows and corridors. Ministry officials are lodged in the castle for the funeral, in rooms not described.
1997 to 1998 under Snape: Neville reports Dumbledore's Army painting slogans on the walls at night.

conflicts.text: The two sets of size clues disagree by nearly three times. One Gryffindor dormitory per year and twenty-place classes give about 280 pupils. A hundred filling coaches, over a hundred exam desks and two hundred in green give 350 to 800.

open: The actual pupil roll. If it is near 800, either Gryffindor is unusually small or some years have more than one dormitory.
How many classrooms exist. Twenty-place classes for 300 to 800 pupils need very different totals.
Where the wings run and which floors they share with the main block.

castle-protections.summary: The magical and practical security covering the whole school, not one room. Nobody can Apparate or Disapparate anywhere in the buildings or grounds, a rule that stops at the boundary, so people leave by the gates and vanish just outside. Enchanted gates, jinxed perimeter walls and ancient charms guard the site, and Muggles reportedly see only a ruin. Exceptions are real: house-elves Apparate freely, a phoenix can carry its owner out, Portkeys work in both directions, and the paired Vanishing Cabinets defeat everything in 1997. Most measures are reported by characters, not observed, and none has visible architecture. Dated layers change the picture: Dementors at every entrance in 1993 to 1994, Floo and owl surveillance in 1996, Secrecy Sensors and Aurors from 1996, and defensive spells and Mandrakes in the 1998 battle.

facts.text: The Apparition ban covers the whole site, buildings and grounds alike, not just the castle.
McGonagall reports an enchantment on every entrance to the castle and a guard on every secret way out, and Aberforth reports old passages watched at both ends. Plan for multiple entrances.
The ban ends at the boundary: fleeing Death Eaters run for the gates in June 1997 and Snape Disapparates just beyond the school's limits.
Perimeter protection is layered outward: Aurors are stationed in Hogsmeade in 1996, and in 1998 Harry treats the village as the place to test the defences.
Muggles reportedly see a decaying ruin with a sign warning of danger, according to Hogwarts: A History.
Electricity, computers and radar reportedly fail near Hogwarts because of the density of magic. Do not give the school any Muggle technology.
Snape says many ancient spells and charms guard the walls and grounds. Dumbledore calls the school a stronghold of ancient magic. Neither describes anything visible.
The site was reportedly chosen far from Muggle eyes when it was founded.
Hogwarts: A History is cited for anti-stealth enchantments, with no Apparating or Disapparating inside. Snape repeats this flatly in 1994 and Hermione again in 1995.
House-elves are exempt: Kreacher and Dobby appear with a crack in the hospital wing and the common room, and Ron says elf magic works in and out of Hogwarts.
Portkeys work both ways: Dumbledore sends pupils out by kettle in 1995 and Harry in by statue head in 1996, and a doctored Cup takes Harry and Cedric out of the grounds in 1995.
A phoenix can leave: Dumbledore vanishes from his office holding Fawkes's tail in 1996, and Umbridge insists he cannot have Disapparated.
The perimeter walls and gates carry jinxes and Dumbledore's own enchantments. Harry's broom shudders crossing the wall in June 1997 as Dumbledore seems to lift them for entry at speed.
facts.because: The shudder and muttering are observed; that Dumbledore is suspending his enchantments is Harry's interpretation.

facts.text: Dumbledore barred Dementors from crossing the castle threshold in 1993. It was a rule rather than a barrier: Fudge brought one inside in June 1995.
Vanishing Cabinets defeat every ward in June 1997: Draco repairs the school's cabinet and Death Eaters step through from Borgin and Burkes.
No check is complete: Secrecy Sensors miss a love potion repackaged as perfume or medicine, and enchanted coins carry messages past monitored post.
September 1993 to June 1994: Dementors at every entrance to the grounds. Lupin reports them resenting exclusion; they return to posts after searches and are withdrawn in June 1994.
February 1994: the front doors are taught to recognise Black's photograph and Filch boards up tiny cracks and mouseholes.
1996: fires are watched for Umbridge, with hers excepted, the Squad opens owl post, and Filch watches secret routes. Fires were also policed through a Floo Network contact.
From autumn 1996: new charms, counter-curses and a small Auror task force, with Dumbledore announcing stronger fortifications. No new masonry is described.
From 1996 Filch screens arrivals and Hogsmeade trips with Secrecy Sensors, and the Ministry arranges a one-off Floo link for the January 1997 return.
February 1997: Dumbledore lifts the Apparition ban for one hour, inside the Great Hall only, for lessons. Nobody can Apparate beyond its walls.
By June 1997 the air is reportedly closed too: McGonagall says they knew nobody could fly in. Earlier flyers, such as the 1992 car, met no such barrier.
June 1997: Dumbledore says he has never left the school unprotected and adds cover the night he leaves. An unlocked front door that spring shows the routine could lapse.
May 1998: Flitwick casts protective spells into the grounds from a broken classroom window, expecting to delay Voldemort, not stop him; Sprout's group carries Mandrakes to throw over the walls.
Before 1981: Hagrid reports Hogwarts as one of the few safe places during Voldemort's first rise. No specific measures are described.

conflicts.text: Hermione says repeatedly that nobody can Apparate inside Hogwarts, yet house-elves do so in view and Ron explains it as a difference in elf magic. Treat her rule as applying to witches and wizards.

open: The exact line of the Apparition boundary, and whether it follows the walls everywhere, including the Forest side.
Whether any protection is visible, for example a shimmer on the wall tops. The text shows none.

grounds-general.summary: The school grounds as a whole: lawns falling away from the castle on its narrated sides, with the lake, the Forbidden Forest, the Quidditch pitch, greenhouses and Hagrid's cabin set among them inside a boundary wall. Every route back to the castle climbs. The site is large: walking along the Forest edge far enough loses sight of both castle and lake, and Krum still thinks Durmstrang's grounds are bigger. Distances are rarely measured; the few figures are two hundred yards near Hagrid's cabin and a quarter of a mile from castle to the merpeople's square. Long views run from castle windows to the pitch and the cabin. The grounds change strongly with the seasons: frost in November, deep snow and a frozen lake by December, thaw and mud in February, hot cloudless June days.

facts.text: Krum says Durmstrang has grounds larger even than Hogwarts's, while its castle is smaller.
Walking along the Forest edge in November 1994, Hagrid's party goes far enough that the castle and the lake both pass out of sight.
The carriage from Beauxbatons parks two hundred yards from Hagrid's door, one of the few measured distances in the grounds.
From the merpeople's statue in the lake, Harry reckons his trunk in the castle to be a quarter of a mile away.
Treat the grounds as at least about a kilometre across. Not canon; no overall dimension exists.
facts.because: A quarter-mile to the merpeople's statue is 400 m, the cabin and carriage add 200 yards near the Forest, and from the pitch the doors are distant. These spans do not lie end to end, but together with a route that loses the castle from view they rule out a compact site.

facts.text: Snow reaches several feet by mid-December 1991 and two feet in late 1995.
Growth runs large: pumpkins reach garden-shed size in October 1992 and greenhouse flowers grow as big as cabbages in spring 1993.
The ground falls from the castle: lawns slope down to the pitch, the cabin and the lake, and pupils return uphill from the Forest and greenhouses.
Castle windows overlook the pitch, Hagrid's usual walks and his cabin frontage far off in the distance.
From the sloping lawns the Forest stands in the distance, and the flying lawn lies on the opposite side of the grounds from it.
Forest trees can be heard creaking from the Gryffindor dormitory in a storm, and Fawkes's lament carries across the grounds into the castle.
There are lonely, secluded corners where pupils can go unobserved. None is named or placed.
A hen-coop exists somewhere in the grounds, reported by Hagrid, with its position unstated.
Mostly grass lawn with flowerbeds. June lawns ripple satin-green; the lake reflects a cloudless sky.
Lupin says he and his school friends roamed the grounds and village at night, the knowledge behind the Marauder's Map.
Pupils cross the grounds freely between castle, pitch and cabin by day. At dusk or after dark the same routes feel empty.
Autumn: damp, days of heavy rain, a raised lake and flowerbeds turned to mud (1992). Hard frosts and first snow on the peaks by November.
Winter: the lake freezes solid by December and pupils skate on it. Deep snow carries trodden channels; pupils toboggan, and snowballs are bewitched up at Gryffindor Tower's windows.
Late winter: endless rain, then thaw, cold rain and slippery mud in February; harsh drying winds in March 1995.
Spring and summer: warm breezy Easter, then hot cloudless June days with pupils on the lawns and the giant squid at the lake's surface.
Blizzards and sleet recur: grey snow darkens the castle in December 1992, sleet drives along the lane in October 1996.
Temporary lessons and exams: Hagrid's bonfire of salamanders, January 1994, and Lupin's obstacle course of pool, potholes and marsh, June 1994. Neither is permanent topography.
June 1997: Fawkes's lament stops and Harry believes the phoenix has left for good.
facts.because: The silence is observed; the permanent departure is Harry's conviction.

open: Overall size and outline of the grounds: no dimension is given.
How the boundary wall runs around the Forest and lake.

surrounding-mountains.summary: Mountains surround the school and rise beyond Hogsmeade, which lies in the shadow of one of them. None is named, measured or placed by bearing. They are seen from castle windows, the High Street and the railway, and one stands between the departing train and the castle. They turn icy grey and carry snow by November. The castle's own site is called a high mountain at first sight. The region lies far to the north, with moors and forest on the rail approach.

facts.text: At first sight the castle's own site is called a high mountain, and later a cliff, so the school stands in high country, not on a hill in a valley.
facts.because: Both words are used of the same site across the lake.

facts.text: A snow-capped mountain stands beside the railway on 1 September 1992, so peaks near the route hold snow in early autumn.
facts.because: The date and the snow come from the same observation; the height is deduced, and that peak's distance from the school is unknown.

facts.text: The narration speaks of the mountains around the school, and Harry notices their absence as soon as a Portkey takes him away.
One mountain overshadows Hogsmeade. A lane from the High Street thins out past cottages to a stile at its foot.
Dark mountains stand beyond the village, seen from the High Street, which curves off towards the school.
A mountain stands between the railway and the castle: the school drops from view behind it soon after the train leaves.
Mountains and forest are visible from the train at dusk near arrival.
Ravenclaw's common-room windows look out on the mountains, and at dawn the sun rises over mountains seen from the Headmaster's office.
Beyond Hogsmeade, Thestral riders pass over mountains, gullies, villages and winding hillside roads heading for London.
The region lies far to the north: dawn has broken at Shell Cottage while Hogsmeade's street is still dark, and a man from Peebles reports the flying car on its way north.
Aberforth says that once out of Hogsmeade on foot and up into the mountains, Disapparating works again. He adds that Hagrid is hiding in a cave up there.
They turn icy grey by November 1991 and are snowcapped by November 1995.

open: Names, heights and bearings of the mountains: the text gives none, and never names the country the school is in.

mountain-caves.summary: Caves in the mountains beyond Hogsmeade, used as hiding places. These are separate reports and must not be merged into one cave. Only Sirius's refuge of 1995 is described: reached by a stile, a boulder-strewn slope and nearly half an hour's climb, then a narrow crack in the rock opening into a cool, dim cave. Hagrid's 1996 hiding place, Grawp's big cave from 1996 and the cave Hagrid shares with him in 1998 are known only from speech.

facts.text: Sirius's cave lies nearly half an hour's climb up a steep, winding, stony path from the mountain's foot.
Inside there is room to sit and pace and to keep a tethered Hippogriff at the far end.
Grawp's cave is called large by Hagrid, big enough to house a giant.
Reached from Hogsmeade's High Street by a winding lane to a stile, then scrubby rising ground and boulders at the mountain's foot.
Sirius's cave has a rock floor, cool dim air and a large rock used as a tether post. The way in is a narrow fissure that people must squeeze through.
In 1995 the floor holds old newspapers and food scraps, with Buckbeak roped at the end.
The way back runs down the path and over the boulders to the stile, through Hogsmeade and uphill to the castle.
Later cave reports: Hagrid hides in one in 1996, Grawp is rehoused in one from September 1996, and Hagrid says he heard Voldemort's magnified voice in his cave in 1998.

conflicts.text: The cave entrance is a fissure that people squeeze through, yet a Hippogriff is tethered inside. The text does not explain how Buckbeak got in.

open: Whether any of the later caves is the same as Sirius's.

kings-cross.summary: The London end of the school railway, included only as the start of the journey. Platform nine and three-quarters is reached by walking straight at the solid-looking barrier between platforms nine and ten. On the far side a wrought-iron archway carries the platform's name, and a long crowded platform holds the scarlet engine. The train leaves at eleven. Nothing here gives a distance to Hogwarts.

facts.text: The platform is long enough that in 2017 another family stands some fifty yards along it, and it is packed with families, trunks, cats and owls on departure day.
The way in is at a ticket box in the barrier between ordinary platforms nine and ten of the Muggle station.
Seen from inside, a wrought-iron arch with the platform's name stands where the barrier was, and a sign overhead shows Hogwarts Express, eleven o'clock.
Travellers walk or run straight at the barrier and pass through without collision. It looks entirely solid.
At the end of term a guard or ticket inspector lets pupils out through it a few at a time, so Muggles do not see a crowd step from a wall.
The train leaves at eleven on 1 September, by the school letter and in the years shown, and returns to the same platform.
On 1 September 1992 the barrier turns solid for Harry and Ron; they hit it and hear no train beyond. Dobby later admits sealing it.
It works the same in the 1971 memory and in 2017.

hogwarts-express.summary: The school train: a scarlet steam engine pulling corridor carriages between King's Cross and Hogsmeade station. It leaves at eleven on 1 September and arrives after dark, running north through fields, moors, a great city and rolling hills to mountains and forest. Inside, a corridor serves compartments with sliding glass-panelled doors, luggage racks and lanterns, with a prefect carriage towards the engine, a toilet and a food trolley. It carries nearly the whole school at once and fills up, so it must be long: at least seven carriages are implied. Near the end of the run the castle can be seen from the window.

facts.text: At least six carriages are walked through in 1995, plus the prefect carriage towards the engine, and the compartments passed are already full.
A compartment takes six: Harry, Neville, Ginny and Luna sit together in 1995 and Ron and Hermione join them.
facts.because: Four take seats at the start of the journey and Ron and Hermione come in after prefect duties; six is the most seen, not a stated limit.

facts.text: To carry 300 to 800 pupils at six to a compartment and eight compartments to a carriage, the train needs about 7 to 17 carriages. Not canon.
facts.because: 6 x 8 = 48 per carriage; 300/48 = 6.3; 800/48 = 16.7. Eight compartments per carriage is an assumption, and the pupil range is itself an estimate.

facts.text: The journey fills the day: departure at eleven, lamps lit when darkness falls, arrival at night.
It runs north: past fields, purple moors, villages and a great city, then wilder rolling hills and a snow-capped mountain, with mountains and forest near the end.
The only named places on the flight north are London, Norfolk and Peebles, from a newspaper report in 1992.
The castle shows from the railway: Malfoy says he can see it just before arrival in 1996, and Harry watches it pass behind a mountain when leaving in 1994.
In 1995 Harry looks for a first distant view from the train, but rain, grime and a moonless night defeat him.
A scarlet steam engine, heavy with smoke and steam at the platform.
A corridor runs along the carriages, serving compartments through sliding doors with glass panels and blinds. Compartments have facing seats, corner window places and swinging lanterns.
Luggage racks over the seats take trunks and owl cages. The train has a toilet and a food trolley.
The prefect carriage lies towards the engine; latecomers end up in the last carriages.
An announcement carries through the train before arrival. Luggage stays aboard and reaches the school by another route.
On 1 September 1993 it stops short of the station, the lights fail, and a Dementor comes aboard in a search for Black.
It leaves an hour after Dumbledore's funeral in June 1997, and also runs home at the end of each year.
The carriages appear unchanged in the 1971 memory and in 2017.

open: The number of carriages, and the route of the last miles to the station.

hogsmeade-station.summary: The school's railhead, a very small, dark platform on the far side of the lake from the castle. Two routes leave it. First-years go down a steep, narrow, pine-lined path with a bend in it to the lakeshore and the boats. Everyone else moves along the platform and out through the station by a narrow doorway to the road, where about a hundred coaches wait. Though called tiny, it must take a full train and hundreds of pupils at once, and the crowd moves slowly.

facts.text: The platform is called tiny in 1991 and 1993.
Small though it is, it must take a full train of at least seven carriages and hundreds of pupils at once, so make it long and narrow, not short.
facts.because: A mass of people shunts the trio along it in 1993 and pupils inch along it in 1994, while the train has at least seven carriages. Tiny can only describe its width and facilities.

facts.text: It lies on the far side of the lake from the castle: the first-years' path ends at the shore with the castle straight across the water.
facts.because: The path from the platform comes out at the lake's edge and the castle stands on the other side.

facts.text: The road and the coach stand lie just outside the station, and the lane to the school starts there.
In 1996, lying on the stopped train, Harry thinks he can hear the trees around the lake and a far-off owl, so the shore may be close.
The castle comes into view from the train just before it stops.
It has a station building or wall: pupils pass through it by a narrow doorway to reach the road.
Pines line the path to the lake and their smell reaches the platform.
First-years gather at the far end of the platform and go down a steep, narrow path round a bend to the lake, led by Hagrid's lamp, or a teacher's lantern in 1995.
All other pupils go along the platform to the road and the coaches.
Arrivals are always after dark, in cold air, with driving rain and a storm in 1993 and 1994.

open: The size of the station building, and how far the station lies from Hogsmeade village.

carriages-and-road.summary: About a hundred coaches carry every pupil above first year from Hogsmeade station to the castle in one long convoy. The route starts as a rough road outside the station and becomes a bending, hedged lane, climbing all the way to the winged-boar gates, where the drive takes over. It is far longer than it feels by coach: Harry is surprised by the distance when he first walks it in 1996. The coaches are closed, with doors, small windows, lumpy seats and a smell of mould and straw, and carry three to five pupils each in the scenes shown. Skeletal winged Thestrals pull them, though to many pupils they appear horseless.

facts.text: A hundred or so coaches: at least a hundred in 1993, a hundred in 1994, about a hundred in 1995.
Riders seen in a coach: three in 1993, four in 1994, five in 1995, when Hermione hurries in case they all fill up.
At four to five riders the fleet carries about 400 to 500 pupils, the whole school less its first-years. Not canon.
facts.because: 100 coaches x 4 to 5 riders = 400 to 500. Assumes the coaches seen are typical. At three riders it would be 300.

facts.text: In single file a hundred coaches make a convoy about 1 km long, so the stand outside the station and the road need that much room. Not canon.
facts.because: 100 x 10 m per coach with its animal and a gap = 1,000 m. The 10 m is an assumption, and the coach stand may be double-parked.

facts.text: Having always gone by coach, Harry had not realised how far the school was from the station until he walked the lane in 1996.
Model the road from station to gates at no less than about 1.5 km. Not canon; the text gives no length.
facts.because: Harry's surprise at the distance suggests at least a 15 to 20 minute walk (assumption); at 5 km/h that is 1.25 to 1.7 km. It must also hold the 1 km convoy.

facts.text: Route order: station, road and lane uphill, gates between boar-topped pillars, then the drive to the front steps.
The village connects to the same lane: from the High Street the road runs uphill to the gates, which lie to the right as you approach them from the village.
facts.because: Leaving the gates one turns left towards the village (B05-078), so the gates are on the right coming the other way. The text never says outright that the station lane and village road are one road.

facts.text: The surface is a rough mud track in the rain of 1993, a rain-washed road in 1995, and a lane with corners, bends and a hedgerow in 1996.
From the air in June 1997 it appears as a dark, twisting lane running to the boundary wall.
Coaches are stagecoach-style with wheels, doors and small windows; inside they are dark and musty, smelling of mould and straw, with lumpy seats. They bump and sway in procession.
Each coach is drawn by skeletal black horse-like animals between the shafts, with dragon-like heads, white pupil-less eyes and vast leathery bat wings.
Harry and Luna can see the animals in 1995; Ron stands right in front of one and cannot.
Luna says they have always pulled the coaches. Hagrid says the Forest herd began with one male and five females and mainly does this work.
At the end of the year coaches come up the drive to collect pupils waiting in the Entrance Hall.
To Harry the coaches look horseless until September 1995: he assumes an invisible horse in 1993.
October 1996: sleet, wind and frozen slush on the lane.
Still in use in 2017.

open: How many Thestrals draw each coach.
Where a hundred coaches are kept and how they turn at the castle.
The true length of the road and the number of bends.

boats-and-harbour.summary: First-years reach the castle by boat, a tradition still running in 2017. A fleet of little boats waits at the shore at the end of the path from the station, each taking no more than four pupils, with Hagrid alone in one. They move off together on his command, cross the lake to the cliff below the castle, pass behind a hanging screen of ivy into a broad opening, and follow a dark tunnel that seems to run beneath the castle to an underground harbour of rocks and pebbles. A passage then climbs through the rock to grass in the castle's shadow, close to the front steps. No dock or building is described at either end.

facts.text: No more than four to a boat: Harry, Ron, Hermione and Neville share one, and Hagrid has one to himself. The boats are small and form a fleet.
At four to a boat, 1991's 24-plus first-years need at least seven boats counting Hagrid's, and a year of 43 to 114 needs about 11 to 29. Not canon.
facts.because: 24/4 = 6, plus Hagrid's boat. 43/4 = 10.75 and 114/4 = 28.5, from the school-roll estimate. The number of boats is never given.

facts.text: The harbour must berth the whole fleet and let every first-year land, so it is a sizeable cavern, though no dimension is given.
facts.because: The boats all arrive there and the passengers climb out together; nothing suggests they unload elsewhere.

facts.text: The rock passage must climb from lake level to the grass at the castle's foot, close to the height of the cliff.
facts.because: It starts at the underground harbour and comes out on grass beside the castle, so it rises about as far as the cliff does. No length or step count is given.

facts.text: Boats wait at the shore at the end of the path from the station, on the far side of the lake from the castle.
The opening is in the cliff face below the castle; the tunnel seems to carry the boats right under it.
The opening is wide but hidden by hanging ivy, and riders must duck to pass.
The tunnel is dark and ends at a kind of underground harbour where passengers climb out on to rocks and pebbles. No quay is described.
The boats move by themselves, all together, on Hagrid's spoken order.
From the harbour a passage climbs through the rock to smooth damp grass in the castle's shadow; a flight of stone steps then leads to the front door.
The crossing is described as traditional in 1993 and 1994 and is still planned in 2017. In the storm of 1994 Dennis Creevey falls in and is pushed back aboard.
At the end of Harry's first year Hagrid takes them down to a fleet of boats to cross the lake before the train.

open: Whether first-years always return by boat, or only in 1992; later years wait for coaches.
The size and shape of the harbour and passage.

main-gates.summary: The main entrance to the grounds: a pair of high wrought-iron gates between tall stone pillars, each topped by a winged boar, at the foot of the long drive. They stand on the lane from Hogsmeade, and leaving them the village road lies to the left. A boundary wall runs away from them around the grounds, far enough from the front of the castle to be out of sight. The gates can be chained and padlocked; in 1996 they resist an Unlocking Charm but open to Snape's wand. There is more than one entrance to the grounds, though only these gates are ever described. The Apparition limit runs along this boundary. Dementors flank them in 1993 to 1994, and the wall is breached by the Forest in 1998.

facts.text: The gates are high, the pillars tall, and no measurement is given.
The boundary lies far from the castle front: in May 1998 people swarming over the walls are heard from the lawn, not seen.
There is more than one entrance to the grounds: Dumbledore speaks of every entrance, and Macnair goes to one of them. Only the main gates are ever described.
facts.because: The plural is used by several speakers in 1993 to 1994, but no second gate is seen.

facts.text: They stand at the bottom of the drive, on the lane to Hogsmeade. Leaving, pupils pass between the pillars and turn left for the village.
Ron says the Marauder's Map stops at the school's boundaries, so the grounds have a defined edge.
From the gates one looks across dark grounds to the castle; from Hagrid's cabin they are a long run away.
A pair of wrought-iron gates between stone columns, each column topped by a winged boar.
A boundary wall runs around the grounds. Walls are mentioned from Book 6 onward; height and material are not given.
On the late night of 1 September 1996 the gates are chained and padlocked. Alohomora fails; Snape taps the padlock, the chains draw back and the gates creak open, then clang shut and relock.
Tonks says Dumbledore bewitched the gates himself and all the perimeter walls carry anti-intruder jinxes.
Apparition is possible just beyond this line: Snape Disapparates outside it in June 1997 as Buckbeak circles the gates.
Vehicles stop outside: the Knight Bus sets pupils down on the road in January 1996.
Dumbledore tells Lupin in June 1994 that his carriage is waiting at the gates.
Pupils with permission walk out through them for Hogsmeade and return uphill by the same road.
September 1993 to June 1994: a tall hooded Dementor stands on each side, with others at every entrance. Fudge removes them after the attack on Harry.
March 1998: in Harry's vision Voldemort waits at the gates before dawn, then goes up through the grounds beside Snape.
May 1998: Dementors are reported around the walls, Grawp smashes through the boundary by the Forest, and allies swarm over the walls at dawn.

open: Height, material and full line of the boundary wall, including whether it encloses the Forest.
Where any other entrances are.

castle-drive.summary: The drive climbs from the main gates to the stone steps at the castle front. It is called long, sloping, sweeping and wide, and carriages gather speed on it. A lantern at the castle's foot looks distant from the gates, and the walk takes long enough for an extended conversation. It is visible from the forecourt, from the Charms classroom, and from the doors at night by the light they throw. The route passes near the lake and the Quidditch stadium.

facts.text: Called long and sloping in 1993, sweeping in 1994, and wide in 1995. No length is given.
The castle's foot looks distant from the gates, and in 1996 the walk up feels long, reaching the steps only at last.
Model the drive at no less than about 400 m. Not canon.
facts.because: A lantern seen bobbing far off, a conversation that lasts all the way down, and gates that only come into view on the descent rule out a short approach. 400 m is an assumed minimum, about a five-minute walk.

facts.text: It rises from the gates to the front steps, so the way out is downhill and the gates lie at its bottom.
It runs near the lake and the stadium: pupils heading for the gates pass the Durmstrang ship in 1995 and the stadium in 1996.
It can be watched from the forecourt, from where the school looks down it to the gates, and from the Charms classroom window.
At night the open front doors throw light on to the drive and lawn.
Its surface is not described, but it turns slippery under snow in January 1996.
Coaches use it in both directions, climbing with arrivals and coming up empty to collect pupils at the end of the year.

open: Its length, bends and surface.

front-steps.summary: A flight of stone steps rises from the end of the drive to the great oak front doors, the castle's main entrance, which open into the Entrance Hall. Coaches stop beside the steps. The doors are called huge, great and giant, are double, and bolt from inside. They stand directly beneath the Astronomy Tower's parapet. The ground before them has held the whole school in rows with a house-sized flying carriage landing in front. From the top step the view runs down the drive and over the grounds to the lake, Hagrid's cabin and the distant Forest. A window of the Great Hall lies close by. The usual routes across the grounds start here, going down sloping lawns. The doors are blasted open in June 1997 and burst again in May 1998.

facts.text: The doors are called huge, great and giant, and are a double pair.
The stairs are always just a flight of stone steps; no count or width is given.
The whole school lines up in rows before the steps in October 1994, first-years in front and Harry's fourth-years in the fourth row.
A carriage the size of a large house with a dozen elephant-sized horses lands just ahead of those rows, and the front three rows draw back.
The ground before the doors needs about 45 to 115 m of open width for those rows, plus clear space for that landing. Not canon.
facts.because: One row per year, as the fourth-years' place suggests: 43 to 114 pupils per row (school-roll estimate) at an assumed 1 m each is about 45 to 115 m. No width is given.

facts.text: The opening clears Hagrid, about twice normal height and three times as broad, who uses these doors, and a palomino centaur walks through it in 1996.
facts.because: Hagrid opens the doors and walks out in B03-091; his size is given at B04-012; nothing says he stoops. No door height is stated.

facts.text: A twenty-foot giant by the doors punches through an upper window and reaches inside, so that window is within about 30 ft of the ground.
facts.because: A giant 20 ft tall reaches to about 30 ft with his arm up (assumed one and a half times height). The window's floor is not named.

facts.text: The front doors lie directly below the Astronomy Tower's parapet.
Coaches halt beside the steps. The doors open into the Entrance Hall, with the Great Hall's doors on the right as you enter.
A brightly lit Great Hall window is close to the steps, and from outside it you can watch the Sorting.
From the top of the steps and lawns the view runs over the grounds to the lake, Hagrid's cabin, the Forest treetops, and the far-off Beauxbatons carriage.
The steps can be seen from the pitch, the broomshed and the Forest edge, all of which are distant.
The grass where the harbour passage comes out is just below these steps.
The usual routes across the grounds start at the foot of the steps: down lawns to the cabin, the pitch, the lake, the Forest edge, and past the vegetable patch.
The doors are heavy oak, with a lintel above the opening, and the steps are stone.
The doors and steps are the everyday way in and out for pupils and staff, and the whole school files out by them to the lake for the June 1997 funeral.
A lock on the inside can be slid back by hand, so pupils can let themselves out at night.
Filch locks the doors at night. In spring 1997 he forgets: Harry walks out at dusk, Slughorn complains of poor security, and the door is still unlocked on Harry's return.
On Hogsmeade days Filch checks pupils against a list at the doors, and from 1996 uses a Secrecy Sensor on the way out and in.
In early 1994 Hagrid collects Harry and Ron from the Entrance Hall at six and walks them to his hut and back, a security escort.
1994: Flitwick teaches the doors to recognise a large photograph of Sirius Black.
June 1997: the doors are blasted open during the Death Eaters' flight; afterwards the crowd spills down the steps to the lawn.
May 1998: giant spiders burst the doors, a giant fights by the shaking steps and leaves a clog as big as a small boat, and the defenders stand on the steps at dawn.

conflicts.text: The doors are repeatedly huge, and the twins ride brooms out of them from fifteen feet up in the Hall, yet in 1996 Ron, carried shoulder-high, bumps his head on the lintel. Either the lintel is lower than the wording suggests or the crowd lifted him high.

open: The number and width of the steps.
The height of the doorway, given the lintel scene.

knight-bus.summary: A vivid purple three-decker bus used once to reach the school, in January 1996, when it runs in magical jumps from London through Hogsmeade to stop on the road outside the gates. Chairs replace its night-time brass beds by day.

facts.text: It has three decks, with stairs to the top and a large front window.
It stops on the deserted road outside the school gates, after passing through Hogsmeade near the Hog's Head side street.
By day it holds mismatched chairs grouped at the windows, which slide about in the jumps. At night it holds brass beds, with candles in brackets.

entrance-hall.summary: The Entrance Hall is the castle’s main junction, on the ground floor directly behind the oak front doors at the top of the stone front steps. It is a vast stone room with a flagged floor, wall torches and a ceiling lost above the torchlight, big enough to take a whole four-bedroom house. The marble staircase faces the front doors. Double doors on the right lead to the Great Hall, and a door to the right of the staircase leads down to the kitchens and the Hufflepuff basement. On the other side of the staircase a door leads down to the Slytherin dungeons, and a corridor runs to classroom eleven. Giant house-point hourglasses stand in wall niches in one corner. Most of the school has stood here at once in a ring round a clear middle, so allow at least 250 m² of open floor and 10 m to the ceiling, as modelling minimums rather than figures from the books.

facts.text: The Dursleys’ entire four-bedroom house would fit inside it, on Harry’s first impression.
Its ceiling is out of sight above the torchlight.
Peeves hovered twenty feet above arriving pupils in 1994; in 1996 two brooms rose fifteen feet inside it, level with him.
Modelling minimum, not canon: at least 10 m from floor to ceiling.
facts.because: Twenty feet (6 m) above pupils about 1.7 m tall puts Peeves near 8 m up, with the ceiling above that. A two-storey house with a pitched roof, assumed 8 to 9 m to the ridge, must also fit under it. A ceiling too high to see by torchlight suggests well over 10 m.

facts.text: The 1994 Age Line ran ten feet out from the Goblet in every direction, a ring about 20 feet across at the centre of the hall, with people moving around it.
In 1996 apparently most of the school stood round the walls in a ring with a clear middle; an earlier packed ring overflowed on to the marble staircase.
Modelling minimum, not canon: about 250 m² of open floor, for example 16 m by 16 m, excluding the staircase.
facts.because: Crowd: most of a school of 500 to 700 is about 400 people. At an assumed 2.5 people per m², a band 3 m deep around a 10 m clear middle holds 390 (156 m² × 2.5), which needs 16 m by 16 m = 256 m². Goblet: a 6 m ring plus an assumed 5 m each side for passing pupils also gives 16 m. House: a two-storey, four-bedroom house, assumed 8 m by 10 m in plan, fits inside.

facts.text: Described as vast and cavernous.
In 1996 Harry, coming down into the hall, judged the diners beyond the Great Hall doors to be about twenty feet away.
On the ground floor, directly behind the oak front doors at the top of the stone front steps.
Seen from the front doors, the marble staircase stands straight ahead and the Great Hall’s double doors are on the right.
Seen from the front doors, the door to the kitchens and Hufflepuff basement is on the Great Hall side of the staircase, and the door down to Slytherin is opposite.
facts.because: Cedric’s door is to the right of the staircase and is the one reached by turning left when coming down it, so it is on the right seen from the front doors. The Slytherin door is on the right when coming down, so on the left seen from the front doors. This puts the kitchen steps on the same side as the Great Hall, which fits the kitchens lying under it.

facts.text: A corridor to classroom eleven leaves the hall on the side opposite the Great Hall.
Stone walls lit by flaming torches and a stone-flagged floor. Footsteps and shouts echo, and it feels cool or gloomy coming in from sunny grounds.
A balcony overlooks the hall, and at least one window lies across the hall from the stairs.

Giant house-point hourglasses stand in wall niches in one corner, holding rubies for Gryffindor, sapphires for Ravenclaw and emeralds for Slytherin. Gems fall as points are won and rise as they are lost.
A noticeboard, plus armour standing by the front door.
The oak front doors have a sliding lock on the inside, and a centaur’s horse body has walked in through them.
On Hogsmeade days Filch checks names at the front doors, from 1996 also with a Secrecy Sensor.
Side chambers, a broom cupboard and at least one corridor door open directly off the hall.
Book 4: a large tournament notice stood at the stair foot in October 1994, then the Goblet of Fire on the Sorting stool at the centre of the floor.

Damage: front doors blasted open and Gryffindor’s hourglass cursed, spilling rubies (June 1997); Slytherin’s hourglass shattered, doors burst by giant spiders, banisters broken, flagstones bloodied (May 1998).

open: Plan shape and the position of each door along its wall. The text fixes only which side each is on, and gives no compass bearing.
What the balcony connects to, and whether it is at first-floor level.
Which wall holds the hourglasses. Slytherin’s is on the left when coming down the stairs, and Hufflepuff’s gem is never named.

marble-staircase.summary: The marble staircase is the castle’s main stair, rising from the Entrance Hall directly opposite the front doors. In most scenes it climbs from the ground floor to the first floor, where other stairs take over; from the seventh floor the way down is six floors and then this staircase. It has marble banisters and a balustrade and at least one landing, and it is the everyday route up for the whole school, carrying whole houses after feasts and hundreds of evacuees in 1998. No width, step count or plan shape is stated, so allow at least 4 m of width as a modelling minimum, not a figure from the books. It was badly damaged in the 1998 battle and no repair is described.

facts.text: Stands across the Entrance Hall directly facing the front doors, and is the main way to the upper floors.
Climbs from the ground floor to the first floor, where other stairs take over: from the seventh floor the route is six floors down, then this staircase.
Carries large crowds: whole houses climb it after feasts, onlookers packed it in 1996, and hundreds of evacuees poured up it in 1998.
Modelling minimum, not canon: at least 4 m wide.
facts.because: No width is given. Gryffindor and Ravenclaw, about half a school of 500 to 700, both live upstairs, so about 300 pupils climb it after a feast. At an assumed 0.5 people per metre of width per second, 300 people in 5 minutes need 2 m. Double that for traffic coming the other way, which also leaves room for Hagrid, at least three times normal breadth, who has run down it.

facts.text: A person at the foot can make out who is at the top: Harry saw Cedric and his friends up there from the bottom.
Marble steps and marble banisters with a balustrade; the banister ends can hold cakes set on them.
It has at least one landing: Filch passes a first landing on the way up, and a portrait of bewigged witches hangs on a landing.
A corridor reached by a concealed staircase and a tapestry joins a landing, from which the rest of the staircase drops to the Entrance Hall.
At the foot, coming down, the door on the left leads to the kitchens, the door on the right to Slytherin, and the front doors lie ahead.
Christmas 1994: everlasting icicles hung from the banisters.
May 1998: the battle left chunks missing from the staircase, parts of the banisters and balustrade gone, and rubble and blood on the steps. No repair is narrated.

conflicts.text: Most scenes end the staircase at the first floor, but Book 5 has Filch reach its first landing on the way up to Umbridge’s office, and in Book 6 the Carrows run down it above a landing with more of it below. That suggests a half-landing or a longer stair.

open: Plan form: one straight flight, a divided stair, or flights with a half-landing. The text gives no shape or step count.

entrance-side-rooms.summary: A group, not one room: small spaces that open directly off the Entrance Hall. Known instances are the small empty chamber where first-years wait before the Sorting, an empty chamber used as a hiding place in 1994, and a broom cupboard of buckets and mops. The text does not say the two chambers are the same, and gives no wall for any of them.

facts.text: The waiting chamber is small: the new first-years, all together, had to press in close.
From that chamber the first-years cross back over the hall to reach the Great Hall’s doors.
A broom cupboard opening off the hall holds buckets and mops, with room for two people and an upturned bucket as a seat.
People hiding in the cupboard or the empty chamber can hear others crossing the hall; from the cupboard, even going down the front steps.
In 1991 about twenty ghosts crossed the waiting chamber, in through the back wall and out through the opposite one.

open: Which wall each room opens from, and whether the 1994 chamber is the 1991 one.

great-hall.summary: The Great Hall is the school’s main dining and assembly room, on the ground floor to the right of the Entrance Hall, with the kitchens directly beneath it. It is a stone room with high windows and an enchanted ceiling that shows the sky. Four long house tables with benches run up the room to a fifth, the staff table, on a raised platform along the top wall. The books never state its dimensions, but every clue points to a very large room: about a hundred dining tables, roughly 1,200 seats, stood in it at once for the 1994 ball, the whole school has slept on its floor, more than a hundred exam desks have filled it, and two duels have been fought fifty yards apart inside it. As a modelling minimum, not a figure from the books, allow at least 1,200 m² of floor, roughly 50 m by 24 m, and at least 12 m to the ceiling. All the furniture is movable, and the room is repeatedly cleared or rearranged for exams, duelling, Apparition lessons and the 1998 battle.

facts.text: Modelling minimum, not canon: at least 1,200 m² of floor (about 13,000 sq ft), for example 50 m by 24 m. Anything much smaller fails several scenes at once.
facts.because: No dimensions are stated; all spacing here is assumed. Seats: about 100 tables × about 12 seats = about 1,200 seats; at an assumed 1 m² per seated diner including aisles, 1,200 m². Grid check: a 1.8 m table, 0.5 m of chairs each side and a 0.6 m aisle makes a 3.4 m grid, and 100 × 3.4 m × 3.4 m = 1,156 m². Length: fifty yards is 46 m between two duellists; an assumed 2 m each end for the crowd along the walls gives 50 m, and 1,200 ÷ 50 = 24 m wide. Width check: four tables at 3 m with benches and diners, plus five 1.6 m aisles, is 20 m, which fits. Sleeping check: 500 to 700 pupils × 1.6 m² per bag (2.0 m by 0.8 m) = 800 to 1,120 m² of bags alone, before walkways and the long tables at the walls. Bench check: 700 pupils ÷ 8 bench sides × 0.5 m each = 44 m of table, which fits a 50 m room. Exam desks (100+ at an assumed 3 m² = 300+ m²) and Apparition spacing (100 pupils on an assumed 2 m grid, five clear feet plus a body, = 400 m²) need less, so they do not set the limit.

facts.text: The Hall must hold the whole school at one sitting, about 500 to 700 pupils plus staff, and must also physically take the roughly 1,200 seats laid out for the 1994 ball.
facts.because: No head-count is ever stated. Coaches: about 100 carry everyone above first year; the observed loads of 4 (1994) and 5 (1995) give 400 to 500 pupils in six years, so about 470 to 580 in seven. Exam desks: more than 100 desks × 7 years gives 700 or more if they held one year group, though in 1996 fifth- and seventh-years were called in together, which could halve that. The ball’s 1,200 counts seats, not people: only fourth-years and above plus invited partners could come, so on these figures at most about 800 attended. Size the room for the largest stated furniture load, because a big room can be under-filled but a small one cannot take the tables.

facts.text: Yule Ball, 1994: about a hundred small lantern-lit tables of about twelve seats each stood in the Hall at once, with a large round table for the judges at the top.
O.W.L. exams: more than a hundred one-person desks, all facing the same way with aisles between them (Snape’s year, about 1976). The same layout was used in 1996.
Hallowe’en night 1993: all four houses slept here together, with hundreds of sleeping bags across the floor and the long tables stood against the walls.
May 1998: two duels ran fifty yards apart inside the Hall, while hundreds of people lined the walls and everyone still on their feet pushed in.
February 1997 Apparition lesson: tables removed, each sixth-year stood with five clear feet ahead and a wooden hoop on the floor. The anti-Apparition enchantment was lifted inside the Hall only.
Duelling Club, December 1992: with the dining tables gone, the bulk of the school crowded in standing, then paired off across the floor.
Narration calls the room huge and the seated school hundreds; in 1994 the two visiting schools added only some twenty. Harry’s walk up to the staff table seemed endless.
Floating candles number in the thousands on feast nights and at the Duelling Club; Book 4 gives hundreds and hundreds.
Owl post arrives in one flock: about a hundred owls in Books 1 and 4, hundreds in Book 5, circling above the tables.
Twelve Christmas trees, called towering, stand around the room every year; one tree alone could hide Hagrid in a corridor.
Modelling minimum, not canon: at least 12 m from floor to ceiling. The text gives no height and never describes the real roof.
facts.because: A fir that can hide Hagrid (about twice normal height, so about 3.5 m) and is called towering once stood up is likely 6 m or more. Grawp, at about 16 ft (4.9 m), can put his face to one window from outside, while the windows in general are called high or upper, so their heads must stand well above him: allow about 10 m, plus 2 m above the window heads to the ceiling. A room 50 m long under a low ceiling would contradict all of this.

facts.text: On the ground floor, entered through double doors on the right of the Entrance Hall as you come in from the front doors. The kitchens lie directly beneath it.
The doors open at the back of the Hall on its Slytherin side: you pass the other tables to reach Gryffindor, the table furthest from the Entrance Hall.
facts.because: In 1994 the walk in passes Slytherin, Ravenclaw and Hufflepuff before Gryffindor. In 1993 Harry skirts the rear of the Hall to get to his table. Book 6 calls Gryffindor the furthest table. One Gryffindor bench faces the doorway and the other has its back to it, which could not happen if the doors lay on the line of the tables.

facts.text: From outside, a lit window near the foot of the front steps looks into the Hall across the tables as far as the staff table.
Stone walls and floor, a raised platform across the top end, winter fires, and high mullioned windows that open for owls and catch the dawn sun (May 1998).
Four long house tables with benches run up the room side by side, in the order Slytherin, Ravenclaw, Hufflepuff, Gryffindor, with aisles between, laid with gold plates and goblets.
The staff table (the High Table) runs along the top wall, staff on one side facing the pupils. The Headmaster’s high-backed gold chair is central; Hagrid’s huge chair is at one end.
Double doors from the Entrance Hall give a view out from the benches. A door behind the staff table at Hagrid’s end leads to a side chamber. The text mentions further entrances in 1993.
The ceiling shows the sky outside, stars, cloud or storm, though a real one exists: a Howler shook dust from it. Food appears and clears itself unseen, by spoken order at the 1994 ball.
At each start of term a stool and the Sorting Hat stand before the staff table, with first-years lined up facing the school; both are removed afterwards.
Furniture moves by magic: tables vanish or line the walls. One table served twelve at Christmas 1993; a stage stood on one wall in 1992, a music platform on the right-hand wall in 1994.

Decorations follow the calendar: 2,000 live bats (1991), hundreds of pumpkins, some able to hold three men, house-colour hangings, huge silk banners (1994), black mourning drapes (1995), Valentine flowers (1993).
Battle of Hogwarts, May 1998: house tables removed, the injured treated on the platform, the dead laid in a row down the middle, the floor cracked, a window smashed; tables later restored.

conflicts.text: House-table order. Book 1 has Ravenclaw second from the left and Hufflepuff on the right, seen from the top of the Hall with Gryffindor far left. From Book 4 on, Hufflepuff sits next to Gryffindor with Ravenclaw beyond it. The later order recurs in at least four scenes.

School size. Two-house classes of twenty imply about 40 pupils a year and about 280 in all. About 100 coaches imply about 500, more than 100 desks up to 700, and 1,200 seats for the top four years alone imply more. These cannot all be right; the room must fit the largest.
The Sorting stool has four legs in Book 1 and three in Books 3 and 4.

open: Exact door position along the back of the Hall, and how that wall relates to the Entrance Hall’s right-hand wall.
Window heights. Most are called high, yet boys on the ground near the front steps can see in (1992) and Grawp’s face reaches one (1998). Decide sill heights and how the ground falls along that wall.
Which walls face the castle front and the sunrise. The text gives no compass bearing for the Hall.
Whether the raised platform is a permanent feature. It is only named in Book 7.

great-hall-side-chamber.summary: A group of small rooms next to the Great Hall, which the text does not say are one room. The best described is the champions’ room, through the door behind the staff table at Hagrid’s end: smaller than the Hall, hung with paintings, with a fire facing the door and a low candle chandelier. Fifth-years waited for practical O.W.L.s in a small chamber beside the Hall in 1996, and Voldemort’s body was laid in a chamber off the Hall in 1998; either may or may not be that same room.

facts.text: The champions’ room is reached through the door behind the staff table, at the end where Hagrid sits.
It is smaller than the Hall, yet held at least eleven people in 1994, and twelve in June 1995 in separate family groups.
A chandelier of candles hangs low enough that Madame Maxime, at full height, brushed it with her head. She is not measured, so this gives only a relative clearance.
Paintings of witches and wizards line the walls, a roaring fire with a mantelpiece faces the door, and parts of the room stay in shadow beyond the firelight.
Violet’s portrait hangs here next to that of a walrus-moustached wizard. Harry reckons she ran through pictures on seven staircases to reach the Fat Lady’s frame.
The door shuts out the noise of the Hall; the voices beyond carry only while it stands open.
In 1996 the fifth-years waited for practical O.W.L.s in a small chamber beside the Hall, went straight into the Hall when called, and did not come back.
Modelling minimum, not canon: about 50 m² if a full year group must wait in the 1996 chamber, despite its being called small.
facts.because: A year group of up to about 100 (see the Great Hall head-count) standing at an assumed 2 people per m² = 50 m². On the smaller class-based figure of 40 pupils it would be 20 m².

facts.text: May 1998: Voldemort’s body was laid in a chamber off the Hall, apart from the fallen defenders.

open: Whether the 1996 waiting chamber and the 1998 chamber are the champions’ room or separate rooms.

staircases.summary: The castle's general staircases, scattered through the whole building rather than gathered in one stairwell. This is a group, not one structure. The text counts 142. Between the ground floor and the seventh floor lie eight levels and seven gaps, which averages about 20 staircases per gap, or about 16 after setting aside a generous 30 for tower spirals and shortcuts. A climb from the ground floor to the seventh floor uses seven staircases, one per gap, so any single route uses about 5 per cent of the total. Each gap must therefore be crossed at many separate points across a wide plan. Forms vary: broad curving flights, thin unsteady ones, narrow stone flights, carpeted stairs, stairs with banisters, portrait-lined flights and tight stone spirals in the towers. Some arrive somewhere else on Fridays, one is called swivelling, and many have a false step that traps a leg. No scene shows a general staircase moving in front of anyone.

facts.text: Hogwarts has 142 staircases.
A climb from ground level to the seventh floor takes seven long staircases, one for each gap between floors.
facts.because: The seventh long staircase from the Great Hall ends on Sir Cadogan's landing (B03-014), which is later placed on the seventh floor (B03-089). Harry also reckons seven staircases from the ground-floor chamber to the Fat Lady (B04-060), and six floors plus the marble staircase make seven (B04-106).

facts.text: About 20 staircases per gap between floors on average, or about 16 after setting aside tower spirals and shortcuts.
facts.because: 142 ÷ 7 gaps (ground to seventh floor, eight levels) = 20.3. Assuming a generous 30 of the 142 are tower spirals, dungeon stairs and shortcuts: 112 ÷ 7 = 16. A staircase spanning two floors (B04-147) counts once, so long stacked stairs raise the crossings per gap rather than lower them.

facts.text: One route uses only about 5 per cent of the staircases; spacing the rest needs at least about 400 m of corridor per floor.
facts.because: 7 ÷ 142 = 4.9%. At an assumed minimum of 25 m between separate staircases, 16 staircases on a floor need 16 × 25 m = 400 m of corridor. A castle built around two or three stair stacks would be short by a factor of five or more.

facts.text: The way from the portrait hole down to the Entrance Hall is described simply as many staircases.
Some are broad and curving, others thin and unsteady.
Narrow stone flights rise towards the Fat Lady's passage, past portraits and armour.
The flight up to the third floor is carpeted.
Some flights have banisters, and the flight below the portrait hole is lined with pictures of old witches and wizards.
Towers are climbed by tight stone spirals, such as the one from the West Tower battlements to a corridor at its foot.
One flight arriving on the seventh floor has a statue of Lachlan the Lanky to the right of its top.
Floors are not perfectly level: a staircase lies on the walk along the seventh floor from Gryffindor to the blank wall.
facts.because: Harry stops at the top of a last staircase after the three have set out along the seventh floor, and only then reaches the tapestry (B05-108). Short stairs within a floor would also help account for so high a total.

facts.text: The flight from the seventh floor down to the sixth near the boys' bathroom is also called marble.
Landings carry windows or single large paintings; Sir Cadogan's seventh-floor landing has little else.
On Fridays some staircases arrive at a different place.
Many stairs are trick stairs: a step partway up gives way or disappears, and pupils learn to jump it.
One false step swallows a leg to above the knee and struggling sinks it deeper; someone else must pull the victim free.
One staircase is called swivelling and offers a way round the corridor to the Defence office.
No scene shows a general staircase moving before anyone's eyes; the only stair seen in motion is the spiral behind the Headmaster's gargoyle.
facts.because: A search of all seven books for staircases moving, shifting, swinging or turning finds only that spiral, the Friday remark and the one swivelling name. Harry's sense that everything moves about is his impression (B01-026).

open: How the 142 are shared between wings and towers is unstated: the modeller must place them, keeping the average of 16 to 20 per gap.
The swivelling staircase is a name only; nothing says what it does or how far it turns.

corridors-general.summary: Stone corridors and landings on every floor, the general fabric linking the castle's rooms. This is a group, not one place. They are long, branching and confusing: Ron allows ten minutes from the Great Hall to the top of North Tower, and two first-years once spent nearly an hour failing to retrace one route. Widths vary from a passage narrow enough for two men to touch a hidden boy to corridors that take crowds and, in 1996, flying firework wheels five feet across. Windows are high and frequent, and many look over the grounds to Hagrid's cabin, the pitch or the lake. Light comes from wall torches, lamps and the occasional chandelier. Contents include rugs, waste-paper baskets, armour, statues, vases on plinths, tapestries, portraits and cupboards. Classrooms open off both sides of some stretches. Some corridors have boarded floors. Damage is dated: fireworks in 1996, a half-collapsed ceiling in 1997, and broken windows in 1998.

facts.text: The walk from the Great Hall to the top of North Tower implies at least several hundred metres of level corridor, roughly 450 m.
facts.because: Ron allows ten minutes (B03-014). Assuming about 3 minutes for seven staircases and 1 minute for the tower spiral leaves 6 minutes; at an assumed 1.25 m/s that is 450 m. A rough figure, since Ron was guessing and the three then lost their way.

facts.text: Two first-years wandered for nearly an hour trying to retrace one route.
One corridor near the library is so narrow that two approaching men would have knocked into an invisible boy.
Corridors one floor below the Defence office exceed five feet in width and height.
facts.because: Firework wheels five feet across flew along them in April 1996 (B05-214).

facts.text: Doors line both sides of some corridors: classes are audible left and right, and door after door opens at once.
A corridor window, once smashed, took Hagrid's whole body thrown in from outside.
Walls are stone: stray curses crack them and blast out fragments.
Some corridors and stairs are floored with boards, which squeak under Harry and quake under Hagrid.
High windows throw moonlight and sunlight in bands across the floor, and one route passes window after window.
Light comes from torches in wall brackets, from lamps in places, and from a chandelier in one corridor.
Rugs, waste-paper baskets, suits of armour and statues on plinths stand along the corridors.
Cupboards open off corridors, including lockable ones for brooms.
Windows on the Gryffindor route and near History of Magic look towards Hagrid's cabin.
Windows in the corridor outside the hospital wing show the Quidditch pitch and the lake.
A large vase stands halfway along the fourth-floor corridor on Harry's way up to the Owlery.
A corridor near the Owlery leads towards the west wing.
Two corridors joined by a corner link the Defence classroom to the staff room.
Fifth-years may stay out in the corridors up to nine in the evening.
April 1996: fireworks fill the corridors one floor below the Defence office, and a rocket blasts a hole in a painting.
June 1997: about half the ceiling falls in at the corridor below the Astronomy Tower stair, and curses crack walls and break a window.
May 1998: dust fills shaking corridors, windows lose panes, and a huge vase bursts from its plinth.

conflicts.text: The 1996 fireworks are one floor below the Defence office, which is on the third floor, yet creatures there flee towards the second floor, as if they were not already on it.

open: Corridor floor material is stated only for boarded stretches; the modeller must choose for the rest.

second-floor-corridor.summary: The corridor outside Moaning Myrtle's bathroom, narrated in Book 2 as the last, empty passage of the second floor. It is stone-walled, with windows and torch brackets, and stairs serve both ends, so crowds from the Great Hall can pour in from either direction at once. Myrtle's door, marked Out of Order, stands a few paces past the spot where Filch kept watch. The corridor is the site of the 1992 wall message, in foot-high letters between two windows, and of a second message in 1993. Water from the bathroom has covered half its length. Its floor number is disputed within Book 2: most journeys support the second floor, but this is not settled.

facts.text: Reached by climbing the marble staircase to the first floor, a further flight, then going round the second floor to its last empty passage.
Myrtle's bathroom door stands a few paces past the place where Filch's chair stood.
Stairs serve both ends: pupils leaving the feast enter from both directions at once.
It must hold a crowd: pupils coming up from the feast pack it from both ends.
facts.because: The text has hundreds of feet on the stairs at either end and the students massing in the passage around the hanging cat (B02-047).

facts.text: The wall is stone, with at least two windows and torch brackets.
The window beside the writing has a small crack in its topmost pane.
The 1992 message stood in foot-high shining letters between two windows.
Filch's cleaning fluid failed to remove the message, and he kept watch from a chair set against that wall.
After the first attack the floor showed scorch marks.
In early 1993 water from Myrtle's bathroom covered half the corridor.
A second message appeared directly below the first in May 1993.
McGonagall's office lies moments away along the corridor, with no stairs mentioned.

conflicts.text: Floor number. Narration runs up to the second floor and round to this passage (B02-046). Hermione places Myrtle's toilet, beside it, on the first floor (B02-045). Lockhart's office is on the second-floor corridor (B02-033), yet it is just upstairs from here (B02-048), and the nearest stairs lead down from it to here (B02-138), which also implies the first floor.
Book 2 also has this corridor one floor above the hospital wing (B02-097), though from Myrtle's bathroom the ward is said to be up (B02-095).
Most journeys, and Book 4's second-floor placing of the bathroom, support the second floor. This is the better-supported reading, not a settled one.

charms-corridor.summary: The corridor serving the Charms classroom, with other classrooms along it. Its floor is never stated, but in 1991 a locked door at its end opened straight into the forbidden third-floor corridor, so the third floor is the likeliest reading. The way there starts up the marble staircase. A hidden passage behind a tapestry comes out near it, and the pupils think of it as very far from the trophy room.

facts.text: Probably on the third floor.
facts.because: A locked door at its end opens directly into the forbidden third-floor corridor, with no stairs between (B01-050).

facts.text: The way there from the Entrance Hall starts up the marble staircase.
A hidden passage behind a tapestry comes out near the Charms classroom, which pupils regard as a very long way from the trophy room.
Classrooms open along it; Peeves and Moody each emerge from one.
It runs on for more than a dozen paces beyond the place where the pupils regrouped.
In 1991 the door at its end was locked, and a simple unlocking charm opened it.
The classroom Harry enters beside it has a window over the grounds.
A picture of drunken monks hangs somewhere near this corridor.

east-wing-fifth-floor.summary: A corridor on the fifth floor of the east wing, with classrooms beyond it, best known as the site of the Weasley twins' Portable Swamp in 1996. The twins call it Gregory the Smarmy's corridor, so that statue probably stands here. It lies above the Defence classroom and well away from the Defence office.

facts.text: The corridor is on the fifth floor of the east wing.
Gregory the Smarmy's statue probably stands in this corridor.
facts.because: The twins send Ron to Gregory the Smarmy's corridor for the diversion they are setting off in the east wing (B05-226). The statue is named in B01-044, with a passage behind it.

facts.text: It lies above the Defence classroom corridor and well away from the Defence office.
facts.because: The uproar is heard from above the classroom corridor (B05-230), and the twins chose the east wing to draw Umbridge right away from her office (B05-226).

facts.text: The swamp filled the corridor, which was roped off, and Filch punted pupils across it to classrooms beyond.
The swamp dates from April 1996, and it lasted until June after Umbridge and Filch failed to remove it.
Flitwick cleared it in about three seconds in June 1996, keeping a tiny roped-off patch under a window.

hidden-shortcuts.summary: Concealed stairs, tapestry openings, wall doors and mirror or panel passages that stay inside the castle. This is a group of separate features, not one passage, and the Marauder's Map shows many of them. The common form is an opening behind a tapestry with a narrower staircase beyond, sometimes with a tapestry at each end. The best described drops two floors in one long flight, apparently from the fourth floor to the second, with a false step halfway. Known instances also include a sliding panel and a hanging tapestry above the marble staircase, a second-floor tapestry used as a regular way up to Gryffindor, a sideways shortcut on the third floor, a fourth-floor alternative route, a door posing as solid wall on the way to Potions, and a tapestry passage coming out near Charms. A roomy passage behind a fourth-floor mirror is reported blocked.

facts.text: The Marauder's Map shows many shortcuts as well as secret passages.
One narrow tapestry staircase drops two floors in a single long flight.
That staircase apparently runs from the fourth floor to the second.
facts.because: It opens halfway along the corridor one flight below the corridor of the fifth-floor Prefects' bathroom (B04-147, B04-131) and descends two floors. The second-floor tapestry shortcut (B06-070) may be its foot.

facts.text: Tapestries hide both its top and bottom openings.
The false-step stair of Books 4 and 6 is probably one staircase.
facts.because: Each is a concealed narrow stair behind a tapestry, with a step halfway that pupils jump (B04-019, B04-148, B06-186). The text never says outright that they are the same.

facts.text: A concealed stair with a vanishing step ends at a tapestry, in a corridor leading to a landing of the marble staircase.
A tapestry on the second floor opens on the usual shortcut up to Gryffindor Tower, with a corridor behind it.
Above the marble staircase, the route to Gryffindor uses doorways hidden behind a sliding panel and a hanging tapestry.
A shortcut opens sideways off a third-floor corridor, on the way up to the Fat Lady.
A familiar shortcut bypasses a jammed fourth-floor door and reaches the portrait hole within five minutes at a run.
A door posing as solid wall opens on a shortcut towards Potions.
A tapestry on the route from the trophy room hides a passage that comes out near the Charms classroom.
Other tapestries hide a door a little way along the fireworks corridor and an opening Filch steps through.
A passage behind a big fourth-floor mirror was roomy enough to practise jinxes, but is reported blocked by a collapse.
From the Room of Requirement refuge a small corner cupboard opens on a long, steep, torchlit stair with unexpected bends, ending at a wall on the fifth floor that night.
That wall melts away when pushed, reseals at once and opens again from the corridor; its destination is reported to change daily.
May 1998: the stair behind one tapestry is flattened into a chute, and its lower tapestry is turned to stone.

conflicts.text: After the two-floor shortcut, Harry and Moody climb to its top and walk to Moody's office (B04-150). That suggests the office is on the fourth floor, whereas it is stated to be on the third (B05-055).

open: The text rarely says which tapestries belong to which stairs, so most entrances and exits must be placed by the modeller.

gryffindor-tower.summary: Gryffindor Tower is the round tower holding the Gryffindor common room and dormitories. It is entered on the seventh floor, the highest floor the books number, through a portrait at the end of a dead-end corridor, and everything above that level lies inside the tower. Its windows face the side of the grounds with Hagrid's cabin, the Forest edge and the lakeside beech. Its height is never stated. A 1998 battle plan names it with Ravenclaw and Astronomy as the three highest towers, and only Astronomy is known to be higher. Counting dormitories gives the modelling figure. The top room stands at the head of a stair with other dormitory doors below it, and a year group seems to keep one room for its whole school career. One room per level for seven years puts the top floor at the fourteenth, which is 15 storeys counting the ground floor. The strict minimum from the text alone is the ninth floor, and a single shared stack for boys and girls would reach the twenty-first. Treat 14 as an estimate, not canon.

facts.text: The entrance is on the seventh floor, the eighth storey counted from the ground: six floors above the head of the marble staircase, seven staircases up in all.
No floor above the seventh is named in any book, so the dormitories lie inside the tower, above the numbered floors of the castle.
facts.because: A search of all seven books finds no eighth floor or higher. The North Tower and Headmaster's stairs also start from the seventh floor.

facts.text: Tower windows overlook the lawn, the Whomping Willow, the lakeside beech, Hagrid's cabin and the Forest edge.
The Tower stands on an outer edge of the castle, with a clear drop from its upper windows to the foot of the walls.
facts.because: From a dormitory sill Harry looks straight down into the shadows at the castle's foot, and no roof or wing is mentioned in between.

facts.text: The tower is circular in plan, though no outside description of it exists.
facts.because: The common room and top dormitory are both called circular, the stairs are spiral, and new pupils deduce a tower from the spiral stair.

facts.text: Pupils on the grounds bewitched snowballs to fly up and strike its windows in 1995.
From the Entrance Hall the way climbs the marble staircase, then portrait-lined corridors, narrower stone stairs, and doors hidden behind tapestries and sliding panels.
Short cuts start behind a second-floor tapestry and on the third floor; one taken after a blocked fourth-floor door reached the portrait within five minutes at a run.
The last stretch passes a stair top with a statue of Lachlan the Lanky, a corner window towards Hagrid's cabin, then a corridor with a wall noticeboard.
No book gives the Tower's height, its number of levels or its number of steps. Every height figure here is derived.
facts.because: No passage counts them. The only count on a dormitory stair is the sixth step of the girls' stair, which measures nothing overall.

facts.text: Rooms stay with a year group: the boys of 1991 took the top room as first-years and still held it in 1996, with only the door sign changing.
facts.because: Same room at the stair's head in 1991, 1992 and 1994, with dormitories below it in 1996. So rooms are not handed up by seniority, and pass to new pupils when a year leaves.

facts.text: Seven year groups with one boys' room and one girls' room each would make 14 dormitories, seven per stair. Only Harry Potter's year is shown to fit this.
facts.because: Seven years are confirmed and all five boys of Harry's year share one room, but no other year's rooms are described.

facts.text: Other dormitories stand below the top room on one shared stair: doors opened along it in 1994, voices rose from rooms below in 1996, and boys of every year use it.
Strict minimum from the text: top floor 9, which is 10 storeys counting the ground floor.
facts.because: The text proves at least two doors below the top room. If they share one level, that is two dormitory levels above the common room: 7 + 2 = 9.

facts.text: A top floor of 10 to 12 means 3 to 5 dormitory levels and 11 to 13 storeys counting the ground floor. It needs two or three rooms sharing a level.
facts.because: Seven rooms stacked 3+3+1 give floor 10, 2+2+2+1 give 11, 2+2+1+1+1 give 12. Round rooms pack badly, so lower rooms would be wedges. If 10 to 12 meant storeys from the ground, the top floor would be 9 to 11.

facts.text: One room to a level gives seven dormitory levels on floors 8 to 14: top floor 14, which is 15 storeys counting the ground floor.
facts.because: 7 + 7 = 14; adding the ground floor gives 15 storeys. Assumes one room per year group on each stair, each filling its own level.

facts.text: A round dormitory cannot contain both spiral stairs side by side, so the stairs must rise outside the room circles.
facts.because: Both stairs already start behind doors in the common-room wall. Assuming rooms 7 m across and stairs 2.5 m across, two shafts would take most of the width at every level.

facts.text: One stack of full-circle rooms would need boys and girls on alternate levels: 14 dormitory levels, top floor 21, which is 22 storeys counting the ground floor.
facts.because: 7 + 14 = 21. Assumes each round room fills its level, so a level can belong to only one stair.

facts.text: Two round stacks side by side, each with its own stair, keep the top floor at 14 but need a plan at least 17 m wide, or two turrets.
facts.because: Assumes a five-bed room 7 m across with 0.75 m walls, so 8.5 m per stack: 2 x 8.5 = 17 m.

facts.text: Top floor 21 looks too high, because the Astronomy Tower would then have to rise above it.
