facts.because: That needs a tower of over 22 storeys, yet its stair is never called long, no landings are mentioned, and fighting at its foot is heard from the top.

facts.text: Best single figure: top floor 14, 15 storeys counting the ground floor. A top floor of 10 is a safe lower limit, not a likely height.
facts.because: Seven levels fit seven year groups and keep the Tower under Astronomy. A larger House could add rooms per level without adding levels. Not stated in the books.

facts.text: At a modest 3.5 m per storey, the top room's floor is about 49 m above the ground floor, and the stair from the common room rises about 25 m, some 120 steps.
facts.because: 14 x 3.5 = 49 m; 7 x 3.5 = 24.5 m; at 0.2 m per step about 120 steps. Storey height and step height are assumptions; the text gives neither.

facts.text: Astronomy must overtop it: with a top floor of 14, the Astronomy ramparts stand at about floor 15 level at least, and higher if Gryffindor Tower has a roof above the top room.
facts.because: Astronomy is the tallest and highest tower. The top room's ceiling is at about floor 15 level, and Astronomy must clear whatever caps Gryffindor Tower.

facts.text: Ravenclaw and Gryffindor are of the same rank, below Astronomy. Neither is stated to be the taller.
facts.because: Kingsley names both among the three highest, and his order is no ranking, since Astronomy, the tallest, comes second.

facts.text: It must overtop the West and North Towers, both of which already rise above the seventh floor, so it cannot stop just above the common room.
facts.because: Neither is among the three highest, yet a flyer climbs from a seventh-floor window to the West Tower top, and the North Tower stair starts on the seventh floor.

conflicts.text: One five-bed room per year on each stair gives 70 beds, but 200 people in Slytherin green at the 1994 final and over 100 exam desks for one year in 1976 imply Houses of about 175 or more.

open: How the boys' and girls' rooms are stacked: two turrets, one stack with alternating levels, or half-round rooms round a shared stair core. Only the top boys' room is known to be a full circle.
Whether the round shaft reaches the ground or springs from the main block near the seventh floor. Counts of 15 storeys are castle floors, not proof of a 15-storey free-standing shaft.
What caps the Tower. No roof is described, nor where the 1998 fighters would stand.

fat-lady-portrait.summary: The Fat Lady portrait is the only entrance to Gryffindor Tower that the books describe. It hangs on the seventh floor at the very end of a corridor that stops there: a large framed oil painting of an extremely fat woman in pink. Given the current password, the painting swings out into the corridor like a door and uncovers a round hole in the wall. The hole is a climb rather than a doorway, passes one person at a time, and opens straight into the common room. The painted occupant acts as the lock: if she is away nobody gets in, and she can refuse or waive the password at will. The canvas was slashed in October 1993, Sir Cadogan's portrait stood in until February 1994, and security trolls then patrolled the corridor.

facts.text: The portrait hangs on the seventh floor at the very end of a corridor that stops there.
The corridor in front is hard-floored and takes moonlight, so it has outside windows along it or close by.
facts.because: Harry finds its floor hard to sit on, and it is described as moonlit at night.

facts.text: A large framed oil painting on canvas of an extremely fat woman in pink hangs over the opening.
It swings out into the corridor on the password, like a door, uncovering a round hole in the wall.
The hole's lower edge sits above floor level: everyone climbs through it, and a short first-year needed a leg up.
facts.because: Every passage has people climbing or scrambling through it, and no step is mentioned.

facts.text: It passes one person at a time, so pupils queue to leave, but adults such as Professor McGonagall get through.
facts.because: A queue forms at it on a school morning, and McGonagall steps out and back through it. No dimension is given.

facts.text: It works from both sides. From inside it is simply pushed open, with no password needed to leave.
Entry needs the current password and the occupant in her frame. When she is away visiting, pupils are locked out.
The occupant judges entry herself: she turned Harry away with a false claim of a change in 1997, and let him in without a password that June.

Passwords named: Caput Draconis, Pig snout, Wattlebird, Fortuna Major, Scurvy cur, Oddsbodikins, Flibbertigibbet, Balderdash, Fairy lights, Banana fritters, Mimbulus mimbletonia, Dilligrout, Baubles, Abstinence, Tapeworm, Quid agis.
31 October 1993: the canvas was slashed, with strips left on the floor. The occupant fled through a fourth-floor landscape and was later found in a second-floor map of Argyllshire.
November 1993 to February 1994: Sir Cadogan's portrait, with his grey pony, replaced her and changed passwords at least twice a day. His own place is a seventh-floor landing.
From February 1994 she was back, restored, with hired security trolls carrying clubs pacing the corridor, still there at Easter.
Christmas 1994: she wore a tinsel hairband and shared her frame with Violet from a downstairs painting, among empty liqueur-chocolate boxes.
She already guarded the entrance in Mrs Weasley's school days and in 1976.

conflicts.text: Her dress is pink silk in most passages and pink satin once in Book 5.

open: Height of the hole and of its lower edge above the corridor floor. Model a raised round opening, not a full-height doorway.

gryffindor-common-room.summary: The Gryffindor common room is a round tower room on the seventh floor, entered by climbing through the portrait hole. It is cosy and shabby but not small: the whole House has packed into it at once. Across the room from the portrait hole are the doors to two separate stairs, boys' and girls', and the noticeboard. The fire, in a brick fireplace with a worn hearthrug, is the room's focus, with the best armchairs round it. The rest is filled with soft, sagging armchairs, a sofa, rickety movable tables, a chest of drawers, a tapestry, two clocks, a lamp and candles. Glazed windows open onto a view of the grounds, Hagrid's cabin and the Forest edge, and owls land on their outside sills. The room is cleaned overnight by house-elves.

facts.text: It is entered directly from the seventh floor through the portrait hole, so it occupies the seventh-floor level of the Tower.
The Defence Against the Dark Arts classroom is four floors below it, which makes that classroom third-floor. The staff room, McGonagall's office and the dungeons also lie below.
facts.because: The text says four floors below; seventh minus four is third.

facts.text: The room is round, called circular in Books 2, 4 and 5 and a tower room.
The whole House has gathered in it at once, in 1992 standing on the furniture, in 1994 waiting up overnight and greeting a new champion.
Fifty people watched a moment at one 1997 party, and it is called crowded or packed on many other nights. Neither sets its limit.
It is wide enough for far corners: in dim light a large boy asleep in a distant chair went unnoticed by someone sure the room was empty.
facts.because: A person in a chair can only be missed like this if the room is well over a few paces across.

facts.text: It should be at least 13 m across, and about 17 m if two dormitory stacks stand on it.
facts.because: Assumes 0.75 m2 a person among furniture. A House of 70 needs 52 m2 (8 m across); a House of 175 needs 131 m2 (13 m across). Over 100 candidates a year, over four Houses and seven years, gives 175. Two 8.5 m stacks need 17 m.

facts.text: Its windows are glazed and can be opened, with sills that take a perching owl. Owls fly in across the room, and a table stands at one window.
The windows overlook the dark grounds, Hagrid's cabin and teaching at the Forest edge, and a low sun over the Forest treetops can be judged from the room.
A fire burns in a grate in a brick fireplace, before a singed, threadbare hearthrug with a hole in it. A lamp and candles add to its light.
Seating is soft, sagging armchairs, some leaking stuffing, the favourites by the fire, plus a sofa with room for a cat beneath it.
Its tables are rickety and lop-sided but portable: one is dragged to a corner, three are spread with one pupil's work, and a small one stands by the fire.
Noticeboards, battered and layered with notices, hang on the far side from the fire.
Other fittings: an old chest of drawers with a low gap beneath it, a wall clock that chimes, a grandfather clock by the door, and a tapestry.
The door to the boys' stair is across the room from the portrait hole. It stands behind anyone facing the fire, with a clear view from it back to the flames.
A separate door leads to the girls' stair, close to the noticeboard: a boy thrown down the slide stopped at the feet of a friend standing there.
facts.because: Harry is at the noticeboard, looks round at the door, and is not said to move before the slide delivers Ron to him.

facts.text: Portrait hole and hearth share one half of the circle; both stair doors and the noticeboard share the other.
facts.because: The boys' door lies opposite both hole and fire, the noticeboard opposite the fire, the girls' door by the noticeboard, and pupils cross the room before dividing.

facts.text: Sound carries from above: the closing of two dormitory doors, early-morning movement, and a yell down the boys' stair are heard from the room. Storms sound louder here than upstairs.
The fire serves as a remote link: a head can appear in the flames to talk, as in 1994 and 1995, and a searching hand reached through in October 1995.
House-elves clear it overnight and can appear in it. From October 1995 only Dobby cleaned the Tower, the others refusing because of hats hidden around the room.
Dated dressings include Dungbombs (1993), party food and banners (1994), practice clutter (1994), an enlarged talking magazine cover on a wall (1996) and careers leaflets (1996).

conflicts.text: The room is called round or circular, yet pupils repeatedly sit in or pull tables into its corners. Recesses or furniture groups would reconcile this; the text does not explain it.

open: The room's diameter and ceiling height, and how far hearth and portrait hole sit from each other on their half of the circle.
The number of windows, and their compass bearing.

gryffindor-boys-dormitory.summary: The boys' dormitories lie up a stone spiral stair behind a door in the common room, with doors opening off the stair. Only one room is described: the top one, at the head of the stair and of the Tower. It is a circular room with five four-poster beds set against the walls, one for each boy of Harry Potter's year. The beds have deep red velvet hangings, with a trunk at each foot and a bedside cabinet or table beside each. High narrow glazed windows look over the lawn, the Whomping Willow, the lakeside beech, Hagrid's cabin and the Forest edge. The same five boys kept this room from 1991 to at least 1996, while the year sign on the door changed. Lower rooms exist but are never seen.

facts.text: The described room stands at the head of the boys' spiral stair and at the top of the Tower.
It is a circular room with a door from the stair, which carried a year sign reading second-years in 1992.
It holds five four-poster beds against the walls, for all five boys of one year.
Allow at least about 7 m across inside.
facts.because: Assumes beds 2.1 m long with heads to the wall and a 0.5 m trunk at each foot: 2 x 2.6 m, plus 1.8 m of central floor, is 7 m.

facts.text: Rooms stay with a year group: the boys of 1991 were still in this room in 1996, and only the door sign changed.
facts.because: The room recurs as their old, familiar room at the stair's head each year, with dormitories below it in 1996.

facts.text: The beds have canopies, posts and closable deep red velvet hangings, called crimson in Book 4.
Each bed has a lockable trunk at its foot and a bedside cabinet or table with a drawer. Headboards and nearby walls take posters and rosettes.
The room also has wardrobes, a long mirror, and a silver water jug with a goblet under a window.
Light comes from a lamp, candles and the moon. No fireplace is mentioned.
The windows are high and narrow, glazed, curtained and rattled by storms. A boy can climb onto a sill, and an owl can get in.
One window is beside Harry's bed and another beside Neville's, which Harry can see from his own bed. Ron's bed is next to Harry's, on his right.
The windows overlook Forest treetops, the Whomping Willow and a lawn. The lakeside beech is directly ahead from Neville's window, with Hagrid's cabin and the Forest edge in view.
A door off the common room opens on a stone spiral stair, cool and quiet, with walls tight enough for a running boy to hit.
The door and stair serve the boys of all years: a first-year in 1992 and a seventh-year in 1995 use them.
Other dormitories lie below the top room: doors opened along the stair in 1994, and pupils were heard in rooms beneath it in 1996.
A shout from the upper rooms carries down the stair and silences the common room.
Another dormitory also has a window on the grounds: a younger boy reports watching the lawn through one in June 1996.
Girls can enter these rooms, unlike the reverse.
Dated damage: Harry's belongings were ransacked in spring 1993, and one side of Ron's hangings was slashed away in February 1994.

conflicts.text: The room is circular, yet in December 1994 a long mirror stands in its corner.

open: The plan, bed count and door positions of every room other than the top one. Do not assume five beds elsewhere.
Whether any bathroom lies inside the Tower. None is described, and the nearest named one is a boys' bathroom on the Room of Requirement corridor.

gryffindor-girls-dormitory.summary: The girls' dormitories lie up a separate stone spiral stair behind their own door in the common room. No interior is ever described, because the narrative never enters them. The stair guards itself: when a boy reaches the sixth step an alarm sounds and the steps merge into a long smooth stone slide that drops him back into the common room. Girls of more than one year ride it down, so several rooms open off it. A window opens to the outside, since books summoned from the Headmaster's study flew straight in through it in 1997.

facts.text: A door of its own off the common room, separate from the boys', leads to the girls' stair and dormitories.
The stair is a stone spiral.
When a boy reaches the sixth step an alarm wails and the steps merge into a long smooth stone slide, which ends on a rug in the common room.
Several rooms open off the stair, and the slide runs some distance.
facts.because: Fourth-year girls and a fifth-year separately ride the slide down, and on an alarm girls come down their stair in nightclothes.

facts.text: Hermione attributes the rule to the founders, who she says trusted boys less. Girls may enter the boys' rooms.
If they share the Tower, no girls' room stands higher than the top boys' room, which is at the top of the Tower.
facts.because: The top boys' room is placed at the top of the Tower. Two turrets could stand level, but the text mentions neither.

facts.text: Hermione's first-year room may be low on the stair: she fetched a book from it in moments in early 1992.
facts.because: The boys barely exchange a look before she is back. This is narrative pace, so a weak hint.

facts.text: A dormitory window opens to the outside: in June 1997 books summoned from the Headmaster's study flew in through it.
The Marauder's Map marks at least one girls' dormitory by name.

open: Everything inside: room shape, bed count, furnishings and how many doors open off the stair. Do not copy the boys' top room without flagging it as assumed.

slytherin-common-room.summary: The Slytherin common room is underground in the dungeons. Coming down the marble staircase, a door on the right leads to stone steps and a passage. The entrance is a concealed stone door in a bare, damp length of wall, which opens to a password. Inside is a long, low room with undressed stone walls and ceiling, round greenish lamps hanging on chains, a fire under an elaborately carved mantelpiece and carved chairs. Harry later says it lies under the lake and that the light is green, but no window is ever described.

facts.text: It lies underground in the dungeons, below the Entrance Hall.
Coming down the marble staircase, a door on the right leads down steps to a passage and on to the common-room wall.
The entrance is a stone door concealed in bare damp wall, sliding open to a password: Pure-blood at Christmas 1992. No handle or portrait marks it.
It is a long, low room under the ground, walled and ceiled in undressed stone, long enough for two boys to sprint its length.
Round greenish lamps hang on chains from the ceiling.
A fire burns under an elaborately carved mantelpiece straight ahead of the entrance, with carved chairs round it and more chairs set back.
Harry tells captors it is under the lake, full of skulls, and that the light is green. His claim was accepted as convincing.
Size it for about 200 people: at least about 150 m2.
facts.because: Two hundred people wore Slytherin green at the 1994 final. If the room takes the whole House as Gryffindor's does, 200 x 0.75 m2 = 150 m2. The per-person area is assumed.

open: Whether it has windows into the lake. The one narrated visit mentions only lamps.
Where the doors to the dormitories are.

slytherin-dormitories.summary: The Slytherin dormitories are in the dungeons, reported by a house-elf and shown on the Marauder's Map, and close enough to the common room for a return trip in about a minute. They are never described.

facts.text: They lie in the dungeons, as Kreacher reports of Draco Malfoy's dormitory in 1997.
They are close to the common room: Malfoy fetched a cutting and came back about a minute later.
facts.because: He leaves to get it and returns a minute later. He may have kept it elsewhere, but no other place is implied.

facts.text: The Marauder's Map shows a Slytherin dormitory.

ravenclaw-tower.summary: Ravenclaw Tower stands in the west of the castle and is named with Astronomy and Gryffindor as one of the three highest towers. It is not the West Tower. A spiral stair, reached on foot from the fifth floor in the one narrated visit, climbs in tight, dizzying circles to a door of plain old wood with no handle or keyhole, only a bronze eagle knocker. The eagle asks a question and the door opens to a well-reasoned answer, not a password. Behind the door lies the common room, with dormitories above it, so the tower must rise well beyond its entrance. Its floor numbers are never given.

facts.text: The Marauder's Map shows Ravenclaws going to a tower in the west of the castle.
It is one of the three highest towers, with Astronomy and Gryffindor, according to the 1998 battle plan.
It stands below Astronomy and level in rank with Gryffindor. Neither is stated to be the taller, and it must overtop the West and North Towers.
facts.because: Astronomy is the highest tower. Kingsley's list is no ranking, since it puts Astronomy second.

facts.text: It is not the West Tower, despite standing in the west.
facts.because: Harry often climbs to the Owlery at the top of West Tower, yet has never been up this stair. Only this one is among the three highest.

facts.text: A spiral stair climbs in tight, dizzying circles to the entrance door.
In May 1998 Harry reached the stair's foot on foot from a fifth-floor corridor. Coming back, the party descended two more floors after the stair and corridors.
The tower holds the common room with dormitories above it, so a House's dormitories rise beyond the door.
facts.because: Footsteps of sleepers above shake the ceiling, and a stair behind a door by the statue leads to their beds.

facts.text: The door is plain old wood with no handle or keyhole, only a bronze knocker shaped like an eagle.
A knock makes the eagle's beak ask a question in a musical voice. A reasoned answer opens the door; after a wrong answer you wait for someone who gets it right.
Force and noise fail: shouting, shaking and loud bangs did not open it in 1998. A teacher from another House got in by answering, and Flitwick had earlier admitted Alecto Carrow.

open: The floor of the stair's foot, the floor of the door, and the tower's plan and diameter. If it mirrors Gryffindor, about seven dormitory levels stand above the common room.

ravenclaw-common-room.summary: The Ravenclaw common room is a wide circular room in Ravenclaw Tower, below the dormitories, and the airiest room Harry has seen at Hogwarts. Graceful arched windows break walls with blue and bronze silk hangings, and by day they show the surrounding mountains. The domed ceiling is painted with stars, echoed by a midnight-blue carpet. Tables, chairs and glass-fronted bookcases furnish it. Opposite the entrance a niche holds a tall white marble statue of Rowena Ravenclaw on a plinth, wearing a carved circlet. Beside the statue a door opens on the stair to the dormitories above.

facts.text: It is wide and circular, and the airiest room Harry has seen at Hogwarts.
Graceful arched windows break walls with blue and bronze silk hangings.
By day the windows would show the surrounding mountains.
The domed ceiling is painted with stars, echoed by a midnight-blue carpet.
Tables, chairs and glass-fronted bookcases furnish the room.
A niche opposite the door holds a tall white marble statue of Rowena Ravenclaw on a plinth a person can climb, with a delicate circlet bearing the House motto.
A door beside the statue leads to a stair and the dormitories above, close enough that running feet make the ceiling tremble.
May 1998: one bookcase front was smashed, and the two Carrows were left hanging in a net under the ceiling.

conflicts.text: The ceiling is star-painted with bronze silks below in one chapter, and described as blue and gold in the next.

open: The room's floor number, diameter and number of windows.

hufflepuff-entrance.summary: The Hufflepuff common room is never seen. The approach is a door to the right of the marble staircase, as you face it from the Entrance Hall, then stone steps down to a broad, torch-lit basement corridor that also leads to the kitchens. Map views place the Hufflepuffs in that basement, close to the kitchens.

facts.text: The way down is a door to the right of the marble staircase seen from the Entrance Hall, which is on the left coming down the stairs. Stone steps lie beyond it.
The steps reach a basement corridor that also serves the kitchens: broad, brightly torch-lit and hung with cheerful food paintings.
The Marauder's Map places Hufflepuffs in a basement close to the kitchens, and Cedric Diggory comes up from their common room into the Entrance Hall.
This door and the Slytherin door lie on opposite sides of the bottom of the marble staircase.
facts.because: Coming down the stairs, the kitchen door is reached by turning left and the Slytherin door is on the right.

open: The common room itself, its entrance, and the dormitories. Nothing is described beyond the corridor.

potions-classroom.summary: The Potions classroom is one of the large dungeons under the castle, one storey below the ground floor, entered off a dim stone passage at the foot of steps from the Entrance Hall. It is colder than the castle above, with a stone floor and pickled animals in glass jars all round the walls. In a normal lesson twenty cauldrons stand among wooden desks or shared tables, with stools for the pupils and a small fire under each cauldron. The teacher's desk and a blackboard stand at the front, a stone basin fed by a gargoyle spout sits in one corner, and an ingredient store cupboard opens from the room. A memory from fifty years before Book 2 shows the same dungeon. It stays the Potions room under Slughorn from 1996, when Snape moves upstairs to teach Defence.

facts.text: A normal 1992 lesson has twenty steaming cauldrons standing among the wooden desks.
The 1996 N.E.W.T. class is twelve pupils at three tables of four.
The room must seat a joint class of about twenty, each with a cauldron, with walking room between lines of desks.
facts.because: Twenty cauldrons in 1992 and twenty brooms for the same two houses in 1991; Umbridge walks between two lines of desks to reach a pupil's cauldron.

facts.text: Allow at least 70 sq m of floor.
facts.because: Twenty pupils at tables of three or four is about six tables. At an assumed 6 sq m per table with stools and cauldrons that is 36 sq m; aisles, teacher's desk and side fittings roughly double it.

facts.text: It is one of the large dungeons, down stone steps from the Entrance Hall, and colder than the castle above.
It lies one storey below the ground floor.
facts.because: The dungeons are eight floors below the seventh floor (B05-C018-P0190), and a single run of stone steps links them to the Entrance Hall.

facts.text: A dim stone passage runs outside, where voices echo and classes queue at a door that creaks open and bangs shut.
A concealed short cut, entered by a door posing as solid wall, runs towards the room.
The floor is stone, and the room is dim enough to have a dark corner where an inspector sits unnoticed at first.
Pickled animals in glass jars stand all round the walls.
A teacher's desk and blackboard stand at the front; pupils use wooden desks or shared tables and stools, with some tables at the back.
Brass scales and ingredient jars stand on the desks, and each cauldron sits over its own small adjustable fire.
A stone basin in one corner takes an icy jet from a gargoyle's mouth, for washing hands and ladles.
An ingredient store cupboard holds unicorn horns, dried herbs and a box of bezoars; a corner cupboard keeps spare textbooks and old scales.
Snape teaches here until 1996, then Slughorn; Snape keeps his dungeon office.
A memory from fifty years before Book 2 shows the same dungeon, torches unlit, with a door that can stand almost closed.
Accidents such as a melted cauldron and spilled potion are cleared by wand and leave no recorded damage.
September 1996: extra cauldrons of finished potions stand near the tables and on the teacher's desk.

open: Layout: the text uses desks, tables, lines and a usual table at the back without giving one plan. Shared tables for three or four, in lines, fit all of it.
Whether the corner cupboard and the ingredient store cupboard are one fixture or two.

defence-classroom.summary: The Defence Against the Dark Arts classroom is a conventional teaching room used by every Defence teacher from 1991. No passage names its floor, but it lies four floors below the Gryffindor common room, which makes it the third floor. Desks stand in rows with chairs and some stools, facing a teacher's desk and a blackboard. There is a back row beside a window, more windows with curtains, a ceiling candelabrum and wall space for pictures. One window shows the top of a ship's sail on the lake. The desks can be swept aside to leave a large clear floor for a whole class to practise. The corridor outside holds a queue, and a side passage opens nearby. The room is separate from the teacher's office: nothing in the text joins them, and pupils reach the office by its own corridor.

facts.text: It is on the third floor, four floors below the seventh-floor common room.
facts.because: B06-C009-P0041 gives four floors below the common room; the Fat Lady's entrance is on the seventh floor (B01-C009-P0200); seven minus four is three.

facts.text: It lies below the fifth floor.
facts.because: During the east-wing diversion that left a swamp on the fifth floor, pupils outside the classroom hear the noise from above and look up at the ceiling.

facts.text: A corridor runs past the door and holds a queue; a side passage with a stone wall opens nearby, with a corner beyond.
One window faces the lake.
facts.because: The top sail of the Durmstrang ship, moored on the lake, shows through it (B04-C029-P0090).

facts.text: In 1995 pupils arrive here ten minutes after the bell at the top of North Tower, by way of the ladder and stairs.
No desk count is given. Desks stand in rows, with at least a front and a back row, and must seat a joint class of about twenty.
facts.because: Rows are named in B02-C006-P0135 and B05-C015-P0112. Twenty is the size of a two-house class elsewhere: twenty brooms and twenty cauldrons.

facts.text: Moody clears the desks with one wand stroke to leave a large open floor in the middle, where the class takes turns.
There are several windows that can be curtained, one beside the back row; winter sun reaches into the room.
A candelabrum hangs from the ceiling; in 1992 it gave way under a swinging pupil.
Furniture: a wooden teacher's desk with a drawer at the front, a blackboard, pupil desks with chairs and some stools, ink bottles and a waste bin.
In 1992 the way in runs from a courtyard side door along a corridor and up one staircase.
The classroom and office are separate rooms; the text describes no door or stair joining them.
facts.because: In 1996 Harry leaves the classroom and runs through other corridors to reach the office corridor (B05-C029-P0175 to P0179). Moody offers to take Neville up to his office. Snape teaches here from a dungeon office.

facts.text: The text treats it as one fixed room across teachers, though less directly than it does the office.
facts.because: Each year it is simply the Defence classroom, and in 1996 it is gloomier than usual, which compares it with its earlier self (B06-C009-P0047). Nothing says the post changed rooms.

facts.text: 1991: the room smells strongly of garlic under Quirrell.
1992: pixies wreck it, breaking a window, tearing down pictures and scattering papers.
1996-97 under Snape: curtains drawn, candles for light, and new wall pictures of people suffering curses and injuries.
Dumbledore says that since Voldemort was refused the post no Defence teacher has lasted more than a year. The curse attaches to the job, not to any fitting in the room.

conflicts.text: Floor. Four floors below the common room gives the third. But Harry runs down only the nearest flight of stairs to McGonagall's first-floor door, which suggests the second; one staircase leads up from a courtyard side door, which suggests the first; and Lupin's class walks to the staff room with no stairs mentioned.
Moody offers to take Neville up to his office from beside the classroom, so the office should be higher, yet the explicit floors put both on the third. The office's fourth-floor hints would fit this.

open: research/places.json describes the teacher's office as adjoining this classroom. No passage supports that, so do not model a connecting door or stair.
Use the third floor unless the classroom's position beside the office is settled another way.

transfiguration-classroom.summary: The Transfiguration classroom is McGonagall's teaching room, on an unstated floor above the ground floor. It has pupil desks, a teacher's desk, a blackboard and windows looking down into the grounds, with enough open floor in the middle for spell practice when the room is empty. In 1992 it lay close enough to a corridor of classrooms for her class to run out to an attack there, and that corridor is one corner from the Headmaster's gargoyle. In 1993 pupils struggled to find it after North Tower, and Ron later called it a very long way from Umbridge's office.

facts.text: It stands above ground level, with a window looking down on a tree in the grounds, close enough to watch a pupil's hand gestures.
facts.because: Pupils stare down from the window at Malfoy under a tree below and can make out what he does with his hand (B04-C031-P0027 to P0029).

facts.text: A girls' bathroom lies on the floor below.
It is close to the dark corridor where two victims were found in December 1992.
facts.because: McGonagall and her class come running as soon as the alarm is raised (B02-C011-P0184).

facts.text: In 1992 Harry passes it on his way from Gryffindor Tower to the library.
In 1993 pupils leaving North Tower take so long to find it that they only just arrive on time.
Ron calls the Transfiguration department miles from Umbridge's office.
No desk count is given. It must seat a joint class of about twenty, at desks reaching to seats at the back.
facts.because: Pupils have their own desks and there are back seats. Twenty is the size of a two-house class elsewhere.

facts.text: Emptied at lunchtime in 1995, it gives three pupils open floor in the middle for spell practice.
Teacher's desk, pupil desks and a blackboard readable from the back; a corner has room for an inspector's seat.
Lesson props include a large cage of guinea-fowl, boxes of mice and, by 1996, mirrors for human transfiguration.
Conjured birds in 1996 and an escaped firework dragon in 1996 fly about the room without lasting effect.

open: Floor is not given. Any floor from the first upward fits, provided a girls' bathroom lies on the floor beneath.

charms-classroom.summary: The Charms classroom is Flitwick's teaching room on the Charms corridor, reached from the Entrance Hall by the marble staircase and further corridors. No passage states its floor. Book 1 implies the third, because the corridor ends at a door into the forbidden third-floor corridor. Pupils sit at tables, and objects can be sent flying across the room into a box on the far side. The room has a chandelier, windows overlooking the front drive, a large cabinet that stores practice cushions, and a teacher's desk that Flitwick can see over only from a pile of books.

facts.text: It is probably on the third floor.
facts.because: The Charms corridor ends at a locked door that opens straight into the forbidden third-floor corridor (B01-C009-P0182 to P0196), and pupils are near the classroom when they enter that corridor.

facts.text: From the Entrance Hall the way goes up the marble staircase and along corridors.
A tapestry-hidden passage comes out near it, and pupils count it as a very long way from the trophy room.
A window overlooks the front drive and the way into the castle.
An empty classroom lies further along the same corridor.
No table count is given. It must seat a joint class of about twenty, each pupil in 1995 with a stack of cushions.
facts.because: Twenty is the size of a two-house class elsewhere. Pupils work at tables, one kept by three friends at the very back.

facts.text: Objects cross the whole room: pupils Banish cushions into a box on the far side and Summon things to themselves, and a misfire carries Flitwick past the back table.
Tables for pupils, and a teacher's desk that Flitwick sees over only by standing on a pile of books.
A large cabinet or cupboard stores the practice cushions; board dusters, wastepaper baskets and Lunascopes are about the room.
A chandelier hangs from the ceiling, windows take the rain, and a jet of water or conjured snow can reach the ceiling.
December 1993: live fairies are hung as Christmas lights.
Lessons bring temporary frogs, ravens, walking teacups and false snow; first-year practical exams in 1992 use the teacher's desk.

conflicts.text: Book 1 joins the Charms corridor to the third-floor forbidden corridor, yet the same night treats Charms as very far from the third-floor trophy room, and in Book 4 the way there starts at the top of the marble staircase, which is the first floor.

open: An unnamed first-floor classroom with a chandelier is used at break straight after a Charms lesson. The text does not say it is Flitwick's room, so keep them apart unless the third-floor reading is dropped.

history-of-magic-classroom.summary: The History of Magic classroom is Binns's teaching room, somewhere above the staff room and below Gryffindor Tower; no floor is stated. It has rows of seats at desks, a teacher's desk and chair, a blackboard that the ghost teacher passes through, lamps, and a thick-glassed window with a sliding catch and a narrow outside ledge. Lupin judged it big enough for Patronus practice. The corridor outside has a view over the grounds towards Hagrid's cabin.

facts.text: It lies above the staff room and below Gryffindor Tower.
facts.because: Harry goes downstairs from its corridor to the staff room (B05-C017-P0077) and upstairs from it towards the common room (B03-C012-P0148, P0155).

facts.text: A window in its corridor overlooks the grounds as far as Hagrid's cabin.
It is probably near the second floor.
facts.because: A class one corridor short of the room is beside a side passage leading towards Myrtle's bathroom (B02-C016-P0052, P0056), which Book 4 puts on the second floor.

facts.text: Lupin picks it as large enough for Patronus practice against a Boggart.
No desk count is given. Seats stand in rows, with a way along a row to the window, and must take a joint class of about twenty.
facts.because: Twenty is the size of a two-house class elsewhere.

facts.text: A window of thick glass with a sliding catch opens onto a narrow outside ledge, wide enough for an owl.
Lamps can be lit by wand; left empty, the room is dark and its floor dusty.
A teacher's desk and chair face pupil desks and chairs, and there is a blackboard.
Binns, a ghost, enters and leaves through the blackboard and floats an inch above his chair.
1994: during Patronus lessons a Boggart kept in a large packing case puts out the lamps and chills the room until it is shut away again.

open: Floor is not given. The second floor fits the Book 2 route, but nothing states it.

divination-classroom.summary: The Divination classroom is a round room at the very top of North Tower, which is also Sybill Trelawney's home. The route climbs to the seventh floor, passes Sir Cadogan's landing, follows a corridor, goes up a tight spiral stair to a tiny doorless landing, then up a silver ladder through a circular trapdoor in the landing's ceiling. Inside, no fewer than twenty small round tables are crammed among chintz armchairs and pouffes. Closed curtains, scarf-draped lamps and a perfumed fire keep the room dim, red and stifling, and shelves run all round the curved wall. Ron allows ten minutes for the journey from the Great Hall. From 1996 Firenze teaches on the ground floor because a centaur cannot use the ladder, while Trelawney stays in the castle.

facts.text: The classroom is at the very top of North Tower.
On the seventh floor pupils are already sitting on the spiral stair that leads up to the room.
Seven long staircases from the ground floor reach Sir Cadogan's landing, which is on the seventh floor.
facts.because: B03-C006-P0034 counts the staircases; B03-C014-P0002 names the floor of that landing.

facts.text: Ron says the passage running right from that landing heads south, since a window there shows part of the lake.
From the landing a corridor leads to a narrow, tightly winding spiral stair hung with pictures of crinolined women and sinister monks.
The stair ends at a tiny doorless landing with a sunny window. A circular trapdoor in its ceiling has a brass nameplate and opens from above to lower a silver ladder.
The landing is tiny, yet most of a class crowds onto it, and in exam week the queue runs back down the stair.
Ron allows ten minutes for the climb from the Great Hall, and the text calls the journey long.
The route from the Great Hall is several hundred metres long.
facts.because: Ten minutes is 600 s. About 8 flights at an assumed 20 s each take under 3 minutes; the remaining 7 minutes at an assumed 1 m/s is about 400 m.

facts.text: At least twenty small round tables are crammed into the room.
The room can seat far more than one class.
facts.because: Three friends share one table (B03-C006-P0062). Twenty tables at three each is sixty places, against a joint class of about twenty.

facts.text: Allow at least 9 m across inside.
facts.because: Twenty tables with their chairs at an assumed 3 sq m each, crammed, is 60 sq m, a circle about 9 m wide, before adding hearth and shelves.

facts.text: The room stands above the seventh floor by a whole spiral stair plus a ladder.
facts.because: The stair is long enough to make climbers dizzy (B03-C006-P0049), and the ladder then rises through the landing's ceiling.

facts.text: Hermione doubts a voice from the top of the tower could carry down to the grounds.
The room is circular, with shelves running round the walls, and looks more like a cluttered attic crossed with a tearoom than a classroom.
Windows are normally curtained, but at least one can be opened an inch for air.
Chintz armchairs and fat pouffes crowd the rickety tables, and the furniture blocks any direct path across the room.
Many lamps draped in red scarves give a dim crimson light.
A perfumed fire under a crowded mantelpiece heats a large copper kettle and keeps the room stifling; Trelawney's high-backed winged chair stands beside it.
Shelves hold feathers, candle stubs, worn playing cards, silvery crystal balls and a great many teacups; a solar-system model under glass is kept beneath her chair.
Trelawney lives in this room and seldom leaves it.
For crystal-gazing lessons a glowing ball stands on every table.
After her 1996 dismissal she stays in the castle and pupils visit her upstairs; classes move to classroom eleven, since a centaur cannot use the ladder.

open: The number of storeys between the seventh floor and the room is not given. Allow at least one full storey for the spiral stair, plus the ladder.
The stair is narrow and the room is wide. Decide whether the stair climbs inside a tower of the room's width or in a thinner turret that opens out at the top.

classroom-eleven.summary: Classroom eleven is a ground-floor room along the corridor that leaves the Entrance Hall on the side opposite the Great Hall. Before 1996 it was one of several rarely used rooms, with the neglected air of a storeroom. From March 1996 Firenze teaches Divination there, in a room Dumbledore has turned into an indoor forest clearing.

facts.text: Ground floor, down a corridor that leaves the Entrance Hall on the far side from the Great Hall.
The school numbers its classrooms, and has at least eleven.
facts.because: The name implies a numbered series; rooms one to ten are never listed.

facts.text: No seat count is given. A class sits on the ground among the trees while a centaur stands in the open middle, so it cannot be a small room.
facts.because: The students lean on trunks and boulders, and Firenze stands in a treeless clearing at the centre (B05-C027-P0020).

facts.text: Before 1996 it was seldom used and felt like a cupboard or storeroom. It has windows, a closing door and a ceiling.
The move from North Tower is made because a centaur cannot climb the ladder; Dumbledore says the new teacher prefers lodgings on the ground floor.
From March 1996: springy moss and earth for a floor, trees growing from it with branches across ceiling and windows, green dappled light, boulders and a stump.
Firenze can dim the room to twilight and show stars overhead, and pupils burn herbs on the floor.
A wastepaper basket survives beside the stump, and a school bell rings right outside the door.

open: The text does not say whether Firenze lodges in this room, or whether the forest stays after he shares Divination with Trelawney from 1996.

wand-weighing-room.summary: A classroom on an unstated floor above the ground floor, used once for the Weighing of the Wands in November 1994. The text calls it fairly small, yet with most desks pushed back it leaves a large space in the middle. A cramped broom cupboard lies nearby.

facts.text: A fairly small classroom: with most desks pushed to the back it still leaves a large central space. No desk count is given.
For the event, three desks stand end to end under velvet before the blackboard, with five judges' chairs behind; a photographer cannot get far enough back to frame the very large Madame Maxime.
It is above the Entrance Hall.
facts.because: Harry reaches it from the steps up to the Entrance Hall and later goes down to dinner (B04-C018-P0118, P0205).

facts.text: A nearby door opens on a cramped broom cupboard, dark when shut, with a bucket, boxes and cleaning fluid.

mirror-of-erised-classroom.summary: A disused classroom off a narrow corridor on an upper floor, near a tall suit of armour, where the Mirror of Erised stood for a short time at Christmas 1991. Harry judged himself about five floors above the kitchens, which puts it around the fourth floor.

facts.text: Harry reckons the corridor outside is five floors above the suit of armour near the kitchens.
That puts the room around the fourth floor.
facts.because: The kitchen corridor is one flight of stone steps below the Entrance Hall (B04-C021-P0099), so five floors above it is the fourth floor. This rests on Harry's guess in the dark.

facts.text: No desk count is given: desks and chairs are piled against the walls, a waste-paper basket is upturned, and the mirror against the wall reaches the ceiling.
The door opens off a narrow corridor beside a tall suit of armour; finding it again from the library takes nearly an hour of wandering, including getting lost.
Christmas 1991 only: Dumbledore says the mirror will move to a new home the next day.

unnamed-classrooms.summary: This group gathers classrooms the text does not name. They are not one room. They matter because they show ordinary teaching rooms at many levels: a free ground-floor room for a wet-weather class, several first-floor rooms, a third-floor room beside the one-eyed witch, rooms on the east wing's fifth floor, and others on unstated floors. Typical fittings are desks, chairs, a blackboard, a waste bin, a door that shuts and a window. Many stand empty and unlocked, and pupils and staff borrow them freely.

facts.text: Ground floor: a free classroom takes a Care of Magical Creatures lesson during a 1995 storm.
First floor: an overcrowded room with seats, windows and a chandelier is used at break in 1995; another empty room opens off the corridor from the head of the marble staircase.
First floor, probably: the room holding the wrecked Vanishing Cabinet, directly above Filch's office.
facts.because: Nick has the cabinet crashed in a classroom right over the office, and in 1996 the twins speak of a Vanishing Cabinet on the first floor. Assumes one cabinet, unmoved.

facts.text: Hermione leaves the others on the first floor for her 1994 Muggle Studies exam, so that room is probably on that floor.
facts.because: The text gives only where she turns off (B03-C016-P0053).

facts.text: Third floor: an empty classroom with desks stands to the left of the one-eyed witch statue.
East wing, fifth floor: classrooms lie beyond the corridor flooded in 1996, and Filch punts pupils across to them.
Other rooms are tied to neighbours: one floor above Lockhart's office, further along from Charms, and the last on Slughorn's corridor.
An unlocked classroom with a teacher's desk lies close to the Fat Lady's corridor, so classrooms probably reach the seventh floor.
facts.because: Harry finds it after stepping out of the portrait hole into a deserted corridor; no stairs are mentioned and the floor is not repeated.

facts.text: One corridor in 1992 has classes on both sides, and door after door opens along it.
Spare rooms are plentiful: pupils and staff find free ones at short notice in most years.
facts.because: Couples, Harry's practice sessions and private talks all find empty rooms without planning; Harry tries doors along the first-floor corridor and soon finds one.

facts.text: A large classroom holds first-year written exams and grows swelteringly hot.
One room on the way back from the library has a second door at its far end.
Common fittings seen: desks, chairs, a blackboard, chalk, a bin that clangs, a closing door.
Windows differ by room: some look on the lake, some on the grounds, and one towards the perimeter wall.
A deserted classroom lies on the left of a corridor two staircases below the West Tower stair, on the way to the hospital wing.
May 1998: Snape escapes through a classroom window, leaving a body-shaped hole; Flitwick then casts protective spells from it.

headmasters-office.summary: The Headmaster's office is a round room at the top of a tower, entered from a corridor on the seventh floor. A lone stone gargoyle guards the way: a spoken password moves it aside, the wall behind opens, and a stone spiral stair carries visitors up by itself to an oak door with a griffin knocker. The text calls the room large, yet eight people fill it. It holds an enormous clawed desk, a fireplace on the Floo network, tables of whirring silver instruments, a black cabinet for the Pensieve, a shelf for the Sorting Hat, a glass case for Gryffindor's sword and a golden perch by the door. Portraits of past heads cover the walls almost to the ceiling. Several windows look down over the grounds as far as the Quidditch stadium, and between them they catch both sunrise and sunset. The same room serves every head from Dippet onward. Book 6 fixes the floor, but Books 2 and 4 describe approaches that read as much lower; see the conflicts.

facts.text: A lone stone gargoyle against a seventh-floor corridor wall hides the entrance; the office is a round room at the top of a tower above that corridor.
The gargoyle stands round a corner, halfway along an otherwise empty stretch of corridor; after a year at school, pupils still do not know where it is and see no sign to it.
From the Fat Lady's corridor it takes a few minutes on foot, and from North Tower a walk along corridors; no stairs are mentioned on either route.
Harry tells a visitor it lies round the far side of the castle from the Room of Requirement, yet in 1997 he walks from one towards the other with no stairs mentioned.
A spoken password makes the gargoyle jump aside and the wall behind it part; the wall shuts again behind those who enter.

Passwords used: Sherbet lemon 1992, Cockroach cluster 1995, Fizzing Whizzbee 1995-96, Acid Pops and Toffee eclairs 1996-97. In 1998 the word Dumbledore works, then the displaced gargoyle simply lets people pass.
Behind the wall a stone spiral stair rises by itself in tight circles to a polished oak door bearing a griffin-shaped brass knocker; it can also be climbed on foot.
The office floor stands at least one storey above the corridor, and possibly more.
facts.because: The moving stair makes repeated circles and leaves a first-time rider dizzy (B02-C011-P0196, B05-C022-P0005). No rise is given.

facts.text: Besides the stair, the office has been entered or left by Floo through its fireplace, by Portkey and by phoenix.
The text calls the room large and people walk around it, yet at a 1996 hearing eight people make it read as full; a ninth then joins them.
A small rock island in a distant cave is measured against it: no bigger than this office.
Allow at least 8 m across inside.
facts.because: A circle 8 m wide has 50 sq m. Assumed: 10 for the enormous desk and chairs, 10 for tables, cabinet, hearth and perch, 9 for nine standing people, 20 for circulation.

facts.text: More than one window looks down across the grounds, as far as the distant Quidditch stadium; one has curtains in an old memory, and an outer ledge collects snow.
Between them the windows see dawn over mountains and also sunset, so they face roughly opposite ways.
facts.because: Sunrise over mountains is seen through a window in B05-C037; sunset is seen through a window in B02-C013 and B06-C025.

facts.text: An enormous claw-footed polished desk has a high-backed chair behind it, visitor seating opposite and a rug in front. The room also has a fireplace, lamps, a clock and carpet.
Spindle-legged tables around the room carry delicate silver instruments that whirr and give off puffs of smoke.
Portraits of past heads fill the walls all round, some as high as the ceiling; named subjects include Dippet, Fortescue, Phineas Nigellus, Everard and Dilys Derwent.
From June 1997 Dumbledore's portrait, the largest, hangs directly behind the head's chair and swings forward from a hidden wall cavity.
A shelf behind the desk holds the Sorting Hat; a wall-mounted glass case beside it holds Gryffindor's ruby-hilted sword, with Phineas's portrait next to the case.
Near the door stand the golden perch, with an ash tray beneath it, and a black cabinet with a sliding catch for the shallow stone Pensieve. Another cupboard once held a kettle.
Hermione says Dumbledore kept books taken from the library in his study, and that they later flew out of its window; his private library passes to the school in 1997.
March 1996: a fight overturns the desk, breaks instruments and tables and fills the room with dust. By June it is whole again, until Harry smashes more instruments.
The room passes from Dippet to Dumbledore, McGonagall and Snape. In 1996 it reportedly sealed itself against Umbridge, and Phineas says it admits only the rightful head.
1997: pupils reportedly smash the sword case, and the displayed sword is sent to Gringotts.
May 1998: the gargoyle is knocked lopsided but still speaks, and the portraits empty and later refill.

conflicts.text: Floor of the gargoyle. Book 6 says a seventh-floor corridor, and Book 5 makes it minutes from the Fat Lady. In Book 4 Harry takes the marble stairs, making for the second floor, and is at it five minutes later.

Books 2 and 4 read as well below the seventh floor. In 1992 it is one corner from a corridor whose victims are taken up to the hospital wing. In 1995 the office is one flight of stairs above that wing, which Book 5 puts two floors above the top of the marble staircase, the third floor.

In 1995 Dumbledore says he will take Harry upstairs from the Defence office, but the narration gives only a dark passage before the gargoyle, which reads as a short walk, not four floors of climbing. Harry's 1992 run round the whole second floor, by contrast, mentions no gargoyle.

open: Place the gargoyle on the seventh floor: it is the only passage that names the corridor's own floor, and it fits Book 5. Books 2 and 4 stay unreconciled, and the hospital wing cannot then be one flight below the office.
How far the stair rises, and how far the tower stands above the seventh floor, is not given.

mcgonagall-office.summary: McGonagall's office, also called her study, is a small room on the first floor, reached from the Entrance Hall by the marble staircase and a corridor. It has a large fire in a grate that can join the Floo network, windows that rattle in storms and look out to the Quidditch pitch, a desk with drawers, visitor chairs, a carpet and a tin of biscuits. The first-floor statement comes from Book 1, and everything later fits it except one short walk from Myrtle's bathroom. From the office the hospital wing and Gryffindor Tower are up, and the Great Hall is down. When lessons end, hundreds of pupils can be heard overhead.

facts.text: It is on the first floor.
From the Entrance Hall the way is the marble staircase, then a corridor.
It is upstairs from ground-floor classroom eleven.
The twins say they must take friends down to it from the library.
From the office the hospital wing is up, the Great Hall is down, and more stairs lead on to the Gryffindor common room.
A corridor outside leads to a stair head with a lower landing and a moonlit window; a corridor on the way to Gryffindor overlooks Hagrid's cabin.
Her window shows the Quidditch pitch.
It is called a small room, with a large fire.
Small as it is, it holds at least eight people at once.
facts.because: May 1993: Mr and Mrs Weasley, Dumbledore, McGonagall, Harry, Ron, Ginny and Lockhart (B02-C018-P0001 to P0004).

facts.text: When the bell rings, hundreds of pupils can be heard moving overhead and all around.
Windows rattle in their frames in sleet, and the room can stay chilly despite the fire.
A fire in a grate with a mantelpiece has chairs beside it; ash on the carpet is a concern when pupils arrive through it.
A desk with drawers faces a visitor's chair and carries piles of papers, pamphlets and a tartan tin of Ginger Newts.
She says she is used to keeping the Quidditch Cup in her study.
The door shuts by itself behind a visitor, and voices carry along the corridor.
January 1997: a one-off Floo link brings pupils back through this fireplace.
February 1995: the second-task hostages are reportedly put into an enchanted sleep here.

conflicts.text: First floor in Book 1, but in 1993 the party leaves Myrtle's bathroom and reaches the office moments later along a corridor, with no stairs mentioned. The bathroom is on the second-floor corridor; Hermione once says first floor, which would fit, but Book 4 says second.

snape-office.summary: Snape's office is a stone-floored room in the dungeons, behind a door halfway along a cold passage reached by a narrow stone stair from the Entrance Hall. He keeps it even after moving to teach Defence in 1996. Shelves of hundreds of glass jars holding preserved creatures line the dim walls. It has a desk with a chair opposite, two chairs by a fireplace that takes Floo travel, a corner cupboard of private ingredients, a table and a large wall clock. Crowd noise from the grounds does not reach it, though a scream from the Entrance Hall does.

facts.text: It lies in the dungeons, down a narrow stone stair from the Entrance Hall, one storey below the ground floor.
facts.because: The stair and dungeon location are explicit. The dungeons are eight floors below the seventh floor (B05-C018-P0190), which makes them one storey down.

facts.text: Its door is halfway along a cold passage.
It must be close to the Potions classroom.
facts.because: In 1992 Hermione slips out of a lesson in the confusion, takes ingredients from his stores and is back in time to hide them under her robes (B02-C011-P0040 to P0044).

facts.text: The Marauder's Map shows it in the bottom left-hand corner.
Walking there from the steps leaves crowd noise from the grounds behind entirely; a scream from the Entrance Hall still reaches it.
Fleeing it in 1996, Harry stops only after putting three floors between himself and Snape.
Shelves carry hundreds of glass jars of animal and plant parts in coloured potions.
Five people meet here in September 1992; in 1996 a staggering pupil covers several steps before hitting the shelves.
The floor is stone and the room is dim, lit by firelight, candles or torches.
A desk with a chair opposite, two chairs by the fire, a table and a large wall clock.
The fireplace works for Floo travel, with powder in a jar nearby; Lupin arrives through it in 1994.
A corner cupboard holds his private ingredients, separate from the classroom store.
Specimens named: a large slimy thing in green liquid behind the desk, a dead frog in purple liquid, an eel, and a jar of cockroaches.
Snape says the office is sealed by a spell only a wizard can break, yet stores vanish from it in 1992-95.
1996: the Pensieve stands on the desk or a shelf during Occlumency lessons.
May 1997: cobwebbed boxes of old punishment cards pile up on the table.
From 1996 he teaches floors above but does not give up this room.

defence-office.summary: The Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher's office is one room that the text says served Lockhart, Lupin, the false Moody and Umbridge in turn, with only the contents changing. Its last stated floor is the third, though Book 2 once sends Harry along the second-floor corridor to it and a Book 4 route reads as the fourth. It is a separate room from the Defence classroom, reached from the marble staircase by its own corridor, which has a large suit of armour and a recess with a stone bust. The room has one lockable door, a window with a sill, a distant view of the Quidditch goalposts and the grounds, a stone floor, a hearth on the Floo network and a desk with drawers. It is a fair size: fourteen people stood in it at once in 1996, and a very large tank fitted in one corner. From 1996 Snape keeps his dungeon office, and the text never returns to this room.

facts.text: The latest explicit statement, in 1995, puts the office on the third floor.
Book 2's routes agree with the third floor, one level above the second-floor attack corridor.
facts.because: Lockhart calls the office just upstairs from that corridor (B02-C009-P0010), and pupils march him down the nearest stairs to it (B02-C016-P0169).

facts.text: An empty classroom lies one floor above it.
The way in goes up the marble staircase, past its first landing, then along a corridor; leaving, one landing down is still above the marble staircase.
It may lie near the Charms corridor.
facts.because: In 1994 Moody leaves a classroom beside that corridor and walks Harry to the office with no stairs mentioned (B04-C020-P0038 to P0043).

facts.text: Its corridor has a large suit of armour, a recess with a muttering stone bust on a column, and another way round by a swivelling staircase.
From the window the Quidditch pitch is visible far off: goalposts and play can be followed until dark, but individual players are hard to make out.
The window also overlooks the grounds; pupils say they saw two friends crossing towards the Forest from it.
Screams from the distant pitch can be heard inside on a June night.
The text states that this one room served Lockhart, Lupin, the false Moody and Umbridge, and speaks of teachers living in it.
It holds at least fourteen people at once.
facts.because: June 1996: Umbridge, Harry, Hermione, Malfoy, Millicent Bulstrode, four captives, four captors, then Snape (B05-C032-P0158 to P0171).

facts.text: In 1992 eight people gather around the desk, some in chairs; in 1993 a very large water tank fits in one corner.
One door with a key lock opens on the corridor. A window with a sill opens to the outside. The floor is stone, carpeted by 1996.
A desk with drawers stays through every occupant; a hearth has a grate, stacked logs and a small box of Floo powder.
1992-93 Lockhart: many candles and walls covered in countless framed photographs of himself, with a life-size poster behind the door.
1993-94 Lupin: kettle, tea things and Dark creatures kept for lessons in cages or tanks.
Lupin says he would keep a Boggart in a cupboard under his desk and spend full-moon nights curled up in the office.
1994-95 false Moody: Sneakoscope on the desk, Secrecy Sensor on a corner table, Foe-Glass on the wall, and a large trunk with seven keyholes under the window.
Moody says his Sneakoscope senses trouble about a mile off and that figures in the Foe-Glass sharpen as enemies near.
The trunk's seventh lock opens on a pit-like space ten feet deep holding the real Moody. It is inside the trunk, not a cellar.
June 1995: Dumbledore blasts the door to splinters.
1995-96 Umbridge: lace cloths, doilies, vases of dried flowers, plates of moving kittens, a chintz armchair, a small table and a block reading HEADMISTRESS.
Spring 1996: brooms chained to an iron peg behind the desk burst through the door, which Filch replaces; Nifflers then wreck the room, put in by the window.
Umbridge says hers is the one unwatched fire in the school, that sensing spells guard her doorway, and that the office has a mirror.
The text is silent on this room after 1996: Snape keeps his dungeon office while teaching Defence.
facts.because: B06-C024-P0144 says he did not vacate the dungeon office; no later scene uses this room.

conflicts.text: Second or third floor. In 1992 Harry walks the second-floor corridor to the office, but in 1995 it is on the third floor, and Book 2's own routes put it one level above the second-floor attack corridor.

Book 5 pulls both ways. Noise is heard several floors below the office, which needs a high floor; yet one floor down fireworks fill the corridors and some escape towards the second floor, which suits an office on the second or fourth floor, not the third.

A fourth-floor reading also exists. In January 1995 Moody and Harry climb the shortcut stair to its top, one floor below the fifth-floor Prefects' bathroom, and walk straight to the office door. Moody's 'up to my office' from the third-floor classroom and the Book 5 fireworks both fit it.
In 1995 Pomfrey is asked to come down to this office from the hospital wing, so the wing is higher. Book 5 puts the wing on the third floor, which would make the office lower than third.

open: Use the third floor: it is the latest explicit statement and Book 2's routes support it. The single second-floor line and the fourth-floor hints stay unexplained.
The text never says where Quirrell or the Defence teachers of 1996-98 had offices, so do not assume this room before 1992 or after 1996.

filch-office.summary: Filch's office is a dingy, windowless room with a low ceiling, directly below a classroom. A single oil lamp hangs from the ceiling, filing cabinets stand around the walls, and polished chains and manacles hang behind the desk. No floor is stated. Book 2 puts it right under the room where the Vanishing Cabinet crashed, and Book 5 puts that cabinet on the first floor, which suggests the ground floor.

facts.text: The room is dingy and windowless with a low ceiling, lit by one oil lamp hanging from it, and it smells faintly of fried fish.
A classroom lies directly above: a cabinet crashed there shakes the lamp.
It is probably on the ground floor.
facts.because: The wrecked cabinet lay right over the office (B02-C008-P0061, P0062). Book 5 places a Vanishing Cabinet on the first floor (B05-C028-P0025), and Book 6 calls it broken and long unused. Assumes one cabinet, unmoved.

facts.text: It is downstairs from a tapestried corridor with a window; a corridor leads from it to stairs going back up.
Wooden filing cabinets stand around the walls, with folders under pupils' names and a whole drawer for the Weasley twins.
Polished chains and manacles hang on the wall behind the desk; the desk has drawers, a quill pot and a moth-eaten chair beside it.
A cabinet drawer labelled for dangerous confiscations once held the Marauder's Map; Filch says he keeps the chains oiled.
Dumbledore says the list of banned items, about 437 by 1994, can be read here, and by 1995 it is fastened to the office door.

open: The floor is inferred from one cabinet remark. If that cabinet moved between 1992 and 1996, the office could be on another floor.

flitwick-office.summary: Flitwick's office is a room on the seventh floor, far above his Charms classroom. Its window is the thirteenth to the right of the West Tower, and it can be picked out from the lake shore. In June 1994 it served as a locked cell.

facts.text: Dumbledore puts it on the seventh floor, at the thirteenth window to the right of the West Tower; Pomfrey says the prisoner is upstairs from the hospital wing.
The window faces the lake side of the castle, to the right of the West Tower as seen from the shore.
facts.because: From the lake shore Harry counts the windows to the right of the tower and then flies straight there (B03-C021-P0315, P0323). If Ron is right that the lake is south, this facade faces south with the West Tower at its west end, which suits the tower's name.

facts.text: The window lies at least about 40 m along the facade from the West Tower.
facts.because: Thirteen windows at an assumed 3 m spacing is 39 m. A modeller should not squeeze thirteen window bays into a short wall.

facts.text: The locked glazed window opens just wide enough for a thin adult to squeeze out; the room has a chair and a door that locks. The text gives no room size.

slughorn-office.summary: Slughorn's office from 1996 is a room up the marble staircase, on a corridor of classrooms and below the hospital wing; no floor is stated. It is much larger than an ordinary teacher's study, whether by building or by magic. For the Christmas party of 1996 it is hung like a tent and packed with guests. In everyday use it is overheated and crowded with armchairs, low tables and a drinks table.

facts.text: It is reached by going up the marble staircase from the Entrance Hall.
Harry says Ron was brought up from here to the hospital wing, so the wing is higher.
It is probably on the first or second floor.
facts.because: It is above the Entrance Hall and below the hospital wing, which Book 5 puts two floors above the top of the marble staircase, the third floor.

facts.text: It opens on a corridor of classroom doors, with one last classroom beyond it and a distant corner.
It is far bigger than an ordinary teacher's study; the text leaves open whether it was built so or magically enlarged.
At the party it is crowded and stuffy, yet singing comes from a distant corner. No head count is given.
Everyday contents: armchairs, a tasselled footstool, a drinks table, a low table and a potion kit, in a very warm room; a gramophone is heard, not seen.
December 1996: emerald, crimson and gold hangings cover walls and ceiling like a vast tent, and a golden lamp of live fairies hangs at the centre.
A memory of Riddle's school days shows a Slughorn's office with a winged armchair, velvet pouffe, a desk with a golden clock, and seats for half a dozen boys.

open: The text calls both rooms Slughorn's office but does not say the 1940s room and the 1996 room are the same.

hooch-office.summary: Madam Hooch has an office that can be locked, where the Bludgers are kept between practices. Nothing else is known of it.

facts.text: Wood says the Bludgers have been locked in her office since the last practice.

open: Floor, size and whether it is in the castle or near the pitch are all unknown.

staff-room.summary: The staff room is a long, large, panelled room shared by the teachers, on the ground floor by inference. Its door, flanked by two talking stone gargoyles by 1995, opens on a corridor that pupils use to reach a courtyard. Dark wooden chairs, old and mismatched, fill it, with a fire, a low armchair and, at the far end, an old wardrobe for spare robes. A class of pupils can stand around its walls with space to spare.

facts.text: It is on the ground floor.
facts.because: The corridor outside carries a crowd straight out into a courtyard (B05-C017-P0104), and Snape heads for it from the Entrance Hall (B01-C016-P0073).

facts.text: Pupils go down to it from the common room, the hospital wing and the History of Magic corridor.
It is described as large and long.
It holds the teaching staff at an emergency meeting, or a whole class standing against its walls with a clear stretch before the wardrobe.
facts.because: All teachers are summoned here in 1993, and in 1993 a Defence class backs against the walls, leaving one pupil alone by the wardrobe (B03-C007-P0145).

facts.text: From inside, hundreds of people are heard moving overhead during the 1993 evacuation.
The walls are panelled, and the door can be shut.
Dark wooden chairs, old and mismatched, fill the room, including a low armchair.
A fire burns here; the tale of Binns's death puts an armchair in front of it.
An ugly old wardrobe of teachers' spare robes stands at the far end, close enough to bang against the wall.
By 1995 two stone gargoyles flank the door and talk to callers; teachers open it from inside. The door also opens to a push.
In 1993 Lupin's class reaches it from the Defence classroom by two corridors, past a broom cupboard.
May 1998: both gargoyles are smashed by a jinx through a broken window; their fragments still stir and speak.

conflicts.text: The ground-floor reading clashes with Lupin's route: his class walks here from the Defence classroom, implied to be on the third floor, by two corridors with no stairs mentioned.

open: No window is described in the room.

library.summary: The school library, a very large upstairs collection entered by a door from a corridor. No floor is stated. Routes climb the marble staircase and go on, it lies above McGonagall's first-floor study, and Harry's guess of five floors above the kitchens puts a nearby corridor at about the fourth floor. The books run to the tens of thousands, the shelves to the thousands and the narrow rows to the hundreds. At an assumed 1.5 m per row, 200 rows need 300 m of row spacing, so this is a hall of at least about 1,500 m² or a suite of rooms, not one ordinary room. Read literally, the same counts keep the collection under 100,000 books and 10,000 shelves, which suits rows about 3 to 4 m long holding thick volumes. Shelves are tall enough to hide people. Tables with lamps stand by mullioned windows and among the shelves at the back. The Restricted Section lies at the far back behind a rope. The library closes in the evening, and its librarian polices noise and food.

facts.text: The books number in the tens of thousands, the shelves in the thousands and the narrow rows in the hundreds.
Limits for any model: 20,000 to 99,999 books, 2,000 to 9,999 shelves, 200 to 999 rows.
facts.because: Each phrase is a plural of its unit, so it means at least two and fewer than ten: tens of thousands stops short of 100,000, thousands short of 10,000, hundreds short of 1,000.

facts.text: Row spacing alone comes to at least 300 m, far beyond any one ordinary room.
facts.because: At an assumed narrow 1.5 m per row (0.9 m walkway plus a 0.6 m double-sided case), 200 rows × 1.5 m = 300 m. Even at a very tight 1.2 m it is 240 m. At 300 rows it is 450 m.

facts.text: The whole library needs at least about 1,500 m²: for example one hall about 50 m by 30 m, or three rooms 50 m by 10 m.
facts.because: 200 rows × 1.5 m × 3 to 4 m = 900 to 1,200 m² of shelving floor. Folded into six banks of 33 rows with 2 m cross-aisles: 50 m deep and 28 to 34 m wide. Tables and the Restricted Section are extra. Check: a 3-minute fetch at 1.2 m/s is 216 m; if half goes on finding the book, about 50 m each way. A minimum, not a measurement.

facts.text: The counts allow 2 to 50 books per shelf on average; at a realistic 25 to 30, only about 3,300 to 4,000 shelves fit under the book limit.
facts.because: 20,000 ÷ 9,999 = 2 and 99,999 ÷ 2,000 = 50. Taking one shelf as one 1 m board of ordinary books: 99,999 ÷ 30 = 3,333 and 99,999 ÷ 25 = 4,000.

facts.text: Rows cannot be long: about 4 m is the limit at six shelves high with shelving both sides, or 200 rows pass 10,000 shelves.
facts.because: Each metre of such a row adds 2 × 6 = 12 shelves (1 m shelf assumed). 200 rows × 4 m × 12 = 9,600 shelves, just under the ceiling. With shelves on one side only the limit doubles to about 8 m. The counts allow 2 to 50 shelves per row in all (2,000 ÷ 999 and 9,999 ÷ 200).

facts.text: Rows 3 to 4 m long fit all three counts only at about 10 to 14 books per shelf, so stock must be thick volumes or shelves part-empty.
facts.because: 200 rows × 3 to 4 m × 12 shelves per metre = 7,200 to 9,600 shelves. 99,999 ÷ 9,600 = 10.4 and 99,999 ÷ 7,200 = 13.9. At 30 books a shelf those rows would hold 216,000 to 288,000 books, over twice the ceiling. The text does show large, heavy volumes (B01-080, B02-061).

facts.text: Long full rows overshoot badly: 200 rows 20 m long would hold about 1.4 million books.
facts.because: 200 × 20 m × 12 shelves per metre = 48,000 shelves, almost five times the ceiling. At 30 books each that is 1.44 million, 14 times the ceiling.

facts.text: Rows are at least about 3 m long, since six or seven girls lurk together in one.
facts.because: Single file in a narrow row at an assumed 0.5 m each: 6 to 7 × 0.5 m = 3 to 3.5 m.

facts.text: Shelving at the back runs in long, tall ranks, and elsewhere the shelves are called lofty.
Fetching one restricted book took the librarian several minutes.
One reading area holds at least sixteen people in sight of one another.
facts.because: Fourteen witnesses saw a pupil jinxed from behind as she worked: fourteen, plus the victim and her attacker (B05-120).

facts.text: No floor is stated; the best single clue is about the fourth floor.
facts.because: Just after fleeing the library, with no stairs narrated, Harry reckons he is five floors over the kitchens (B01-081). The kitchens lie one flight below the Entrance Hall (B04-106), so five floors up is the fourth floor. It is a panicked guess about a corridor, not the library itself.

facts.text: It lies above McGonagall's first-floor study: pupils are taken down from it to her.
It is reached up the marble staircase and on through corridors, and left by corridor and stairs down to the Entrance Hall.
It is about five minutes' walk from Myrtle's bathroom and within fifteen of Gryffindor, and Harry judges it nearer the Room of Requirement than the dormitories.
The only entrance mentioned is one door from a corridor.
It shuts at night, with the lamps out by eight in February 1995, yet Harry twice walked in after hours and no lock is described.
Talk is kept to whispers and food is banned; in 1996 enchanted books drove two offenders out.
Windows are mullioned and show open sky, and one faces a reader seated at a table.
Shelves stand taller than the pupils, who spy and listen unseen behind them, and books rise above seated readers.
facts.because: Pupils repeatedly hide behind shelves while standing or moving about (B02-079, B04-073, B04-105), someone stays unseen close to a table until the librarian rounds a corner (B06-079), and Ron looks upward at the books around him (NEW-inner-5).

facts.text: Tables and desks stand near windows and deep among the shelves at the back, and the librarian stamps loans several shelves from them.
Lamps stand at the tables and candles can be moved about; at night it is pitch dark and needs a carried lamp or wand.
An Invisibility section stands towards the back, and Hermione reports a whole collection of old Daily Prophets.
Dumbledore is reported to have taken every book on Horcruxes off the shelves at some unknown date. His private library went to Hogwarts in 1997; nothing says it joined this collection.

conflicts.text: Shelving at the back reads as long ranks (B02-079), while the counts cap a row at about 4 m (B01-073, by the estimates above). The two fit if short rows stand end to end across cross-aisles, making lines of 30 m or more; the text does not say so.

open: One great room or a suite: the text mentions only a back, corners and one door.
Whether a shelf means one board, as assumed here, or a whole bookcase. As bookcases six boards high, even 2,000 could hold only about 8 books per board, so the board reading fits better.
How the height of tall shelves is reached: ladders and upper galleries are not mentioned.
Whether a row means a walkway lined on both sides, as assumed here (Ron walks down one and girls lurk in one), or a single face of shelving.

restricted-section.summary: The restricted part of the library, at its very back, marked off from the rest only by a rope low enough to step over. It holds books of powerful Dark Magic, and a signed note from a teacher is needed to read or borrow them. The bar is a rule, not a lock: no magical barrier is described. Its size is not given, but the librarian needed several minutes to fetch a book from it and one pupil claims to have gone right through it. Volumes include old works with peeling gilt titles in unknown languages, some with no title, and large heavy books that cry out when handled.

facts.text: It lies at the very back of the library.
Only a rope separates it from the other shelves, low enough to step over.
A fetch from it took the librarian several minutes, so it stands well away from where she took the note.
facts.because: She walks off among the tall shelves and is gone several minutes (NEW-inner-1), though some of that time went on finding the book.

facts.text: It is much smaller than the main stacks, since one pupil reports going right through it.
