facts.because: Hermione claims to have been through all of it for one subject (B06-101), whereas three pupils searching the open shelves for a fortnight made little headway (B01-073).

facts.text: It holds books of powerful Dark Magic, read by older pupils in advanced Defence.
Titles are in peeling, faded gold, in languages Harry cannot read, or absent; one book has a stain resembling blood.
Known volumes include a heavy black-and-silver book on a bottom shelf and the large, mouldy Moste Potente Potions.
Reading or borrowing needs a teacher's signed note, which the librarian inspects before fetching the book herself.
The bar is a rule, not a lock.
facts.because: Harry simply stepped over the rope at night and took a book down (B01-079). The alarm was the book itself (B01-080).

facts.text: Some books react aloud: one screams without stopping when opened, another wails when slammed shut.
At night its shelves are unlit, and a reader must carry a lamp in.

open: How many rows or shelves the section takes up is unstated.

hospital-wing.summary: The school's hospital on an upper floor: a ward with a distinct far end, also called a dormitory, off a corridor. Double doors open at the near end, and Madam Pomfrey's office opens off the far end. Beds with white linen and feather mattresses stand in lines with others opposite, so the ward has two sides and a way down the middle. High bed curtains and movable screens give privacy, and each bed has a cabinet or table and room for chairs. Windows with sills and curtains look outside, and the corridor beyond overlooks the Quidditch pitch and the lake. At least eight beds are implied, and six visitors at a bed is the matron's limit. The text never numbers the floor, and journeys disagree, though floors lie above and below it. The one counted journey, two floors down to the first-floor head of the marble staircase, gives the third floor. One Book 2 journey implies the first floor and one Book 6 journey the seventh or higher. Most journeys fit a floor above the second and below the seventh, and the third floor is the best-supported reading, but it is not settled.

facts.text: The only journey that counts floors puts the ward on the third floor.
facts.because: From the corridor outside the ward Harry goes two floors down to the top of the marble staircase, then along the first-floor corridor (B05-268). Two floors above the first floor is the third.

facts.text: Floors lie above and below it: at the bell, which sounds just outside, pupils are heard in corridors over and under the ward.
The way up from the Entrance Hall is the marble staircase, portrait-lined corridors and then more flights of stairs.
It lies above the Great Hall, staff room, dungeons, Slughorn's room, McGonagall's first-floor study and the corridor of the December 1992 attack: people go up to it from all of them.
A single flight of stairs is mentioned between the Headmaster's office and the ward.
From the West Tower top, with ten minutes allowed, the way down is a tight spiral, two more staircases and a new corridor.
A distant roar on the night Sirius left the seventh-floor office came from above the ward.
Windows in the corridor outside show the Quidditch pitch and the lake.
Match commentary from the pitch can be heard from a bed.
Only one ward is described, also called a dormitory, with beds near the doors and others at a distinct far end.
The entrance is a pair of doors opening from a corridor.
Beds stand on both sides with a way down the middle.
facts.because: One bed faces others across the ward (B05-298), and people walk up the ward past beds to a far one (B03-138, B06-191).

facts.text: Windows have sills and curtains, show the sky, and let moonlight fall across beds.
Madam Pomfrey's office has its own door at the far end of the ward.
She appears to sleep beyond that door.
facts.because: She retires through it at bedtime (B06-116) and is fetched from that direction at night in her nightclothes (B02-069).

facts.text: At least four beds stand in one line, and at least eight if both sides match; the text never counts them.
facts.because: Colin's bed is three beds from Harry's (B02-069), and more beds stand opposite (B05-298).

facts.text: It held at least four long-stay patients at once in 1993.
facts.because: Colin, Justin, Penelope and Hermione were all petrified by spring 1993, and none is cured before the book's end.

facts.text: The matron's limit is six visitors at one bed.
Beds have white linen sheets, pillows and feather mattresses, and each has a table or cabinet with room for a water jug, books and gifts.
High curtains and movable screens can be drawn round a bed, and they block the view across the ward.
Lamps light the ward; at bedtime they dim and the matron closes all the curtains with one wave of her wand.
Chairs are pulled up around beds, the matron conjures more when needed, and the ward keeps bedpans.
The door can be locked by wand, and the matron can bar visitors altogether, as in spring 1993.
House-elves arrive and vanish inside the ward with a crack.

conflicts.text: Third floor against first floor. The one counted journey gives the third floor (B05-268). But in 1993, leaving the ward for Gryffindor, the boys climb to the floor above and find the corridor outside Myrtle's bathroom, narrated as the second floor (B02-097, B02-046). In 1997 three people walk along the corridor to the marble staircase with no stairs mentioned (B06-112), and in 1993 that staircase is the only climb named on the way from the pitch (B02-110). These suggest the first floor.

Book 2 disagrees with itself: from Myrtle's bathroom the ward is up (B02-095), yet from the ward Myrtle's corridor is up (B02-097). McGonagall's first-floor study also has the ward above it (B02-159, B01-103), against a first-floor ward.

Seventh floor or higher. In 1997 Harry and Ron leave the ward going down to breakfast and turn into a seventh-floor corridor (B06-118), with no detour upwards stated. That sets the ward at or above the seventh floor, against a roar from a seventh-floor office coming from above it (B03-157, B03-139).

Above the Defence office. In 1995 the matron is told to come down to it and later to go down to it (NEW-inner-2). That office is stated to be on the third floor (B05-055), which would put the ward on the fourth floor or higher, not the third.

One flight below the Headmaster's office (B04-234). That office's gargoyle is approached towards the second floor in Book 4 (B04-188) and stands on the seventh floor in Book 6 (B06-035), so this relation fixes no floor. West Tower routes are no firmer: a spiral and two staircases down from the top (B03-156) cannot be turned into a floor count.

Weight of the journeys, not a settled answer: most put the ward above the second floor and below the seventh, floors lie above and below it, and the only journey that counts floors gives the third floor. The third floor is the best-supported reading.

open: Which floor to model: the third is the best-supported reading, not a settled one.
The number of beds and the ward's length are never given.

myrtles-bathroom.summary: A neglected girls' toilet opening off the attack corridor, on the second floor by most evidence, though one character says the first. The door has a brass knob and an Out of Order sign. Inside, one big cracked mirror hangs over a row of stone sinks, the stone floor is damp, stubs of candle give dim light, and wooden cubicles with scratched doors stand in a line, at least four by inference, with Myrtle's at the end. Cubicles are small: three pupils fit in one only with difficulty. The sink in front of Myrtle's cubicle hides the way to the Chamber of Secrets: a copper tap marked with a tiny snake answers Parseltongue, and the sink drops away to expose a pipe big enough for a grown man. Other pupils avoid the room, which Myrtle's tantrums flood. Its floor is disputed: most journeys and both Book 4 statements support the second floor, but this is not settled.

facts.text: Book 4 places it on the second floor, three floors below the fifth-floor Prefects' bathroom.
Its door opens straight off the attack corridor, a few paces past Filch's chair.
It is about five minutes' walk from the library.
From the dungeons the way runs up to the Entrance Hall and on up the marble staircase.
One big mirror, cracked and spotted, hangs over a row of stone sinks with chipped edges.
The floor is stone and usually damp, lit dimly by low candle stubs in holders.
Cubicles have wooden doors, flaking and scratched, and one door hangs off its hinges.
Cubicle doors have working locks with keyholes.
The sinks face the cubicles.
facts.because: Myrtle points to the sink in front of her own toilet, and it is that sink which hides the pipe (B02-139, B02-140).

facts.text: At least four cubicles stand in a line, with Myrtle's at the end.
facts.because: Ron says she was three toilets from their brewing cubicle (B02-130), and hers is the end one (B02-059). Harry also uses a middle one (B02-089).

facts.text: Three pupils fit into one cubicle only with difficulty, and transformed bodies would not fit together at all.
Myrtle's cubicle has a toilet with a cistern, on which she sits, and a bowl she dives into.
The door's sign says Out of Order, and other pupils stay away, which makes it private.
One copper tap on the sink before Myrtle's cubicle bears a tiny engraved snake; spoken Parseltongue makes it glow and spin, and the sink sinks from view.
The pipe exposed beneath that sink is big enough for an adult man to go down.
The sink slid back into place by itself when four people flew up out of the pipe.
It has been out of order because Myrtle's tantrums flood it.
In early 1993 a flood soaked walls and floor, put out the candles and spread under the door.
In late 1992 a cauldron sat on one cubicle's toilet over a portable waterproof fire.
Myrtle travels by pipes: she appears on the Prefects' bathroom taps and says a flush can carry her down to the lake.
Myrtle says she died here fifty years earlier, in the end cubicle.

conflicts.text: First floor against second. Hermione says the first floor (B02-045). Narration takes Harry up the marble staircase to the first floor, up a further flight and round the second floor to the corridor outside this door (B02-046, B02-057). Book 4 says the second floor outright, and three floors below the fifth-floor bathroom (B04-115, B04-145, B04-131).

Lockhart's office supports the first floor. It lies on the second-floor corridor (B02-033), yet it is just upstairs from this corridor (B02-048), and the nearest stairs lead down from it to here (B02-138).
McGonagall's first-floor study is reached moments after leaving the bathroom, with no stairs mentioned (B02-157, B01-103). This is a weak point for the first floor.
Against the hospital wing, Book 2 has it both ways: the ward is up from here (B02-095), yet this corridor is one floor up from the ward (B02-097).

Weight of the journeys, not a settled answer: the narrated climb, both Book 4 statements and the fifth-floor count all support the second floor. The first-floor reading rests on Hermione's remark and on Lockhart's office.

open: The total number of cubicles and sinks is never given.

prefects-bathroom.summary: The prefects' private bathroom on the fifth floor, four doors along to the left of the statue of Boris the Bewildered. It is a large room of white marble lit by a chandelier of candles, with windows hung in long white linen. A rectangular bath the size of a swimming pool lies sunken in the centre of the floor, deep enough that Harry can hardly stand in it, with a diving board and about a hundred golden taps around its edge, each with a jewel of a different colour in the handle. Taps pour hot water with bubbles, foam and scented clouds. One gold-framed painting of a sleeping mermaid hangs on the wall, and a big pile of towels sits in a corner. The door opens to a password and bolts from inside. Prefects and, from 1996, Quidditch captains may use it.

facts.text: It is on the fifth floor, four doors along to the left of the statue of Boris the Bewildered.
Myrtle's toilets lie three floors below it.
The nearest staircase lies along the corridor in the direction away from Gryffindor Tower.
The sunken rectangular bath is the size of a swimming pool.
About a hundred golden taps stand around its edge.
Harry can hardly stand in the deep water, and he swims lengths.
The bath is at least about 15 m by 5 m, in a room of at least about 20 m by 10 m.
facts.because: About 100 taps at an assumed 0.4 m each need 40 m of edge: 2 × (15 + 5) = 40. An assumed 2.5 m of floor all round gives 20 m by 10 m, or 200 m².

facts.text: Walls, floor and bath are white marble, under a chandelier filled with candles.
Windows are hung with long white linen curtains.
A diving board stands at the bath.
Footsteps and loud sounds echo off the marble.
No two tap handles share a jewel colour.
Fluffy white towels are piled in a corner.
The only painting is a gold-framed blonde mermaid asleep on a rock, her hair moving as she snores.
The door opens to a password, Pine-fresh in January 1995, and bolts from inside.
Use is limited to prefects, and a Quidditch captain ranks with them.
Different taps give football-sized pink and blue bubbles, thick white foam, scented purple clouds or bouncing jets.
The bath fills very quickly for its size.
Myrtle appeared sitting on a tap and left up it.

sixth-floor-boys-bathroom.summary: A tiled boys' bathroom on the sixth floor, one floor below the seventh-floor corridor, reached by a staircase and a passage. It has a sink facing a cracked mirror, toilet cubicles with cisterns, a wall lamp and a bin. A duel wrecked and flooded it in May 1997.

facts.text: It is on the sixth floor, reached from the seventh by a marble staircase and a passage.
facts.because: The Map shows it one floor below the seventh-floor corridor, and Harry takes the staircase down to it (B06-152).

facts.text: A flat run from the Room of Requirement to this bathroom took Harry about a minute.
The room is tiled, with a grimy sink facing a cracked mirror, cubicles, cisterns, a wall lamp and a bin.
May 1997: spells shattered the lamp, blew up the bin and smashed a cistern, and water spread across the slippery floor.

open: The text does not say whether this is the cracked-mirror boys' bathroom of B06-130, which Harry visits after Defence; that one is filed separately.

troll-toilets.summary: The girls' toilets where a twelve-foot troll was fought on Hallowe'en 1991: an upstairs room off a side passage, floor not stated. The door has a key in its outer lock. Inside are toilets and sinks fixed to the walls, with metal pipes. The room must clear a twelve-foot troll swinging a club. The text never links it to Myrtle's bathroom.

facts.text: It lies upstairs from the Great Hall, off a passage reached by side corridors; no floor is stated.
It is probably below the third floor.
facts.because: On the corridor before the toilets, Harry says Snape is heading for the third floor (B01-057), which suggests they are still below it. It is a remark, not a statement of floor.

facts.text: It lies at least two floors below the Fat Lady's portrait.
facts.because: Harry and Ron climb two floors before they even start talking, and only then reach the portrait (B01-060).

facts.text: A twelve-foot troll walked through its door and moved around inside, so door and ceiling must clear it unless it stooped.
facts.because: The troll's height is narrated and it enters the room through the doorway (NEW-inner-4).

facts.text: The door has a key in its outer lock; inside are toilets and wall-fixed sinks with taps and metal pipes.
31 October 1991: the troll knocked sinks off the walls, and noise of the fight carried to floors below.

open: Whether this is Myrtle's bathroom or another room: the text never says, and this room's door has a key where Myrtle's has a sign.

other-bathrooms.summary: Other washing places around the castle. This is a group of separate rooms, not one bathroom. Known instances: a boys' bathroom near the Room of Requirement on the seventh floor, a toilet on the fourth floor, several bathrooms on the second floor, a girls' bathroom one floor below Transfiguration, an old tiled boys' bathroom with a cracked mirror, and unlocated toilets. What they share is cubicles, sinks and mirrors, and that Myrtle can turn up in them. Their spread implies washing places on many floors.

facts.text: Bathrooms exist on at least the second, fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh floors.
facts.because: Each floor has a named example: seventh (B05-199), sixth (B06-152), fifth (B04-131), fourth (B05-209), second (B05-239).

facts.text: A boys' bathroom stands along the seventh-floor corridor, to the right of the Room of Requirement.
Montague is reported found jammed in a toilet on the fourth floor.
The second floor has more than one bathroom.
A girls' bathroom lies one floor below the Transfiguration classroom.
An old tiled boys' bathroom, visited after Defence, has a cracked mirror and toilets in cubicles.
Girls' toilets have several cubicles, all occupied at once in one report.
Neville's toad turned up in a corner of some unlocated toilets.
In spring 1993 pupils could use bathrooms only with a teacher.
May 1996: Peeves tore the taps from the second-floor bathrooms and flooded that floor.
Myrtle says she can visit bathrooms other than her own, and is reported appearing in all of them.

seventh-floor-corridor.summary: This seventh-floor corridor holds the entrance to the Room of Requirement. On one side hangs an enormous moving tapestry of Barnabas the Barmy trying to teach trolls ballet. Facing it is a stretch of blank stone wall where the Room's door appears, with a window just beyond the stretch and a man-sized vase at its other end. Further along are a boys' bathroom, niches holding vases, and corners where lookouts can wait. The corridor can be walked to along the seventh floor from the Gryffindor portrait; the Headmaster's gargoyle, on the same floor, is on the far side of the castle. In May 1998 a blast tore away the castle wall along it.

facts.text: The Room's entrance is on the seventh floor, facing the tapestry of Barnabas the Barmy.
The tapestry is enormous and its figures move: trolls in tutus club Barnabas, who is trying to teach them ballet, and a moth-eaten troll pauses to watch passers-by.
Opposite it is a stretch of smooth, blank stone wall, solid to a push or kick when no door is present.
The Room's door appears in that wall when called and vanishes into the stone afterwards, leaving no sign.
A window just beyond the stretch and a man-sized vase at its other end mark the length walked to open the door. The distance is not given.
The corridor runs both ways from the door. To the right lie a niche under an ugly dragon-shaped vase, a boys' bathroom and another corner.
A large blue-and-white vase stands in a niche nearby. Whether it is one of the other two vases is unknown.
Coming round a nearby corner, the tapestry is on your right and the blank wall on your left. The corner gives lookouts somewhere to wait.
It is reached from the Gryffindor portrait by walking along the seventh floor.
The Headmaster's gargoyle is also on the seventh floor, on the far side of the castle, though Umbridge marched Harry there from here within minutes.
A boys' bathroom lies a floor below, on the sixth floor, reached by a stair the text calls marble.
The corridor runs along an outer wall of the castle.
facts.because: It has a window, corridor windows near the refuge stair look down on the castle's foot, and in 1998 a blast here opened it to cold air and a drop. That scene names no floor.

facts.text: June 1997: Darkness Powder filled the corridor with black that no light spell could pierce, while Death Eaters left the Room.
May 1998: an explosion blew away the castle side, leaving stone and wood wreckage. Giant spiders tried to climb in through the hole, and the windows lost their glass.

conflicts.text: Portrait and corridor are both on the seventh floor, yet in 1995 the walk between them passes the top of a final staircase.
A 1997 route from the hospital wing down to breakfast passes through a seventh-floor corridor with this tapestry, which puts the ward at or above the seventh floor unless the route doubled back.

open: Whether the blank stretch backs on to the outer wall. If the window beyond it is in the same wall, nothing ordinary can stand behind the door.

ror-general.summary: The Room of Requirement, also called the Come and Go Room, is a room on the seventh floor that exists only for someone who needs it. To open it you walk three times past a blank stretch of wall, concentrating on what you need. A polished door with a brass handle then appears, and it melts back into stone when the room is left. Inside, the Room supplies what the seeker needs, at any size: it has been a broom cupboard, a room of chamber pots, a practice room for 28, a store as big as a large cathedral and an enormous refuge. It will not supply food and does not show on the Marauder's Map. In 1997 it stayed shut to repeated requests to see what another user was doing.

facts.text: Its concealed entrance is on the seventh floor, in the blank wall facing the Barnabas tapestry.
You walk past the wall three times thinking hard of what you need. A door then appears: highly polished with a brass handle on its first narrated use.
When the last user leaves, the door melts back into stone at once.
Dobby says it can be entered only by someone in real need, comes and goes, and is equipped for what the seeker needs. Few know of it.
Its inside is not tied to its outside: the same stretch of wall has opened on a broom cupboard, a room for 28 and a cathedral-sized store.
facts.because: All three are reached through this one door place, and the store is far taller and larger than any space on the seventh floor could hold.

facts.text: Reported earlier forms include an elf-sized bed with Butterbeer antidotes, extra cleaning supplies and a well-proportioned room of chamber pots that was gone later.
Asking in the wrong words fails: in 1997 repeated requests to see what Malfoy was doing left the wall doorless.
A user can exclude others: the 1998 refuge stayed shut to the Carrows while one defender stayed inside, and Trelawney reports being thrown out in 1997.
It cannot change form while anyone remains inside, so it had to be emptied in 1998 before being asked for a new room.
It can grow in use: the refuge expanded and added hammocks and a bathroom as people arrived.
It does not make food. After about a day and a half of hunger it opened a passage to the Hog's Head instead.
Harry has never seen it on the Marauder's Map, and Hermione suggests it is unplottable.
Closing its door shuts out outside sound completely: a battle fell silent in 1998.
After the 1998 fire its door vanished, and Ron asks whether it still works. The books do not answer.

open: Whether to model the Room as a true room in the castle or as a separate volume behind a door. The text supports a separate volume, but never says so.

ror-da-room.summary: This is the Room of Requirement as Dumbledore's Army used it from October 1995 to spring 1996: a spacious stone-walled room lit by flickering torches, its walls lined with wooden bookcases holding hundreds of books, large silk cushions in place of chairs, and shelves of Dark detectors at the far end. It seats all 28 members on cushions and takes 14 duelling pairs, but it is too tight for everyone to practise Stunning at once. The door has a working key. Its contents shift from meeting to meeting.

facts.text: It is a spacious room seating all 28 members on large silk cushions, with room for them to duel in pairs.
It is too confined for all 28 to practise Stunning at once: half watch while half cast.
Allow at least about 85 m2.
facts.because: Assumes 6 m2 for a duelling pair: 14 pairs x 6 m2 = 84 m2. The room copes with this, but not with 28 pupils Stunning onto cushions.

facts.text: It has stone walls and flickering torches like those of the dungeons eight floors below, and it can be brightly lit.
Wooden bookcases line the walls with hundreds of large leather-bound defence books.
Far-end shelves hold Dark detectors: Sneakoscopes, Secrecy Sensors and a big cracked Foe-Glass. A later table of Sneakoscopes was reduced to dust.
The door has a key standing in a working lock, and pupils rushing out formed a scrum at it.
December 1995: a hundred golden baubles with Harry's face hung from the ceiling, with a large clump of mistletoe.
From October 1995 the signed Dumbledore's Army list was pinned to a wall, until it was taken in spring 1996.

open: Room dimensions and ceiling height. This state is a dated requirement, not a permanent layout.

ror-hidden-things.summary: The Room of Hidden Things is the Room of Requirement as a hiding place, seen in May 1997 and May 1998. It is as big as a large cathedral, with high windows sending shafts of light over what looks like a city: towering walls of hidden objects, alleyways and roads between them. Things have been left there for centuries, including thousands and thousands of books, broken furniture, weapons and broomsticks, and one wall of junk stands fifty feet high. A stuffed troll, a broken Vanishing Cabinet and a blistered cupboard mark one route in. Crabbe's cursed fire destroyed much of it in May 1998.

facts.text: It is as big as a large cathedral, a gigantic labyrinth, with towering walls of stored objects laid out like a city.
One wall of junk is fifty feet high, about 15 m. That is the heap, not the ceiling.
Allow at least 100 m by 30 m on plan and a ceiling well above 15 m.
facts.because: A large cathedral is taken as at least 100 m long and 30 m wide (assumed). The ceiling must clear 15 m heaps with room for broom flight above them.

facts.text: It cannot physically sit behind a seventh-floor wall.
facts.because: A height over 15 m is more than four storeys at 3.5 m, and no floor above the seventh is named. Treat the interior as a separate volume.

facts.text: High windows send shafts of daylight down into it.
Alleyways, roads and aisles run between the piles, wide enough to run along and with walls high enough to hide people in the next aisle.
It holds thousands and thousands of books, among centuries of objects left by earlier inhabitants.

Piles hold broken furniture, trunks, robes, crates, bottles of congealed potion, hats, jewels, cloaks, swords, a bloodstained axe, broomsticks, Fanged Frisbees and winged catapults, a few still hovering.
One route in: right at an enormous stuffed troll, a short run, left at a broken Vanishing Cabinet, to a large blistered cupboard.
The cupboard holds a cage with a five-legged skeleton. On it stood a chipped bust of an old warlock with a dusty wig and a tarnished tiara, placed there in 1997.
The Vanishing Cabinet is one of a pair, its mate in Borgin and Burkes. Repaired by 1997, it gave a route into the school.
It opens to a request for a hiding place or for where things are hidden. A summoning charm fails inside, and the huge space echoes.
May 1998: Crabbe's spell made a fifty-foot wall collapse into the next aisle, and a curse blasted the bust.
May 1998: cursed fire swept the heaps to soot, forming fiery beasts and thick black smoke. The diadem was recovered and destroyed in the corridor outside.

open: Whether anything survived the fire, and whether the Room can take this form again.

ror-refuge.summary: The refuge is the Room of Requirement as students' hideout in spring 1998. It began small, with one hammock and Gryffindor hangings, and grew until it was enormous, resembling a sumptuous tree house or a gigantic ship's cabin: windowless walls of dark wood panelling, a balcony running round them, multicoloured hammocks strung from ceiling and balcony, and bright House tapestries for all but Slytherin. Bookcases, broomsticks, lamps and a wireless furnish it, and a bathroom opens off it. A passage leads to the Hog's Head, and a cupboard in a corner opens on a long steep stair whose exit changes daily. Hundreds of evacuees passed through it on the night of the battle.

facts.text: It is enormous, like a sumptuous tree house or gigantic ship's cabin. More than twenty people crowded round Harry there on his arrival.
It is reported to have started much smaller, with one hammock, and to have grown over nearly two weeks as more people arrived.
On the battle night it took hundreds: evacuees streamed to it and out through the Hog's Head passage, after it had been packed with fighters.
facts.because: Harry's map shows a dense crowd heading there, he hears hundreds marching towards it, and Aberforth reports hundreds through his pub.

facts.text: The walls are dark wood panelling without windows, with a balcony running round them.
Multicoloured hammocks hang from ceiling and balcony, and it makes more as needed.
Bright tapestries show the Gryffindor lion on scarlet, the Hufflepuff badger on yellow and the Ravenclaw eagle on blue. Slytherin's are absent.
Bulging bookcases, broomsticks against the walls, lamps, chairs and a large wooden-cased wireless in a corner furnish it.
A bathroom opens directly off the room by an open doorway. It is reported to have appeared when girls arrived.
A short flight of steps and a small door at the far end of the Hog's Head passage open into the room.
A small corner cupboard opens on a steep, long torch-lit stair with unexpected bends, ending at a wall that melts to a push and reseals at once.
Neville says the stair's outlet moves each day. On the night of the battle, May 1998, it came out on the fifth floor.
While one defender stays inside, the door will not open to the Carrows or their supporters.
Mrs Longbottom sealed the Hog's Head passage behind her, and the last occupants left by the stone steps so the Room could be asked for something else.

conflicts.text: The Room's door is on the seventh floor, yet the refuge stair runs up to a fifth-floor corridor, which puts this state below the fifth floor that night. Neville's moving outlet explains the exit but not the depth.

open: Size and height of the room at its largest, and where the seventh-floor door opens into it.

third-floor-corridor.summary: A corridor on the third floor, shut behind a locked door and out of bounds to everyone during 1991–92, when it held the first guard on the way to the Philosopher’s Stone. The door closes off the end of the Charms corridor, a few seconds from the head of a carpeted staircase. Behind it a three-headed dog, Fluffy, stood floor to ceiling on a ringed trapdoor let into the corridor floor. The trapdoor lifts upward on to a black shaft with no ladder or steps and no visible bottom, the only known way down to the Stone chambers. Because that shaft starts three storeys above the ground and ends at dungeon level or deeper, it needs a clear vertical run through the second, first and ground floors, at a spot no other scene mentions. The corridor’s length, width and ceiling height are unstated, and nothing is recorded of it after June 1992.

facts.text: On the third floor. Dumbledore’s 1991 notice places it on the right-hand side, without saying whose right or seen from where.
Its door is at the far end of the Charms corridor.
The Charms corridor must therefore also be on the third floor.
facts.because: That corridor’s end door opens straight into the forbidden corridor, with no stairs between them.

facts.text: The door is only seconds from the top of a carpeted staircase climbing to the third floor.
Pupils pass the door on everyday journeys: in spring 1992 they stop to press an ear to it and hear the dog growling.
The door opens directly into the dog’s space: in 1991 the pupils shut it and took the place for a room before turning to find Fluffy.
Ceiling height is tied only to the dog: standing in 1991, Fluffy reaches from the floor right up to the ceiling.
The ceiling is not cathedral height: asleep, the dog is low enough for Ron to see past its back and step across its legs.
facts.because: A body that an eleven-year-old can look across when slumped cannot stand many times his height.

facts.text: The floor at the trapdoor cannot lie over ordinary rooms: the shaft under it needs a clear run down past the second, first and ground floors.
facts.because: The opening is in a third-floor floor and the pupils land far below it, at least four floors down if they reach dungeon level.

facts.text: It is a true corridor, not a room, with the trapdoor set in its floor.
The trapdoor has a ring; pulled, it swings up and open.
Hermione alone notices in 1991 that the dog is standing on a trapdoor.
Under the opening is only blackness: no bottom in sight and no ladder, steps or other way of climbing down, so entrants have to hang and drop.
The door was locked in September 1991, resisted forcing, gave to Alohomora, and stood ajar on the night in June 1992.
Hagrid claims only he and Dumbledore know how to get past the dog.
Harry’s way out from below is to fly: brooms from the key room, up through the trapdoor and past the dog.
Meeting Hermione and Ron in the Entrance Hall, Dumbledore rushes straight to the third floor, which fits the trapdoor being the way in.
In 1991–92 a three-headed dog guards the trapdoor: Hagrid’s Fluffy, on loan to Dumbledore. His thunderous growl carries through the shut door.
Music puts Fluffy to sleep and he stirs the moment it stops; his three noses still follow people hidden under a Cloak.
A harp lay at the dog’s feet on the night of June 1992.
Closed for the 1991–92 school year, with Dumbledore warning pupils of a painful death.

open: Whether this is the same corridor as the third-floor corridor with the one-eyed witch. Both are on the third floor, but no text links them.
Its length, and whether it continues beyond the trapdoor or stops there.
Whether the dog and trapdoor stayed after June 1992. No later scene returns here.

devils-snare-chamber.summary: The chamber at the foot of the trapdoor shaft, under the forbidden third-floor corridor and at dungeon level or deeper. The drop is long enough to shrink the open trapdoor to no bigger than a postage stamp. In June 1992 a mass of Devil’s Snare covered the floor to break the fall, and one stone passage led on.

facts.text: The drop is a long free fall through cold, damp air; from the landing the open trapdoor is a speck of light no bigger than a postage stamp.
Modelling minimum: a drop of about 15 m. An opening 1 m wide that looks like a 2.5 cm stamp held 30–60 cm from the eye is 12–24 m away.
facts.because: The text gives only the stamp comparison; trapdoor width, stamp size and viewing distance are assumptions. Four storeys at an assumed 4 m each give a matching 16 m to dungeon level.

facts.text: The shaft falls from the third floor past the second, first and ground floors to dungeon level or below, so it needs a sealed vertical run through or beside each of them.
facts.because: The trapdoor is in a third-floor floor, the pupils land far below, and the dungeons lie four floors under the third floor (eight under the seventh). No lower floor ever shows the shaft, so it must be walled off.

facts.text: In June 1992 long snaking Devil’s Snare covers the floor and tightens on whatever struggles. The room otherwise offers damp walls and a single stone passage as the only way on.

open: Where the shaft and this chamber fall in plan relative to the rooms on the floors above.

winged-key-chamber.summary: A tall stone chamber at the bottom of a sloping, dripping passage from the Devil’s Snare chamber, with a heavy wooden door in the opposite wall leading to the chess chamber. The vault is high enough for three people on brooms to chase a key through the air, and Ron still manages to ride into it. In June 1992 hundreds of winged keys filled the space. Its light source is never described.

facts.text: Entered from a stone passage that slopes downward from the plant chamber, with water trickling down its walls.
The heavy wooden door to the chess chamber is directly across the room from the entrance.
The ceiling arches high above; the room is called high, and a flying Ron can still reach and hit the ceiling.
In June 1992 hundreds of keys fly here, enough to read as one whirling cloud.
Modelling minimum: about 10 m high and 15 m across. Three riders above, level with and below a dodging key need about 3 m of height each; the sprint across takes seconds.
facts.because: No dimensions are given. Rider spacing and a dash of 3 seconds at 5 m/s are assumptions.

facts.text: Stone walls, brilliantly lit throughout, with no lamps, torches or windows mentioned.
The door has a silver handle and a lock that defeats force and Alohomora; only the one big key opens it.
Broomsticks are left in the room, at least three.
Harry names this room’s brooms as the way back up and out through the trapdoor.
The June 1992 flock has rainbow feathers. The right key is large and silver, with bright-blue wings, one already bent. Once used, it flies off again.

chess-chamber.summary: The chamber beyond the key room, filled by a huge chessboard with stone pieces taller than the pupils. Entrants arrive behind the black men and the door onward stands behind the white men at the far side, so the board has to be crossed by playing. It is dark until someone steps in, then light floods it.

facts.text: Entered from the key room on the black side; another door stands behind the white men on the far side, opening on to a passage that climbs.
A huge board: the black men all stand taller than the pupils, the white men tower a long way off across the room, and knights ride stone horses.
Modelling minimum: a board 16 m square in a room about 20 m across. Eight squares at 2 m each hold a mounted stone knight, plus a strip by the wall for taken men.
facts.because: Pieces obey real chess rules, so a standard eight-by-eight board is assumed; the text never counts squares. The 2 m square and the wall strip are assumptions.

facts.text: Entry floods the dark room with light. In June 1992 the stone men wake, take orders, strike down captured men and drag them to the wall, then part to clear the door.

troll-chamber.summary: A foul-smelling chamber between the chess room and the potion room, reached up a passage from the chess chamber and through a door. In June 1992 it held a troll bigger than the twelve-foot Hallowe’en troll, already knocked out, with one huge leg lying in the way to the next door.

facts.text: Lies at the top of the climbing passage from the chess chamber, behind a door; a further door leads straight on to the potion room.
The troll here is larger than the Hallowe’en troll, which stands twelve feet tall.
Modelling minimum: a ceiling above 4.5 m and a floor about 6 m long. A troll over 3.7 m tall must have stood here, and it lies flat with room to step past.
facts.because: Twelve feet is 3.7 m and this troll is larger; headroom and floor margins are assumptions. The text gives the room no size.

facts.text: In June 1992 the troll lies unconscious with a bleeding swelling on its skull, and Quirrell claims the work. Its stench drives the pupils straight on.

potion-chamber.summary: A room between the troll chamber and the last chamber, with a doorway at each end. In June 1992 a table held seven different bottles in a line with a written riddle beside them, and crossing the threshold lit purple fire in the doorway behind and black fire in the doorway ahead.

facts.text: Entered by the door out of the troll chamber; a second doorway leads on to the last chamber.
A table holds seven differently shaped bottles in one line, beside a roll of paper with the riddle: three poisons, two nettle wines, two passage drinks.
No size is given. The room needs only the table, two doorways and floor enough for Hermione to walk up and down beside the bottles.
facts.because: Those are the only physical demands the scene makes on the room.

facts.text: In June 1992 fire fills both doorways once the threshold is crossed: purple behind, black ahead. The tiny smallest bottle passes the black, a round bottle at the right-hand end the purple.

mirror-chamber.summary: The last underground chamber, behind the black fire at the end of the Stone defences. It held the Mirror of Erised, free-standing, with room to walk all round it and more open floor beyond.

facts.text: The end of the chain, entered only through the black flames from the potion room; that flame doorway is also the only exit named.
Quirrell walks right round the Mirror and behind it, and Harry gets a few paces clear of it, so there is open floor on all sides. No dimensions are given.
The Mirror of Erised stands here in June 1992, a free-standing framed mirror brought from a disused classroom. No pedestal, steps or pit are described.
The Stone lay hidden by the Mirror’s rule: it would come only to someone who sought it with no wish to use it. It reached Harry’s pocket; Dumbledore later reports it destroyed.

stone-defences-general.summary: The chain of seven guarded stages below the forbidden corridor, set up for 1991–92 to protect the Philosopher’s Stone: Fluffy, Devil’s Snare, winged keys, giant chess, a troll, the potion fires and the Mirror of Erised. The route starts at the third-floor trapdoor, drops at least four storeys to dungeon level or lower, then runs in single file through the plant chamber, down a sloping passage to the key and chess chambers, up another passage to the troll chamber, and on through the potion room to the last chamber. Two big rooms sit in that run: the key chamber needs a high vault and the chess chamber a wide floor, so the whole chain takes a large block of space that must lie beneath, or out to the side of, the dungeon rooms. No link to the dungeons, or to any other floor, is described.

facts.text: Seven stages in all: Hagrid’s dog, then work credited to Sprout, Flitwick, McGonagall, Quirrell, Snape and Dumbledore.
On landing at the foot of the shaft, Hermione guesses they must be miles beneath the school. It is a guess, not a measurement.
The chain is not literally miles down: Harry’s shout from the bottom reaches Ron at the trapdoor, and the flute above is faintly audible below.
facts.because: Voice and music both cross the whole height of the shaft, and all three pupils survive the jump.

facts.text: Dumbledore afterwards speaks of the last events as taking place down in the dungeons.
The chain sits at dungeon level or deeper, but apart from the working dungeons: no scene joins it to the Potions rooms or any dungeon corridor.
facts.because: Every entry and planned exit in the text uses the third-floor trapdoor; the only underground label is Dumbledore’s passing remark.

facts.text: Levels shift along the way: the passage after the plant chamber slopes down, and the one after the chess chamber goes up. Other stages connect by doors.
Modelling minimum: chambers end to end run about 55 m, and about 70 m with passages. They need not lie straight, but the block is far bigger than a cellar.
facts.because: Adds assumed minimums: plant 5 m, key 15 m, chess 20 m, troll 6 m, potion 4 m, last 5 m, passages about 15 m. No length is stated anywhere.

facts.text: A single-file chain with no side branches: each stage has one way on, and the trapdoor is the only known way in.
facts.because: The passage from the plant chamber is called the only way on, and every later room shows just one onward door.

facts.text: The exit used in fact is undescribed: Hermione says only that she got back, revived Ron and was heading for the owlery when they met Dumbledore in the Entrance Hall.
All this is dated to 1991–92. Quirrell admits scouting the guards at Hallowe’en 1991; the Stone is destroyed in June 1992, and no later scene visits the chambers.

conflicts.text: Hermione guesses miles under the school; Dumbledore says the dungeons. Neither is a survey, and they imply very different depths.

Harry’s plan was to fly out through the trapdoor and past Fluffy, but Hermione’s account has the pair meeting Dumbledore in the Entrance Hall on the way up to the owlery, with no mention of brooms or the third floor.

open: How the shaft is hidden on the second, first and ground floors, and where it falls in plan.
Whether the chambers lie directly under the third-floor corridor or run off beneath another part of the castle or the grounds.

chamber-entrance.summary: The way down to the Chamber of Secrets starts at a sink in Moaning Myrtle’s girls’ bathroom, on the second floor by most evidence. A tiny snake scratched on one copper tap marks it. Spoken Parseltongue makes the tap glow and spin and the whole sink sinks away, exposing a pipe a grown man could fit into. The pipe plunges steeply and twists, past smaller branches, down through the castle to below the dungeons, then levels out and ends in a stone tunnel. Nobody can climb back up it on foot; Fawkes carried four people out in 1993.

facts.text: The entrance is a sink in Moaning Myrtle’s bathroom, the one in front of her toilet.
That bathroom is on the second floor by narration and by its place beside the second-floor writing corridor, three floors under the fifth-floor Prefects’ bathroom.
A tiny snake is scratched into one copper tap, the tap Myrtle says has never worked.
English has no effect. Parseltongue makes the tap shine white and spin, and the sink drops out of sight.
In 1998 Ron opens it by copying Harry’s hissing after several tries, so no born Parselmouth is required.
The exposed pipe is large: a grown man can slide into it.
It is the largest pipe in view; smaller ones branch off in every direction.
The ride goes deeper under the school than the dungeons before the pipe levels out, and feels endless to Harry.
At the bottom Harry guesses they are miles under the school, and Ron guesses they are under the lake. Both are characters’ guesses.
From the second floor the pipe must pass the first and ground floors and the dungeon level, so it descends more than three storeys inside walls and then rock.
facts.because: The dungeons lie one level under the ground floor, and the narration takes the descent below them.

facts.text: Modelling minimum: a vertical drop of at least 16 m, and about 30 m if the Chamber lies under the dungeons. The pipe itself is much longer, because it slants and twists.
facts.because: Three storeys to the dungeon floor at an assumed 4 m is 12 m, and going deeper than that means at least 16 m. The Chamber’s estimated 15 m height, plus some rock over it, gives about 30 m if it lies directly beneath the dungeons.

facts.text: Dark, slimy and steep, it bends repeatedly, then levels off and throws riders out on to wet stone.
It cannot be climbed unaided: from the bottom Harry sees only a long dark shaft. Holding Fawkes’s tail, four people fly up in a chain, and the sink slides shut behind them.
By Harry’s reasoning the basilisk reached the upper floors through this plumbing, moving inside the walls.
Ron returns from the Chamber in 1998 carrying a broomstick, which suggests a way back up the pipe.
facts.because: The text does not say how they got out, but the pipe cannot be climbed and the broom is the only aid mentioned.

conflicts.text: Hermione says Myrtle haunts the toilet on the first floor, and the 1993 walk from Lockhart’s second-floor office goes down stairs to reach it. Other scenes put it on the second floor.

open: How the system reaches other floors. Every branch seen is narrower than the main pipe, yet a snake as thick as an oak trunk travelled through the castle walls.

chamber-tunnels.summary: The stone tunnels between the foot of the pipe and the serpent doors of the Chamber of Secrets. They lie below the dungeons, unlit, wet and high enough to stand in, and they bend repeatedly. In 1993 they held small animal bones, a shed basilisk skin from a snake of twenty feet or more and, after Lockhart’s failed spell, a rockfall that blocked the way until Ron cleared a gap.

facts.text: Runs from where the pipe levels out to the solid serpent wall of the Chamber.
The Chamber end may be the lower: the walk back to the pipe is described as going up the tunnel.
facts.because: The wording is the only evidence of slope, and it may be loose.

facts.text: High enough to stand in. Width is not given.
Modelling minimum: about 200 m from pipe to Chamber. From the serpent doors it takes a few minutes to come within earshot of the rockfall, and the pipe is further on.
facts.because: Three minutes at an assumed 65 m a minute is about 200 m, before the stretch from the rockfall back to the pipe. No length is stated.

facts.text: A shed snake skin lies coiled right across the tunnel, vivid green and huge; the narration judges the snake that shed it at twenty feet or more.
Dark stone with wet, slimy walls and a wet floor; footsteps and voices ring in it.
The tunnel keeps bending: one bend comes before the skin, and it turns again and again beyond it.
No light of its own: only wand light, and in 1993 the glow of Fawkes’s wings.
Small animal bones, including a rat’s skull, litter the floor.
In May 1993 Ron’s damaged wand explodes and large chunks of ceiling come down, forming a solid rock barrier and leaving huge cracks overhead.
Ron later shifts enough rock by hand to leave a gap that Ginny, Fawkes and Harry can squeeze through. Nothing says the fall was ever fully cleared.
The way was still passable in 1998, since Ron and Hermione reach the basilisk’s skull beyond it.
facts.because: They return with fangs from the Chamber, which lies past the rockfall.

chamber-of-secrets.summary: A very long pillared stone hall hidden far below Hogwarts, deeper than the dungeons and reached by the pipe from Moaning Myrtle’s bathroom and a winding tunnel. Its door is a solid wall carved with two serpents that parts at a hissed command. Inside, a dim space runs between paired rows of towering stone pillars wound with carved serpents, up to a vaulted ceiling lost in shadow. At the far end a statue of Salazar Slytherin, as tall as the hall itself, stands against the back wall with enormous feet on the smooth floor. Its mouth opens on command into a dark cavity of unknown depth, from which the basilisk emerges. The hall gave a snake as thick as an oak trunk room to rear, thrash and turn among the pillars, so it is far larger than any dungeon classroom. No figure for its length, width or height is given. The dead basilisk was left lying there in 1993 and its skull was still there in 1998.

facts.text: At the end of the tunnels, below the dungeons. The only route ever seen is the bathroom pipe followed by the tunnels.
By legend Slytherin built it secretly in the castle, unknown to the other founders; repeated searches by scholars and heads of the school found nothing.
A single very long, dim hall. The statue at its far end comes into sight only once Harry reaches the final pair of pillars.
Towering stone pillars stand in pairs down its length and rise to a vaulted ceiling that is lost in darkness.
A statue as high as the Chamber stands against the back wall. Harry must crane to see its giant face; Ginny lies between its enormous feet, and the diary by its toes.
The basilisk is thick as an oak trunk, with fangs as long as Harry’s sword and a mouth that could take him whole.
It rears high, its head moving among the pillars, while its tail sweeps the floor and its body strikes pillars as it turns.
Fawkes, the size of a swan, appears on top of a pillar and circles the snake’s raised head.
Pillars must stand far enough apart for that snake to turn between them, with space along the walls for a boy to dodge it.
facts.because: The snake rears, coils round and lunges among pillars and at the wall while Harry runs and dodges there.

facts.text: Modelling minimum: statue and ceiling at least 15 m high. A mouth 0.7 m wide for the snake suggests a face over 2 m tall, and a figure eight faces high.
facts.because: Human proportions are assumed: a face about three mouth-openings tall, a figure eight faces tall. The 0.7 m comes from an oak-thick body that can still be stepped over when dead.

facts.text: Modelling minimum: at least 45 m long and 15 m wide. A very long room should be several times its height, and the rows need about 8 m between them plus side aisles.
facts.because: Three times the 15 m height is an assumption, as is the row spacing for a snake to turn. No length or width is stated.

facts.text: Modelling allowance: a snake from 6 m (the text’s twenty-foot floor) up to about 15 m. Its oak-trunk thickness would make twenty feet oddly stout.
facts.because: Assumes a body 0.6 m thick and a large snake’s length of about 25 times its thickness. The text gives only twenty feet or more.

facts.text: The door is a solid wall closing the tunnel, carved with two intertwined snakes whose eyes are set with big emeralds.
Pillars are wound with carved serpents, and other stone snakes have hollow eye sockets.
Smooth, dusty stone floor and dark walls; footsteps and laughter ring loudly.
An odd greenish half-light fills the hall and throws long shadows, with no source named.
The statue shows an old wizard with a monkey-like face and a long thin beard reaching nearly to the hem of sweeping stone robes.
A hissed command splits the wall and its halves slide away out of sight; the doors shut by themselves, with a soft hiss, behind people leaving.
By legend only Slytherin’s heir could unseal it. Riddle says finding the entrance took him five years.
Addressed in Parseltongue, the statue’s stone face moves and its mouth gapes into a huge black hole; the basilisk climbs out and drops to the floor.
Behind the statue’s mouth is a hollow, passage or lair of unknown depth, wide enough for the snake’s body.
facts.because: The snake rises from somewhere inside the statue, and it must pass through the mouth.

facts.text: Reported openings: fifty years before 1992–93, when a girl died in a bathroom and a pupil was expelled; then in 1992–93, when Riddle says Ginny opened it through the diary.
After May 1993 the dead basilisk stays on the floor among blood and ink.
In 1998 Ron and Hermione tear curved yellow fangs from its skull, so the remains are still there five years later.

open: Where the hall lies in plan: under the castle or, as Ron only guessed, under the lake.
How many pairs of pillars stand in it.
What lies behind the statue’s mouth, and whether it joins the pipes.

dungeon-corridors.summary: The dungeon corridors are the underground passages of the castle, a group rather than one corridor, lying exactly one storey below the ground floor and reached by stone steps from the Entrance Hall. They are dim, cold and rough-walled, lit by torches in brackets, and they link the Potions classroom, Snape’s office, the Slytherin common room and other dungeon rooms. Known stretches include the passage with Snape’s office door halfway along it, the waiting space outside the Potions door, the way to the 1992 Deathday party, and a maze of deserted passages leading to the Slytherin wall. Only one dungeon level is ever counted, though the way to Slytherin is said to run deeper under the school.

facts.text: Eight floors below the seventh floor, in British numbering, is exactly one level under the ground floor, so that is where the dungeons lie.
facts.because: The narrator places them eight floors below the seventh floor. In British numbering seven floors down from the seventh reach the ground floor (7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, ground), so the eighth is the first level under it. British numbering is confirmed by the route of six floors plus the marble staircase from the seventh floor to the Entrance Hall, and by seven staircases from the ground floor to the Fat Lady.

facts.text: The text firmly supports only this one level. No second level is counted, though passages towards the Slytherin common room run deeper under the school, so parts may lie lower.
facts.because: The eight floors is the only count, and each route described from the Entrance Hall is a single run of stone steps. The only hints of greater depth are the Book 2 walk towards the Slytherin wall and Harry’s later claim that the common room lies under the lake.

facts.text: The ways in described are stone steps down from the Entrance Hall. A door on the right as you come down the marble staircase leads towards Slytherin; Snape’s stairs also open off the hall.
These are not the deepest spaces under the school: the pipe to the Chamber of Secrets drops well below them.
Snape’s office door stands halfway along a cold passage, and the Potions door has space outside it for a class to queue, at the foot of the steps.
Harry’s flight from Snape’s office in 1996, three floors up, would end on the second floor.
facts.because: One level below ground plus three floors is the second floor in British numbering.

facts.text: The passages form a maze: in 1992 two boys walked deserted passages for about a quarter of an hour before meeting anyone. That time includes searching.
In a diary memory, following footsteps from the Potions room took perhaps five minutes before a corner and a door.
The way down to Snape’s passage is a narrow stone staircase.
Stadium crowd noise dies away completely as you walk in from the steps.
Walls of rough stone with bracket-mounted torches; dim, gloomy and colder than the main castle.
Side rooms and corners open off the passages, voices echo along them, and a stair rises close to the Potions exit.
Hallowe’en 1992: the passage to the Deathday party was lined with thin black candles burning blue.

conflicts.text: Harry says the Slytherin common room is under the lake, yet the castle stands on a high cliff over the lake and the dungeons are one storey below ground. Both hold only if the passages descend a long way.

open: How far the passages descend past the first level to reach the Slytherin common room.
Whether the Slytherin door and the stairs to Snape’s office are one door or two.

deathday-dungeon.summary: One of the larger dungeons, used for Nearly Headless Nick’s party on 31 October 1992, at the end of a passage from the dungeon steps. It took hundreds of ghosts on a dance floor, a thirty-strong orchestra on a platform and a long table across the room. No permanent fittings are described; everything on record is party dressing.

facts.text: Called one of the roomier dungeons; in 1992 it held hundreds of ghosts, most of them on a crowded dance floor.
It also took an orchestra of thirty musical saws on a platform, a chandelier of a thousand black candles, and a long table on the far side.
Modelling minimum, not canon: at least 300 m² of floor, for example 20 m by 15 m.
facts.because: Hundreds means at least 200 ghosts; at an assumed 1 m² per dancer, 200 m². Thirty players at an assumed 1.5 m² each, 45 m². A long table with walking space, assumed 10 m by 3 m, 30 m². A margin for the walkway round the dance floor brings it to about 300 m². Ghosts need no floor, but the room must read as holding this crowd.

facts.text: Reached along a passage from the dungeon steps and round a corner to a doorway; the way out returns up that passage to the steps into the Entrance Hall.
Cold enough for living visitors’ breath to mist.
All dressing was for 31 October 1992: black velvet door drapes, draped platform, podium and velvet-covered table. A dozen ghost horses came in through the wall.

open: Which numbered dungeon this is, and where it lies relative to Snape’s rooms.

other-dungeon-rooms.summary: A catch-all for dungeon rooms the text does not connect to the named ones, known only from passing mentions, with nothing to show that any two are the same room. The instances are dungeon five, a room behind a door beyond the Potions room in Riddle’s memory, and the unnamed place where Harry’s Firebolt was held in 1996.

facts.text: Dungeons carry numbers, so at least five exist.
facts.because: Nearly Headless Nick refers to dungeon five, which needs at least four others unless the numbering skips.

facts.text: A memory from about fifty years earlier shows a door round a corner beyond the Potions room, with a very large box beside it.
In 1992 third-years coated dungeon five’s ceiling in frog brains, and Filch spent a morning cleaning it.
In May 1996 Filch took Harry’s Firebolt below to the dungeons. Umbridge said it was strictly guarded; a security troll watching it is only a rumour.

kitchens.summary: The Hogwarts kitchens are one enormous high-ceilinged stone room in the basement, directly beneath the Great Hall and equal to it in size, so the floor shares the Hall’s modelling minimum of about 1,200 m². Four long wooden tables stand exactly under the four house tables above, and Harry supposes that food rises from them to the matching tables overhead. Brass pots and pans are heaped around the walls and a large brick fireplace fills the far end. At least a hundred house-elves work here. The way in starts at the door to the right of the marble staircase, descends one stone flight to a broad, bright corridor hung with pictures of food, and passes through a painting of a silver fruit bowl, opened by tickling its pear. The same basement corridor serves the Hufflepuffs.

facts.text: An enormous room with a high ceiling, matching the Great Hall overhead in size.
Modelling minimum, not canon: at least 1,200 m² of floor, for example 50 m by 24 m, the same as the Great Hall.
facts.because: The text equates the two rooms, so the Great Hall’s minimum carries straight over: about 100 tables × about 12 seats × an assumed 1 m² per seat = about 1,200 m², fitted to a span of fifty yards (46 m). The four long tables here lie under the house tables, so the plan has to match the Hall’s as well. Anything smaller could not keep those tables in line with the ones above.

facts.text: At least a hundred house-elves stood in the room at once in 1994, all wearing Hogwarts-crested tea-towels.
Nearly Headless Nick says the school has over a hundred house-elves, more than any other dwelling in Britain, mostly in the kitchens by day and out cleaning at night.
The 1994 Christmas lunch needed a hundred or more turkeys.
In the basement, directly under the Great Hall, on the same corridor that serves the Hufflepuffs.
The floor lies one storey below the ground floor, at the same depth as the dungeons.
facts.because: The kitchens sit under the Great Hall, the way in is one flight of stone steps below the Entrance Hall, and the narrator expects that flight to end in a passage like the one to Snape’s dungeon. The dungeons are eight floors below the seventh floor, which in British numbering is one level under the ground floor.

facts.text: Harry’s 1991 belief that he was five floors above the kitchens would put that dark corridor near the library on the fourth floor.
facts.because: One level below ground plus five floors is the fourth floor in British numbering. It is only Harry’s guess, made in the dark in a corridor he did not recognise.

facts.text: Way in: the door to the right of the marble staircase (left when coming down it), then a flight of stone steps to a broad, brightly torch-lit stone corridor hung with food paintings.
Partway along the corridor a painting of a giant silver fruit bowl hides the door: tickling its green pear turns the pear into a door handle.
Pupils can get in: Fred and George report repeated visits for food, and the elves press snacks on visitors.
Stone walls and a stone-flagged floor, with a large brick fireplace at the far end, its brickwork blackened by smoke, and a stool beside it.
Four long wooden tables stand exactly under the four house tables, bare after dinner. Brass pots and pans lie heaped around the walls.
Harry remembers armour standing close to the kitchens.
Harry supposes food is laid on these tables, then rises through the ceiling to the matching tables in the Hall. No one sees this happen.
Nick reports that Peeves threw the pots and pans about and flooded the room with soup before the feast on 1 September 1994.
Kreacher was sent to work here in summer 1996.
May 1998: the door leading here from the Entrance Hall was blasted off its hinges as the house-elves charged out with kitchen knives.

open: The room is high-ceilinged yet only one flight of steps below the Entrance Hall, with the Great Hall floor over it. Decide how that works: a long flight, or a kitchen floor sunk below corridor level.
No ovens, ranges, sinks, stores or windows are described, and nothing says which end of the Hall the fireplace lies under.

owlery.summary: The Owlery is a circular stone room at the top of West Tower, home to the school owls and pupils' own owls. Its windows have no glass, so it is cold, windy and bright. Hundreds upon hundreds of owls of all breeds roost on long lines of perches and on rafters that climb all the way to the tower's top, under a vaulted ceiling. Straw, droppings and small skeletons cover the floor. It is reached by a spiral stair and steps up to a door with a handle. Its windows look over the Forest, Hagrid's cabin and the grounds, and a thrown owl fell twelve feet there before flying.

facts.text: It stands at the top of West Tower.
It is a circular stone room, cold and windy since its windows are unglazed holes in the wall.
It houses hundreds upon hundreds of owls of all breeds.
Perches in long lines climb all the way to the tower's top, with high rafters and a vaulted ceiling far enough up that Hedwig can sit out of reach.
Allow at least 10 m across and about two storeys high.
facts.because: Assumes 0.3 m of perch per bird: 300 owls need 90 m of perch. A 10 m circle has 31 m of wall, so three rings of perches at the least, stacked upwards.

facts.text: The floor is covered with straw, owl droppings and the bones of mice and voles coughed up by the birds. It is slippery and crunches underfoot.
Pupils' owls roost and feed here with the school owls, which anyone can borrow. About half the perches were empty at one dawn as owls came back from hunting.
A spiral stair and steps climb to a hinged door with a handle.
Routes from the seventh-floor portrait are described as going up to it. A longer way in 1995 passed many windows and a statue of Wilfred the Wistful.
Leaving it, the way comes to the entrance of a corridor running towards the castle's west wing.
From the Room of Requirement, on the seventh floor, Harry judged it nearer than the dormitories.
Its windows overlook Forest treetops, Hagrid's cabin and the misty grounds, and in 1995 the Durmstrang ship's sails and the Beauxbatons carriage too.
An owl thrown from a window dropped twelve feet clear before recovering. That is the air below the sill, not the height above ground.
Owls can be seen flying round the Owlery tower from the lawns near the Quidditch pitch.

conflicts.text: Book 4 sends Harry up from the seventh-floor portrait yet past a vase on the fourth-floor corridor. Either he first went down to reach the West Tower, or the text is inconsistent.
The Owlery has rafters, a vaulted ceiling and perches up to the tower's top, yet the same tower top has walkable battlements. A vault with a walkway round or above it could fit both.

open: Which floor the spiral stair starts from. That also decides whether the fourth-floor route was a real detour.

west-tower.summary: West Tower carries the Owlery at its top and battlements that took a landing Hippogriff with three riders. A doorway at the top leads down a tightly spiralling stone stair to a corridor. Seen from the lake shore it is a landmark for counting windows: Professor Flitwick's seventh-floor office is window thirteen counting to its right. Its top stands above the seventh floor, but it is not one of the three highest towers, so it must be lower than Gryffindor Tower.

facts.text: The Owlery is at the top of West Tower.
Flitwick's seventh-floor office is window thirteen counting to the right from West Tower, and those windows can be counted from the lake shore.
The office window is at least about 36 m along the wall from the tower.
facts.because: Twelve window spaces at an assumed minimum of 3 m each: 12 x 3 = 36 m. The text gives no spacing.

facts.text: Its top stands above the seventh floor.
facts.because: A Hippogriff flies upwards from the seventh-floor office window to reach the battlements.

facts.text: It is lower than Gryffindor, Ravenclaw and Astronomy Towers.
facts.because: A 1998 plan names those three as the highest, leaving West Tower out.

facts.text: The top has battlements that took a landing Hippogriff, with three people on it.
A doorway at the top opens on a tightly spiralling stone stair down to a corridor.
From that corridor the way to the hospital wing ran down one staircase, then another. Stair counts here do not give a floor count.

open: How the battlements sit relative to the Owlery's vault, and which floor the corridor at the stair's foot is on.

astronomy-tower.summary: The Astronomy Tower is the tallest tower of Hogwarts, standing at the front of the castle: a parapet at its top lies directly above the front doors, and its foot is on the grass near them. A steep spiral stair rises from a corridor, floor unstated, to a door with an iron ring, which opens on an open-air top with crenellated ramparts, a parapet and a wall. Classes and exams use it at night with telescopes on stands, and pupils may go there only for lessons. It must overtop Gryffindor Tower: if that reaches a fourteenth floor, these ramparts stand at about the fifteenth-floor level or higher. Dumbledore fell from it in June 1997.

facts.text: It is the tallest tower of Hogwarts and the highest of the castle.
It is named with Ravenclaw and Gryffindor as the three highest towers.
Its ramparts must clear Gryffindor Tower: at about floor 15 level or more if that tower's top floor is 14, which is about 52 m above the ground floor at 3.5 m a storey.
facts.because: It is the highest tower, and Gryffindor's top room has its ceiling at about floor 15 level: 15 x 3.5 = 52 m. The storey height and the top floor of 14 are estimates.

facts.text: A parapet at the top stands directly above the castle's front doors.
Its foot is on the grass at the castle front, near the oak doors, and a fall over the battlements lands there.
The top looks over the lawn, the grounds and Hagrid's lit cabin, far enough for walkers to be hard to see, yet a roar from the cabin carries up.
A steep spiral stair rises from a corridor to the top, its foot reached by the marble staircase, more stairs and corridors. Harry leapt its last ten steps; ten is not its length.
The stair ends at a door with an iron ring.
Pupils may go there only for lessons.
The top is open to the sky, with crenellated ramparts, a parapet and a wall to lean on. No roof or dome is described.
It holds an exam sitting with telescopes and examiners walking among them, and took four broom riders with a slung crate.
Allow a top at least about 14 m across.
facts.because: If the whole fifth year sat there, and a year group was over 100 at a 1976 exam, then 100 x 1.5 m2 per telescope and user = 150 m2, a circle about 14 m across.

facts.text: Telescopes stand on stands set up by the users, who carry them in holders. Astronomy exams are held here at night.
June 1997: the Dark Mark hung over the tower, casting green light, and the Headmaster fell from the battlements.
June 1997: a curse sealed the stair behind the Death Eaters, and a later hex brought down half the corridor ceiling at its foot, breaking the curse.
The Bloody Baron is said to go groaning and clanking up there as a favourite pastime.

conflicts.text: One Book 1 passage says the tallest astronomy tower, which could imply several. Every later passage has a single Astronomy Tower.

open: The floor of the corridor at the stair's foot. Death Eaters headed for it from the seventh floor, which suggests a high floor, but the books do not say.
The tower's total height and plan. A long stair is implied if Gryffindor reaches floor 14, though none is described.

hagrid-cabin.summary: Hagrid’s cabin is a one-room wooden house where the sloping lawns below the castle meet the Forbidden Forest, roughly five minutes’ walk from the front doors. The books call it small, but its owner stands about double normal height and three or more times normal breadth, and everything in it is built for him, so it must be far larger than an ordinary hut. The single room has an open fire in one corner, a gigantic patchwork-covered bed in another, an enormous central table with chairs, and a wardrobe, dresser, chest of drawers and cupboards. Hams, birds and pots hang from a ceiling his head can just brush. A wooden front door with bolt and keyhole faces the lawns; a back door opens into the fenced pumpkin garden, which ends only yards from the first trees. There is a chimney, curtained glass windows and a water barrel outside. It has held a Hippogriff, six raiders at once and most of a class. Fire wrecked it in June 1997, yet it stands in May 1998. The roof is never described.

facts.text: Hagrid stands about double a normal man’s height and three or more times his breadth; other passages simply say twice normal size.
Against people: Umbridge barely reaches his navel, Harry and Slughorn only his elbow; bent double he tops a stand by four feet; a photograph shows him seven or eight feet tall at eleven.
When he jumps up from his seat his head brushes the ceiling.
Give the room at least 3.4 m (11 ft) of clear height, about one and a half times a normal cottage’s.
facts.because: Twice a 1.7 m man is 3.4 m, and his elbow would then sit near 2.1 m, within Harry’s reach. He grazes the ceiling only on leaping up, so it sits close to his height. A cottage room is about 2.3 m.

facts.text: Make both doors at least 1.4 m wide and about 3 m high; a normal door would not pass him.
facts.because: Three times a 0.45 m shoulder is 1.35 m. At 3.4 m tall he needs about 3 m with a slight stoop. No passage has him forcing his way through here, and a Hippogriff has gone through one door at a canter.

facts.text: Capacity: most of a two-house class shelters inside at once (1994); six raiders enter with Hagrid and Fang within (1996); a Hippogriff lives indoors in winter 1993–94, on bed and floor.
Allow a rectangular floor of at least 8 m by 6 m, despite the word small.
facts.because: Umbridge walks the cabin’s length, and corners hold bed, fire and barrel. A 3.7 m bed, a central 3 m by 1.5 m table with chairs and a 1 m walk all round (about 6.5 m by 5 m), plus hearth, wardrobe and dresser, need no less.

facts.text: A wooden house of one room, called small, little or a hut throughout.
The front door is wood with a bolt and a keyhole; a back door opens straight into the garden, and people can walk right round the building.
Windows are glazed, curtained and can open: one beside the front door, one with the water barrel outside it and a view of the carriage, and one at the rear over the garden.
Outside stand a chimney, a water barrel, a bush some twenty feet off, a crossbow and galoshes by the door, in summer an armchair, and from 1996 Buckbeak on a tether in front.
A gigantic bed under a patchwork quilt stands in one corner, with space to peer underneath; a Hippogriff with folded wings has lain on it.
An open fire with a grate and mantelpiece occupies another corner, heating a copper kettle.
An enormous scrubbed wooden table, which once held a dragon steak bigger than a car tyre, stands mid-room before the fire, with equally huge chairs and a walkway round it.
Storage comprises a wardrobe, a chest of drawers beside the bed, a dresser with drawers and cups, and more than one cupboard.
Cured hams and dead birds hang from the ceiling over the table; by 1997 brass pots and a long skein of unicorn hair hang there too.

Household goods match him: bucket-sized mugs and cups, an enormous kettle and cooking cauldron, Fang’s cushioned basket, a haversack fit for several small children, and in 1996 a large barrel of foot-long grubs.
The cabin stands on the edge of the Forest at the foot of the sloping lawns: every visit goes downhill from the castle and every return climbs.
Its front looks towards the lawns and castle approach; the back garden lies towards the trees.
facts.because: Officials walking down from the castle reach the front while pupils leave unseen by the back, and a rear window overlooks the patch beside the trees. No compass bearing is given.

facts.text: From the castle front doors the walk takes roughly five minutes; Harry allows about half an hour from Gryffindor Tower under the Cloak.
facts.because: Harry and Ron leave the castle at five to three for tea at about three. Officials seen on the steps knock soon afterwards. Harry sets out at half past eleven for a midnight meeting.

facts.text: Site the cabin at least about 350 m from the front steps.
facts.because: Five minutes at 4 to 5 km/h is 330 to 420 m. Cabin and castle steps are each called distant from the other, and Fang looks tiny from the Astronomy Tower.

facts.text: It is in view from Gryffindor common-room and dormitory windows, the Owlery, the top of the Astronomy Tower and corridor windows; one cabin window shows the far-off castle steps.
It is Harry’s closest refuge from the stadium; Hagrid says he watched a match from it by binoculars. The lake is a run from its door, and people heading for the gates pass nearby.
Shut up and dark in January 1995 and from September to November 1995, raided at night in June 1996 when its door burst open, and closed to pupils’ evening visits in 1994 and 1996.
A spell sets it alight in June 1997; water jets leave a smoking wreck. It is reported in use by spring 1998 and still stands that May, with no rebuilding described.

conflicts.text: Breadth differs: five or more times normal width in Book 1, three or more times normal breadth in Book 4. Use the smaller figure as a minimum.
Height readings differ: twice a normal man implies about 3.4 m, but head and shoulders above a street crowd, or Umbridge at his navel, read closer to 2.2 to 2.6 m.

open: Roof form and covering are never described; the only fixed points are a chimney and a ceiling that clears Hagrid.
The number of windows and the fire’s corner relative to the doors are unstated.

hagrid-garden.summary: Hagrid’s garden is the fenced plot behind his cabin, entered by the back door and overlooked by the rear window, running towards the first trees of the Forest. It holds the pumpkin patch, runner beans and a compost heap, and from spring 1997 Aragog’s grave mound just beyond the patch. Its pumpkins reached boulder size and then shed size in 1992, so even a plot called small needs real ground.

facts.text: The garden lies behind the cabin, reached through the back door and overlooked by the rear window.
In June 1994 a spot ten feet short of the Forest was still in plain view of the back door, and a tether lay a few yards from that door.
The patch’s Forest side lies only yards from the first trees, close enough for sounds at the back door to carry into the wood.
facts.because: Harry darts from the trees to vault the fence, and is soon only ten feet from the Forest while leading Buckbeak away at a walk.

facts.text: A 1997 remark calls the ground before the cabin his front garden, apparently the plot dug for the Niffler lesson.
In 1992 the plot, called small, held about a dozen pumpkins the size of large boulders; rain and magical help swelled them to garden-shed size by October.
Carved for that Hallowe’en, they became lanterns that three men could sit inside.
Allow at least about 7 m by 10 m for the pumpkin bed.
facts.because: Twelve pumpkins 2 m across with 0.5 m gaps, in a three-by-four grid, take 7 m by 9.5 m.

facts.text: Aragog’s grave, dug in spring 1997 just beyond the pumpkin patch, was a massive pit with dug earth heaped ten feet high beside it; the ten feet is the spoil, not the spider.
