Allow a pit of at least about 50 m³, for example 5 m by 4 m and 2.5 m deep.
facts.because: A conical heap 3 m high and 8 m across holds about 50 m³.

facts.text: A fence surrounds the patch, low enough to vault and to lean on; a Hippogriff’s rope has been tied to it, and an axe was apparently swung into it in 1994.
Crops include pumpkins and runner beans; a compost heap stands near the grave site, and at least one tree grows behind the patch.
Blast-Ended Skrewts were boxed here: about twenty nearly three feet long in October 1994, then ten nearly six feet long, which burst enormous boxes that December and withered plants.
Once filled, the grave remains as a smooth mound of earth in the back garden from 1997.

conflicts.text: Buckbeak’s tether in June 1994 is a tree behind the patch in one chapter and the patch fence in another.
That tether lies only a few yards from the back door, beyond the patch, which leaves little depth for a bed that held a dozen shed-sized pumpkins in 1992.

open: The garden’s overall size and fence line are unstated; keep the patch, then the grave, then the first trees in that order from the back door.

creature-lesson-grounds.summary: These are the outdoor sites used for Care of Magical Creatures, not one place. There is no classroom or stable: lessons for two houses together happen on open ground around Hagrid’s cabin and along the Forest edge. Known instances are the fenced Hippogriff paddock five minutes round the trees from the cabin (1993); crates and lawn by the cabin and a rear trestle table (1994); an edge tree beyond the horse paddock and a muddy foal site (early 1995); a dug Niffler plot before the cabin (spring 1995); a trestle table ten yards from the door (1995); and the Forest-edge lawn of the 1996 examination. The sites of the Flobberworm and salamander lessons are unstated.

facts.text: No classroom or animal house is used; every described lesson is in the open or at a temporary table or crate.
facts.because: All lessons narrated are outdoors, and no stable or roofed outbuilding is ever mentioned.

facts.text: A lesson is a joint class of two houses, such as Gryffindors with Slytherins, so each site must take both at once.
The Hippogriff paddock is about five minutes’ walk from the cabin, round the edge of the trees without entering them.
That paddock is a fenced grass enclosure with a gate; the fence takes tether chains and pupils climb over it.
It held twelve Hippogriffs on long chains and a class spread among them; wings are given as twelve feet, and one animal flew a full circuit of it.
Make that paddock at least 40 m across.
facts.because: A Hippogriff with twelve-foot wings spans up to 7 m and flies one circuit before landing, while a dozen animals and a class spread out inside. The text gives no size.

facts.text: In September 1995 a long trestle table stood about ten yards from Hagrid’s front door, with pupils working on the grass around it.
Skrewts: crates of about a hundred six-inch hatchlings stood by the cabin in September 1994; by November pupils walked leashed three-foot Skrewts over the lawn, each blasting several yards at a time.
In December 1994 pupils worked at a trestle table behind the cabin, using the building as shelter.
In January 1995 the class passed the horse paddock to a unicorn tied at an edge tree, with the boys left at the paddock fence. Muddy ground served for foals early that year.
In spring 1995 a large patch of freshly dug earth before the cabin held a hundred buried coins for Nifflers, within sight of the carriage window; crates were stacked at the cabin wall.
The June 1996 practical examination, with a Knarl among a dozen hedgehogs, filled the lawn at the Forest edge in sight of Hagrid’s window; lessons there can be seen from Gryffindor’s common room.
Flobberworm lessons (1993) and a salamander bonfire (January 1994) have no stated site.
Classes climb back uphill to the castle steps, or cross the vegetable patch to the greenhouses; the school bell carries faintly across the grounds to them.
Hagrid says he has raised a special herd for lessons over the years; it proves to be the Thestrals, shown inside the Forest.

open: The position of the 1993 paddock relative to the carriage site and Hagrid’s garden is unknown; it should not be merged with the Beauxbatons horse paddock.

beauxbatons-carriage.summary: The Beauxbatons carriage is a powder-blue flying vehicle as big as a large house, drawn by twelve elephant-sized winged palominos. It stayed at Hogwarts from 30 October 1994 to June 1995, standing two hundred yards from Hagrid’s front door near the Forest edge, with a makeshift horse paddock alongside, and served as sleeping quarters for Madame Maxime and about a dozen pupils. It came back briefly in June 1997. Treat it as a dated visitor, not a fixture.

facts.text: Powder-blue and as big as a large house (simply a house in 1997), it looked far bigger than a hundred broomsticks in the sky.
Make the body at least 12 m long and 8 m high.
facts.because: A large house is about 12 m by 10 m over two or more storeys, and inside it must clear a headmistress of about Hagrid’s height, taken as 3.4 m.

facts.text: Twelve winged palomino horses draw it, each the size of an elephant, with hooves larger than dinner plates.
Madame Maxime is within an inch of Hagrid’s height, with a shoe like a child’s sled, and her size is said to explain the carriage and horses.
It must work as a dormitory for about thirteen for eight months, with a door, steps and rooms that admit a person of Hagrid’s size.
facts.because: Pupils are seen climbing in to sleep and the party numbers Maxime plus about a dozen, from late October to June. The interior is never described.

facts.text: It has vast wheels, a door bearing two crossed golden wands each giving off three stars, fold-out golden steps, and windows lit from within at night.
It stood two hundred yards (about 180 m) from Hagrid’s front door, near the edge of the Forest.
A makeshift fenced paddock lies alongside for grazing, with a trough of single-malt whisky in one corner.
Make the paddock at least 40 m square.
facts.because: Twelve elephant-sized horses at 8 m by 4 m each need about 380 m² just to stand, about 20 m square. Grazing, wings and fence walking at least double each side.

facts.text: It is in view from a cabin window and the Owlery, and from the castle entrance the harnessing is seen far across the grounds.
Forest trees begin a short way beyond the paddock; an edge tree used for a lesson and the spot where Crouch appeared both lie just past it.
The walk to the dragon enclosure starts by rounding the paddock’s edge from the carriage door.
It flew in over the Forest canopy on 30 October 1994 and landed before the castle; by next day it stood near the cabin. It left in June 1995.
It returned on the afternoon before the June 1997 funeral, landing at the Forest edge; its distance from the cabin then is unstated.

conflicts.text: The measured two hundred yards sits uneasily with other cues: Harry hears Maxime inside it from Hagrid’s door, in snow it seems to stand next to the cabin, and whisky fumes reach Hagrid’s class. Keep the measured figure.

open: No interior is ever described; layout, rooms and storeys must be designed.
Which side of the cabin it stood on is unstated, beyond being near the Forest edge and in view of one cabin window.

lake.summary: The lake is the large dark body of water in the Hogwarts grounds, lying between the station path and the castle. The castle's cliff rises from its far shore, and the front lawns slope down to it on another side. It can be walked right round: three laps fit into one morning, which limits the shoreline to a few miles. The books give no width, length or depth. The clues suggest an elongated basin, a few hundred yards across where people watch each other over the water at night, at least half a mile on the line from the far bank to the castle, and deep enough in the middle to hide a masted ship. Ron takes it to lie south of the castle. No window is said to show all of it: a high landing shows a piece, classroom windows a wide sheet. The water is usually still and dark, freezes in hard winters, and holds a giant squid, merpeople and Grindylows.

facts.text: Narration calls it great at first sight, and from classroom windows it reads as a wide grey expanse.
Before he has entered it, Harry pictures it as huge and extremely deep, with merpeople living on the bed.
Allow at least half a mile (about 800 m) on the line from the far bank to the castle.
facts.because: The merpeople square is a quarter of a mile (400 m) from the castle, reached by a swim that felt like over twenty minutes from the far bank. Assuming only 0.5 m/s, twenty minutes is 600 m, so about 1,000 m if straight; rounded down because the swim was not straight. A minimum, not a survey.

facts.text: Between Hagrid's side and the site of the Dementor attack the water is probably only a few hundred yards across.
facts.because: By moonlight the watchers on one bank could see Snape conjure stretchers and load bodies on the other, and a Dementor lower its hood, yet a figure there was too distant to make out properly.

facts.text: The whole shore can be walked: two pupils circle it three times one Sunday after breakfast, then go to the library.
One lap is probably no more than two or three miles.
facts.because: Three laps fit between breakfast and a session in the library. At walking pace a long morning covers six to nine miles.

facts.text: The middle must be deep enough to cover a masted ship, which came up there from under the surface.
facts.because: Mast, rigging and hull rose in turn at the centre of the lake until the ship floated clear. This holds unless the whirlpool was a magical gateway; the text does not say.

facts.text: A path from the station ends on one shore; the castle stands on a high cliff on the far side, and the water reaches the foot of that cliff.
Ron reads a high passage with a partial lake view as the south side of the castle, so the lake lies at least partly south.
Lawns run down from the castle front to the water, and the walk from the doors to the gates passes it.
From the top of the lawns the surface is in open view out to its centre, with the muddy banks visible.
Indoor views differ: a small piece from a landing seven flights up, a wide stretch from classrooms, swimmers from a corridor near the hospital wing, the shore beech from a dormitory.
Treat castle views as partial: no passage shows the whole lake, and Moody's classroom window shows only the top sail of the moored ship.
facts.because: Every indoor view is described as a part. The hull of a ship anchored in the shallows is not mentioned from that window, so terrain or angle hides the near shore there.

facts.text: Reports put the Slytherin common room and the Chamber tunnels beneath it, and Myrtle says a flush can carry her down to it.
The surface is normally calm: black at night, steel or iron grey in cold weather, blue or clear green in summer sun.
A giant squid lives in it, lying in warm shallow water close enough for pupils to touch its tentacles, and lifting them clear of the surface in summer.
Merpeople live in it, and Grindylows lurk in the deep weed.
First-years cross in a fleet of small self-moving boats, four to a boat, from the station shore to the cliff.
People can swim in it: Krum dives in from the ship in January 1995, and pupils swim near the squid in June 1996.
Hard winters freeze it: solid in December 1991, skated on in late 1995. It stays open water in January 1995.
Autumn rain raises its level (October 1992), and a storm roughens it for the crossing of 1 September 1994.
The Durmstrang ship lies moored on it from 30 October 1994 to the end of that school year.
During the battle of May 1998 it breaks like rough sea although the night is windless.

conflicts.text: Harry sees the water a mile below the flying car, yet moments later the dead car falls towards the castle wall just ahead. Treat the mile as loose; it is not a cliff height.

open: Outline of the lake. No length, width or shape is given; an elongated basin satisfies the night sightlines and the long swim together.
How far the water runs against or under the castle rock, given the reported Slytherin common room beneath it.

lake-shore.summary: The lakeshore is the band of bank, shallows and lakeside grass around the lake, reached from the castle down the lawns and from the station by a steep path through pines. The banks are soft and muddy, and the water deepens gradually from knee to waist height over silt and slick flat stones. The chief landmark is a large beech at the water's edge, tall enough to pick out directly from a Gryffindor dormitory window, with dense bushes nearby and open grass where pupils sit. Other bushes and shrubs stand along the bank, one at the very edge on Hagrid's side. Banks are fixed only as pairs: the beech looks across to the funeral site, and a spot near Hagrid's looks straight across to where Sirius collapsed in 1994. The far-side bank is within a ten-minute run of the library.

facts.text: On 24 February 1995 Harry ran from the library to the judges' bank round the far side in under ten minutes.
By the shore route the far-side bank is probably under a mile from the front doors.
facts.because: After waking at 9.20, talking, and running through the castle, Harry had perhaps seven minutes on open ground. A flat-out run, ending with a stitch, covers about a mile at most in that time.

facts.text: A short walk round from the lawns reaches a bank hidden from passers-by behind shrubs.
Wading out, the water passes the knee and reaches the waist before there is any need to swim.
The beech is large and, seen from a dormitory, towering; its shade takes a group of four sitting on the grass.
The beech stands on the water's edge, and the same tree is in use in the parents' generation and in the 1990s.
A window beside one bed in the Gryffindor boys' dormitory looks directly towards the beech.
From the beech the funeral site and tomb lie across the water, reflected in it.
A spot a short way round from the lawns looks straight across to where Sirius collapsed in June 1994; that bank can be picked out by eye in daylight.
Hagrid's front door looks out towards the lake, and a bush right at the waterline on that side faces the attack site across the water.
A grassy slope climbs from the lakeside towards Hagrid's and the Forest.
The funeral seats stood very close to the bank where the judges met the Merchieftainess in 1995.
A steep narrow path from the station bends down through pines to the shore facing the castle.
From the waterside bush the castle front is clear enough to count windows along from the West Tower.
Banks are soft and muddy with lakeside grass behind them; underfoot in the water are silt and slick flat stones.
Dense bushes stand near the beech with open grass between, and pupils sit on the bank with bare feet in the water.
Elsewhere are a tangle of shrubs and a waterline bush with a branch low enough to serve as a step.
From the castle the way is down the lawns. A path also runs up from the lake towards the castle, and the edge can be followed round.
Second task, 24 February 1995: seats from the dragon enclosure stood in packed stands along the bank facing the lawns.
The same day the judges' gold-draped table stood at the muddy water's edge on another bank, with champions spaced ten feet apart beside it.
Judges and stands faced each other over open water, close enough for the crowd to see a waist-deep swimmer.
facts.because: Bagman's magnified voice went out across the water towards the stands, and Harry hears the crowd laughing at him as he stands in the shallows.

facts.text: June 1994: at least a hundred Dementors ring a group on the lakeside grass, the nearest about ten feet away.
From 30 October 1994 the Durmstrang ship lies anchored in the shallows with a plank to the bank.

open: Positions of the beech, Hagrid's side, the funeral bank and the second-task stands around the shore. The text gives pairs of opposite banks, not a plan.

lake-underwater.summary: The underwater terrain is the lake floor beyond the shallows, known only from the swim of the second task in Book 4. The bottom drops out of sight soon after the wading margin. Heading for the middle, a swimmer passes tangled black weed and wide mud plains strewn with dull stones, then a light-green weed bed two feet deep that runs beyond sight, then great stretches of black mud that cloud when stirred, ending at a large painted rock near the merpeople village. Visibility is about ten feet. The light is a failing grey, and the water overhead stays dark until close to the surface. No depth is stated: an aside says fathoms, and every clue points to a basin far deeper than a swimmer's dive, so model at least 100 feet.

facts.text: No depth figure is given. An aside calls the lake fathoms deep, and Harry thinks of it as very deep.
Swimming out, Harry soon loses sight of the bottom even with improved eyesight, then dives and keeps going deeper towards the middle.
Rising from the village with two passengers is slow work, and he judges himself still very deep because the water above is so dark.
Daylight shows only near the top, and Harry's breath fails with about ten feet left to climb. That is the last stretch, not the depth.
Allow at least 100 feet (30 m) of water over the deep basin.
facts.because: A whole masted ship rose from under the middle, and a mast alone is likely to exceed 60 feet. Daylight fails well above the bottom; water with ten-foot visibility goes dark at roughly 60 to 100 feet. Assumptions from real lakes, not text.

facts.text: Visibility is about ten feet, so obstacles appear with little warning.
The light-green weed bed is two feet deep and extends beyond the limit of sight.
Beyond the weed the black mud is so extensive that Harry crosses it for what feels like at least twenty minutes.
The round trip took about an hour: Cedric, after getting lost, came back one minute over; Harry, first to arrive, came back well after.
On Harry's route the order from the bank is silt and stones, dark weed forests and mud plains, light-green weed, black mud, painted rock, village.
The light is a dim grey that weakens with depth, the distance turns opaque, and mud rises in clouds when disturbed.
Small silver fish, large blackened logs and dense clumps of weed lie along the way.
Grindylows hide in the light-green weed and seize ankles and clothing from below.
Champions reach it by Gillyweed, Bubble-Head Charm or part Transfiguration. Harry's Gillyweed lasts a little over an hour.
Underwater, speech gives only bubbles and a spell makes jets of hot water, while ghost and merpeople voices still carry.

open: How the shallows step down to the basin. The bottom drops out of view quickly, but the text does not say whether by a slope or a shelf.

merpeople-village.summary: The merpeople village is a settlement of stone dwellings on the lake bed, in deep water well out from the second-task starting bank and about a quarter of a mile from the castle. It is reached across black mud past a large rock painted with a hunting scene. Rough stone houses streaked with algae have dark windows and doors, and some are also called caves. They grow more numerous further in, some with weed gardens, and they line a central square. There a gigantic merperson statue, roughly cut from a boulder, rises behind an open space where a choir sang during the second task of Book 4. Loose rocks litter the floor. It is big enough to have a corner, a square and a crowd of residents, but no count is given.

facts.text: The square is about a quarter of a mile from Harry's trunk in the castle.
It lies on the lake bed, with the water above it still deep and dark.
It is reached beyond the weed bed by what feels like at least twenty minutes' swim over black mud, past a large painted rock.
Houses surround the swimmer at once and grow more numerous further in, enough to make a corner and a house-lined square.
A whole crowd floats in the square; one merman is seven feet tall, and about twenty escort the swimmers on the surface.
The statue is a gigantic merperson cut from a single boulder.
The statue's tail is several feet across at least.
facts.because: Four people are bound along the tail, with one tied between two others.

facts.text: Houses are rough stone streaked with algae, with dark window openings and doors; the text also calls them caves.
Some houses have weed gardens, and a pet Grindylow is tethered outside one door.
A large rock on the approach is painted with spear-carrying merpeople hunting what seems to be the giant squid.
Loose rocks, some sharp enough to cut weed rope, lie on the lake bed by the statue.
Second task, 24 February 1995: a choir sang in the square, and four hostages were tied to the statue's tail with thick weed rope.
During the task spear-carrying merpeople kept champions from freeing other hostages until Harry threatened them.

conflicts.text: A quarter of a mile from the castle sits oddly with a swim of well over twenty minutes by a fast swimmer. Either the swim started far off and wandered, or the quarter mile is loose.

open: Number of dwellings and height of the statue. Neither is given; allow enough houses for a village with a corner and a square.

durmstrang-ship.summary: The Durmstrang ship is the visiting school's vessel, moored in the lake shallows from 30 October 1994 until the end of that school year. It is a dark masted sailing ship with rigging, black sails, portholes and a deck, looking like a wreck brought back up, and it serves as the delegation's lodging. It arrived by rising whole out of the middle of the lake, then glided to the bank and anchored with a plank to the shore. It lay in sight of the top of the lawns and was passed on the walk from the front doors to the gates. Its sails show from the Owlery, and its top sail from Moody's classroom. Its length is never given, but about a dozen students and their headmaster lived aboard for most of a year, so it cannot be small.

facts.text: It lodges the delegation for the whole school year: the headmaster in his own cabin, his students sent back to it after the feast.
Crouch, when deranged, puts the Durmstrang party at a round dozen students.
Its sails can be seen from the Owlery, and its top sail from Moody's classroom window.
Allow a ship of at least 100 feet with masts of 60 feet or more.
facts.because: Portholes imply a deck below the main deck. About thirteen people live aboard for eight months and the students work the ship, and its top sail shows from a castle window. Sizes assume a small square-rigged ship.

facts.text: A masted sailing ship with rigging, black sails, a deck and dim lights at the portholes, with a thin bony look, as if a sunken wreck had been raised.
It lies anchored in the lake shallows, near enough for a plank to reach the bank.
The lawns lead down to it from the front doors, and the anchor and plank can be heard from the top of them.
The walk from the front doors to the gates passes it, and so does the way from the pitch back to the castle.
A plank links ship and bank, and the party walks uphill across the lawns to the front doors, cutting channels in winter snow.
The side can be climbed from the deck for a dive into the lake.
30 October 1994: after bubbles and a whirlpool at the centre of the lake, it rises, floats clear and glides to the bank.
Winter 1994: it pitches in high wind with sails billowing, and has ice on the portholes and frost on the rigging at Christmas.
Still moored in June 1995. Krum says the students did the sailing, so they can take it home; the departure is not shown.

open: Number of masts. The arrival names one mast; later passages speak of sails and a topmost sail.

dumbledores-tomb.summary: Dumbledore's tomb is a white marble tomb beside the lake, permanent from June 1997. It stands near the water's edge, by the bank the judges used for the second task, and is reflected in the lake, so that it shows from the beech across the water. It formed on the day of the funeral, when white flames around the body and its marble table left a marble tomb encasing both. For that one day hundreds of golden chairs stood in rows with a central aisle, all facing the table, on the bank beside the water, with a view across the lake to the Forest. Outside mourners already filled half of them when the school arrived. In March 1998 Voldemort split the tomb lengthwise, and no repair is described.

facts.text: It stands beside the lake and is reflected in the water.
It lies across the lake from the beech, and the two are linked by a walk round the bank.
The funeral seats were very close to the bank where Dumbledore spoke with the Merchieftainess in February 1995.
From the site the view across the water runs to the Forest edge. The route from the castle leaves the front doors and heads down to the lake.
It is larger than a tall man lying down, since it encases a long thin body and the table under it.
facts.because: No dimensions are given. It replaced the table with the body on it, and it splits along the full length of the body.

facts.text: Allow at least 800 chairs for the funeral; that is still hundreds.
facts.because: Mourners held half the chairs before the school sat. If 400 pupils and staff took the rest, even with some pupils gone home, the total is 800. At 0.5 m a chair and 1 m a row, twenty rows of forty fill about 21 m by 20 m.

facts.text: It is white marble, the same material as the Potters' headstone in Godric's Hollow, and Harry remembers it as grand.
June 1997: hundreds of chairs in rows with a central aisle stood on the bank, all facing a marble table at the front.
The chairs were golden, and at least one row ended beside the water.
Outside mourners already filled half the chairs when the school arrived, and more kept coming; some pupils had been taken home.
The block was deep: from a row end by the lake only scraps of the address carried, over hundreds of heads, and the front was not clearly visible.
The back row held Grawp, a giant in clothes each as big as a small marquee; Madame Maxime took two and a half chairs.
Merpeople sang just under the surface by the seats, and centaurs stood in the distant trees; their arrows landed well away from the crowd.
White flames took body and table, and when the fire vanished the tomb stood in their place.
March 1998: Voldemort splits it along its whole length and takes the wand from under the hands. No repair is described.

open: Size of the tomb. It must read as a white shape from across the water, so avoid a small marker.
State after March 1998: split open or repaired. The text does not say.

forest-general.summary: The Forbidden Forest is the great old wood on the school grounds, forbidden to pupils. Its near edge lies at Hagrid’s cabin, at the foot of the lawns, and from the front doors its treetops stand in the distance, towards the June sunset. No size is given, but times on foot show it is very large: twenty minutes on a path takes you out of sight of the sky, and the deepest known sites are an hour or more in. Near the edge a class can walk among the trees; further in they crowd together, branches tangle, the canopy shuts out all light, and paths fade into roots, brambles, thorn and nettles. Narrow earth tracks run inward and fork, and at least two separate routes exist. Clearings large and small open within it. Oak, beech, yew, sycamore and pine are named. The only height given is twenty feet, for pines a giant can uproot, and others tower well above that. Centaurs, unicorns, Thestrals, giant spiders and Bowtruckles live here. The text supplies no map.

facts.text: Dumbledore places it in the school grounds; Hagrid’s cabin at the foot of the lawns marks its near edge.
From the front steps and lawns it stands towards the setting sun in spring and summer, so broadly west of the castle front.
facts.because: The sun sinks behind or towards its treetops on three evenings, seen from the steps and from Gryffindor Tower. One morning passage disagrees; see conflicts.

facts.text: Its treetops look distant from the front doors; the flying lawn lies across the grounds from it, and it stands to the right on the way down to the pitch.
Part of its margin faces the lake.
facts.because: From the funeral seats on the shore Harry looks out over the water towards the Forest and sees centaurs among its trees.

facts.text: A school boundary lies on this side of the grounds: Hagrid says Grawp smashed through it by the Forest in 1998.
Treat the Forest as at least 4 km across and do not model it as a strip of woodland behind the cabin.
facts.because: Twenty minutes on a path at 4 km/h is 1.3 km and half an hour off it at 1.5 km/h is 0.75 km, about 2 km before the last carried stretch. Ten minutes by car at 15 km/h agrees. If that is near the middle, the wood is at least 4 km wide.

facts.text: Deep sites lie an hour or so from the edge: twenty minutes on a path and half an hour off it still leave the spider hollow further on.
facts.because: Those are the timed legs of the 1993 walk; the unicorn and Grawp routes also add half an hour or more beyond untimed earlier stretches.

facts.text: The only stated tree height is Hermione’s twenty feet, for the pines Grawp rips up.
Many trees stand well above that: Harry lands a broom in a towering beech, an oak towers too, and Grawp’s head fits just under the boughs at a clearing edge.
facts.because: Towering is the narrator’s word for beech and oak. The sixteen-foot giant’s head gives a floor for the lowest branches, not the treetops.

facts.text: Model mature oak and beech at no less than about 20 m, and treat 6 m pines as the small end of the wood.
facts.because: Twenty feet is about 6 m. Real trees of these species reach 25 to 30 m, and a flyer lowers himself through the top branches here; the text gives no figure.

facts.text: Density rises inward: from the air the canopy hides a running man, after twenty minutes no stars show, and further in no light reaches the ground.
The trees are old, close-set and gnarled, with tangled branches; Harry contrasts a younger, wider-spaced wood with clearer ground.
Gaps still pass large bodies on some routes: spiders with heads ten feet up carry boys between the trees, and a car winds out by the widest gaps, losing a mirror to an oak.
facts.because: Off-path movement is narrated, not surveyed. A car needs gaps of about 2 m on that one route, so spacing is tight but not solid.

facts.text: Single trees are massive: one oak takes Hagrid and two pupils behind it.
A narrow winding earth track leaves the edge and forks left and right a little way in; deeper in, paths become overgrown and nearly impossible to trace.
At least two inward routes exist: Hagrid’s way towards Grawp and the older path Harry followed towards Aragog.
facts.because: Harry notes that Hermione has taken a different path from the Grawp visit. Any junction between them is unstated.

facts.text: The floor is leaf-covered earth with roots and stumps; brambles, thorn, nettles and knotgrass fill the off-path ground, which falls towards the hollow. Running water is heard near one path.
Smaller clearings occur throughout, such as a shadowy one below a beech (1992) and a ring of thick trees under a branch roof with room for a car (1993).
Inhabitants include centaurs, unicorns, Thestrals, giant spiders, Bowtruckles, birds and deer; Hippogriffs come out of it in 1993 and a car ran wild in it. Werewolves are only rumoured.
Pupils are barred by a rule repeated year after year, not by any barrier; Hagrid, detentions, lessons and work parties all go in.
A gale in its trees is heard in Gryffindor Tower, birds bursting from it are seen from the front doors, and walkers entering it are visible from Umbridge’s office window.
From the Owlery one looks down on its canopy beyond Hagrid’s cabin, swaying in any breeze.
Giants damage it: Grawp uproots and smashes trees from 1996, and two others knock trees down on the march out in May 1998.
Sirius Black says he lived here as a dog during 1993–94; no den or shelter is described.
In May 1998 it creaks on a windless night, and Harry drops the Resurrection Stone somewhere in it, never recovered.

conflicts.text: Evening passages put the setting sun behind the Forest as seen from the steps and Gryffindor Tower, yet one clear morning Harry squints into the sun while watching its edge from a Gryffindor dormitory.

open: Size and outline are never given. Keep the walking times, choose a shape no smaller than the estimated extent, and do not fix bearings between sites.
Whether the wood continues past the school boundary is unstated.

forest-edge.summary: The Forest edge is the line where the lawns meet the trees, running past Hagrid’s cabin and on around the grounds. Its outermost ground is earthy and scattered with twigs, with single landmark trees: a large sycamore near the cabin, wide and tall oaks, and clumps that screen whatever lies behind them. Coming out of the Forest the trees thin gradually, then stop at open grass. It is long: about five minutes’ walk separates the cabin from the 1993 creature paddock, and further round it goes so far that castle and lake vanish. Gryffindor Tower overlooks it, and from the edge near the cabin one can see the castle’s front doors and the Whomping Willow; elsewhere the stadium is in view. A few minutes’ run uphill leads back to the castle.

facts.text: The edge lies across the grounds from the castle, with Hagrid’s cabin standing on it.
It runs a long way: five minutes’ walk from the cabin to the creature paddock, and far enough round beyond the horse paddock to lose sight of castle and lake.
facts.because: Both walks follow the tree line. The first is timed; the second is judged from Harry’s impatience and his hurried return.

facts.text: From trees near the cabin one sees its front door and, with a small head movement, the distant castle doors; a clump further round commands the Whomping Willow.
A route from the greenhouses past the Whomping Willow reaches the trees while staying hidden from Hagrid’s front door.
From the trees at the end of one Forest path the Quidditch stadium is in view, with sloping lawns leading up from it to the castle.
Gryffindor Tower overlooks it: dormitory and common-room windows show figures moving along the edge, teaching there or leaving the trees.
Named edge trees are a large sycamore near the cabin, a wide oak that hides two people, a tall oak beyond the horse paddock, and screening clumps.
The outer ground is earthy and strewn with twigs, with roots among the first trees; it was dry under one clump in June 1994.
Coming out of the Forest the trees thin gradually until sky shows, and then open ground begins.
The screen closes fast: a short way inside the trees Harry cannot see Hagrid’s garden at all, though he can still hear the back door and voices.
A narrow earth track starts at the very edge not far from the cabin; elsewhere people simply step in among the trees or come out of them near his door.
From the trees just past the horse paddock the front doors are only minutes away uphill at a run.
facts.because: Harry sprints up through the grounds and into the castle, and is in a second-floor corridor about five minutes later.

facts.text: In May 1998 Dementors patrol the outer trees, and Voldemort halts here to address the castle before marching up the lawn.
The open margin takes temporary set-ups: a champions’ tent before the screening trees (1994), a tethered unicorn (1995), and the house-sized carriage landing here (1997).

open: The order of features along the edge is only partly fixed: cabin, then carriage and horse paddock, then the dragon site. Where the 1993 paddock, the Willow clump and the stadium view fall in that line is unknown.

aragogs-hollow.summary: Aragog’s hollow is a vast, tree-free depression deep in the Forest, towards its heart, where the giant spider colony lived. About twenty minutes on a path, then at least half an hour off it going downhill, still leaves you short of it; the car escape to the Forest edge took ten minutes. A steep slope falls to a leaf-covered floor open to the stars, with a dome of misty webbing at the centre. Aragog was as big as a small elephant, his descendants as big as carthorses, and they packed the hollow in 1993. Voldemort camped here in May 1998, with the spiders driven out.

facts.text: It lies deep in the Forest; the captives are carried towards its very heart.
On foot: about twenty minutes along a path until no stars show, then what seems at least half an hour off it, slowly and downhill, then an untimed carried stretch.
The car takes about ten rough minutes from the hollow to the Forest edge, by the widest gaps.
Place it at least about 2 km inside the Forest.
facts.because: Twenty minutes at 4 km/h plus half an hour at 1.5 km/h is about 2 km before the carried stretch; ten minutes by car at 15 km/h is 2.5 km.

facts.text: A vast hollow cleared of trees and open to the stars, with a leaf-strewn floor and a steep rim a car can drive down and climb.
Make the hollow at least 100 m across at the rim.
facts.because: Fifty carthorse-sized spiders needing 10 m by 10 m each take 5,000 m², a circle about 80 m wide, before adding the web and a slope for a car.

facts.text: Colony spiders are black, hairy and eight-eyed, as big as carthorses in 1993 and compared with a small car in 1998.
A full-grown spider’s head can reach about ten feet above the ground.
facts.because: Ron stares at a point that high just behind Harry at the moment one seizes him. This is one observation, not a rule for all of them.

facts.text: Aragog is as big as a small elephant, grey-flecked and blind; he hatched at about Pekinese size. Hagrid got his dead body out of the Forest and heaved it into a pit.
No count is given, but the colony must number dozens at the very least.
facts.because: From one pair it spread across the hollow, closed on the captives from all sides as a solid wall, and several were knocked aside by the car.

facts.text: A dome of misty webbing stands at the centre, and Aragog comes out of it and backs into it.
Allow the web dome at least 5 m of height and 10 m of width.
facts.because: It shelters a spider as big as a small elephant, about 3 m high, with legs spreading several metres wider.

facts.text: Harry recognises the 1993 route in June 1996, by then obstructed by brambles, undergrowth and a fallen sapling.
Hagrid alone could approach safely: he calls it unsafe for others in 1996, and after Aragog’s death in 1997 the colony no longer lets him near its webs.
In May 1998 Harry reaches it minutes after meeting a patrol in deep trees; the march back runs through close-growing trees that gradually thin.
In May 1998 Death Eaters camp here round a central fire, with two giants at the margin, Hagrid tied to a nearby tree and only remnants of the web.
By then the spiders have been driven out, and some climb the castle walls during the battle.

conflicts.text: In 1993 it is a steep-sided hollow; in 1998 the same site is called a clearing, with no slope mentioned.

open: Depth of the hollow and its exact rim width are unstated.

centaur-territory.summary: The centaurs’ territory has no fixed boundary or settlement: the herd treats the whole Forest as its own, and what the books show are clearings where they are met. A dim clearing far along the old spider path held about fifty in June 1996. Smaller groups appear elsewhere, and in 1997 they watched a funeral from the trees towards the lake.

facts.text: About fifty armed centaurs surround three humans in one clearing in June 1996; Hagrid earlier says only that there are a fair few.
Make that clearing at least 30 m across.
facts.because: Fifty horse-bodied centaurs in one ring at 1.5 m spacing make a circle about 75 m round and 24 m wide, with the centre clear and room to move behind them.

facts.text: Elsewhere they appear in small groups: Ronan and Bane in 1992, Magorian with four or five others in 1996.
The 1996 clearing is dim and damp, on the old path towards Aragog after a long walk, past where the canopy shuts out light. Harry thinks it the middle of the Forest.
Other meetings happen in a clearing beyond the left fork (1992) and in thick knotgrass on the way back from Grawp’s clearing (1996).
In June 1997 they stand half-hidden among trees across the water from the funeral seats; their arrows fall far short of the crowd.
No dwelling, camp or settlement is ever described; treat the clearings as meeting grounds, not a village.
facts.because: Every sighting is of centaurs among trees or in clearings, and nothing built is mentioned.

facts.text: Classroom eleven, made to imitate Firenze’s natural habitat, suggests mossy earth, leafy trees, dappled green light, boulders and stumps.
facts.because: Firenze says the room copies his home in the Forest. It is an enchanted classroom, not the place itself, so it shows character rather than layout.

facts.text: They bar Hagrid from 1996 after his rescue of Firenze, and Firenze, banished, says that even going too near could start a fight.
In June 1996 Grawp breaks into the clearing between two trunks, scatters the herd and smashes more trees chasing it.
In May 1998 centaurs are present near the thinning trees as Voldemort’s march leaves the Forest.

conflicts.text: Ownership is disputed: centaurs call it their Forest, Umbridge says the Ministry permits them certain land, and Hagrid denies they control who comes and goes.

open: Where the herd actually lives, and the limits of the ground it claims, are never shown.

unicorn-clearing.summary: The unicorn clearing is a deep-Forest clearing where a dead unicorn was found in 1992, nearly half an hour’s walk past the point where the two detention parties regrouped, with the path almost lost among thick trees. It is seen through the boughs of an ancient oak, with a bush at its edge.

facts.text: Nearly half an hour’s walk beyond the regrouping point, itself reached by an untimed stretch, until the path is almost lost among thick trees.
It is seen through the tangled boughs of an ancient oak; a bush grows at its edge, and dark leaves cover the ground.
In 1992 a dead white unicorn lay here, and a hooded figure fed on it until a centaur drove the figure off.
The way back to the path runs through a dense patch of trees, with low branches that a centaur’s rider must duck.

thestral-clearing.summary: This is the place about ten minutes’ walk into the Forest where Hagrid feeds the Hogwarts Thestrals, a dark stand of close-set trees that keeps out the snow, with gnarled yews among them. The herd’s real home is the Forest at large: it began with six animals and, if each of the hundred or so school coaches takes one, must now number about a hundred.

facts.text: About ten minutes’ walk in from the Forest edge with a class in winter, and not far in by Hagrid’s own account.
The trees stand so close that it is as dark as twilight and no snow lies on the ground; gnarled yews are named.
A double class fits among the trunks, with half a cow laid on the ground and animals coming in between the trees.
Hagrid says the herd grew from one male and five females, and that Tenebrus was the first foal born in the Forest.
If each of the hundred or so school coaches has its own animal, the herd numbers about a hundred.
facts.because: About a hundred coaches wait at the start of term, each with a creature between its shafts, and Hagrid says pulling them is the herd’s main work. No census exists.

facts.text: At least four come to one feed; eight or nine gather around two pupils deep in the Forest in June 1996.
They range well beyond this spot: one rose above the treetops in view of the Owlery in 1995, and others came to pupils near the centaur clearing, on a different path.
The route to Grawp’s clearing passes this site and carries on a long way past it.
Only people who have seen death can see the animals; in 1995 Harry, Neville and one Slytherin could. Hagrid has trained them to leave owls alone.
They are large enough to ride with no saddle: in June 1996 Harry mounts from a stump, and they climb out steeply through the topmost branches.

conflicts.text: The feeding place is a close stand of trees in the lesson chapter but is called a clearing when passed in May 1996.

open: Where the site lies relative to the track from the edge is unstated.

grawps-clearing.summary: Grawp’s clearing is the bare patch deep in the Forest where Hagrid kept his sixteen-foot half-brother tied up in 1996. It lies a long way past the Thestral site, off the path, through brambles and thorn and then fifteen more minutes past nettles. The giant had uprooted the trees around him, leaving bare ground ringed by heaped trunks and boughs, with ropes running from his wrists and ankles to the biggest surviving trees. He broke free in June 1996 and had moved to a mountain cave by that September.

facts.text: From the cabin: a path past the Thestral site and a long way beyond, then off it towards the Forest’s heart through brambles and thorn that hold pupils up for minutes at a time.
After a halt, fifteen more minutes past nettles bring the party to the barricade.
The walk in takes at least 25 minutes and probably well over 40.
facts.because: Ten minutes to the Thestral site and the final fifteen are the only timed parts. The long stretch past the Thestrals and the slow off-path struggle come on top.

facts.text: Place it at least about 1.5 km inside the Forest.
facts.because: Ten minutes at 4 km/h plus fifteen at 2 km/h give 1.2 km, before adding the untimed stretches.

facts.text: The way out skirts the same nettles to rejoin the path, then runs ten minutes to thinning trees with the stadium in view.
A bare patch of earth with trees torn up at the roots all round; the trunks and boughs lie heaped into a rough fence.
Make the bare ground at least 15 m across.
facts.because: A 5 m giant lies curled near the middle, Hagrid stands 3 m from him with a long bough and backs away from him, and the ring of heaped trunks lies beyond that.

facts.text: Grawp is at least sixteen feet tall yet called small for a giant, with feet like sledges nearly Harry’s length and hands the size of beach umbrellas.
Asleep, his curled back looks like an earth mound nearly Hagrid’s height and broad enough for three to stand on, with a boulder-sized head beside it.
Inside the ring Hagrid can stand about ten feet from him.
Ropes as thick as saplings run from his wrists and ankles to the largest nearby trunks, which creak when he stands.
A towering pine with a nest in its upper branches stands within his reach; Hermione later puts such pines at twenty feet.
No other creature is met near it, which Harry puts down to the giant. Hagrid says Grawp feeds himself on birds and deer.
From the castle front doors Harry thinks he sees birds burst up over distant treetops soon after, as though another tree had been pulled up.
He bends that pine until the roots crack and has brought it down by the time the visitors are walking away.
By June 1996 he had snapped his ankle ropes and left. Hagrid later reports him calmer, and by September 1996 he has a mountain cave instead.

conflicts.text: Going in, they pass a site ten minutes from the edge and continue a long way before leaving the path; coming out, they rejoin a path only ten minutes from thinning trees, near the stadium.

open: Its bearing and its position relative to Aragog’s hollow are unstated; both lie towards the dark centre, on different paths.

dragon-enclosure.summary: The dragon enclosure was a temporary fenced compound for the first Triwizard task, set up in November 1994 well round the Forest edge, behind a clump of trees and out of sight of castle and lake. Thick plank fencing held four full-grown dragons that reared to fifty feet and lay like small hills when felled, with at least thirty keepers. On task day conjured stands with hundreds of spectators surrounded the same spot. It is a dated set-up, not a permanent site.

facts.text: It lies round the Forest perimeter beyond the horse paddock, so far that castle and lake are out of sight, behind a clump of trees.
Hurrying, Harry covers most of the way back to the castle in about ten minutes.
facts.because: He has just under fifteen minutes left as he speeds up along the edge and under five on reaching the castle, with a stop of a minute or more on the way.

facts.text: The outward stroll from the cabin is long; walk and viewing together fit within about 45 minutes.
facts.because: Hagrid meets Harry at midnight, and Harry turns back with about fifteen minutes left before his one o’clock deadline.

facts.text: Place it at least 1 km from the castle front doors by the walking route.
facts.because: Ten hurried minutes at 6 km/h is 1 km, and the site must also be beyond view of castle and lake.

facts.text: Four full-grown dragons rear inside, their heads reaching fifty feet up on stretched necks; felled, each lies like a small hill and weighs several tons.
A keeper gives their fire a twenty-foot range and says he has seen the Horntail reach forty feet.
At least thirty keepers work here, seven or eight to a dragon, and five of them carry the eggs in a blanket.
Make the fenced area at least 70 m across.
facts.because: Four animals each 15 to 20 m long, kept beyond 12 m (forty feet) of each other’s fire, need about 35 m per dragon in a two-by-two layout, before any room for keepers.

facts.text: The fence is of thick wooden planks with a gap serving as the entrance; nothing roofs it, and the ground inside is hard.
Chains from heavy leather straps at neck and legs are made fast to iron pegs driven deep into the ground.
Occupants are a blue-grey Swedish Short-Snout, a smaller Common Welsh Green, a red Chinese Fireball and a black Hungarian Horntail with bronze tail spikes, plus huge grey eggs.
The Horntail’s spread wings match a small aeroplane’s and her tail cuts yard-long gouges; a flyer climbs high enough for her to look dog-sized.
For the 24 November task stands were conjured at the same spot, seating hundreds around the enclosure.
A champions’ tent facing the approach blocks the view of the dragons; a separate first-aid tent stands outside the fence.
By February 1995 the same seating stands at the lake, so the installation did not last.
facts.because: The narrator says the seats that circled the enclosure in November are now ranged along the far bank.

facts.text: On task day lessons stop at midday so the whole school can walk down to it.

open: Its bearing from the castle is unstated beyond being round the Forest edge past the horse paddock.

quidditch-pitch.summary: The Quidditch pitch is the school's flying field, a flat grass ground inside the stadium, set downhill from the castle at the foot of sloping lawns. Three hoops on golden poles stand at each end, fifty feet high. No dimensions are stated, but the maze of 1995 shows how large it is: the Cup stood at the centre with a straight hundred-yard run to it, and the outer hedge followed the pitch's edge, so the pitch is at least about 200 yards long on that line. The castle overlooks it from a distance, with players visible but not recognisable from the third floor, and from the pitch the front doors appear far off. The Forest lies to the right of anyone walking down, and Hagrid's cabin is the nearest shelter. Compass clues put it west or north-west of the castle. The ground turns to mud in rain and freezes hard in winter.

facts.text: Three goal hoops stand at each end, six in all, each a golden pole ending in a ring.
The hoops are fifty feet high, a figure given twice for Hogwarts and again for the World Cup.
The pitch is at least about 200 yards (180 m) long on one line.
facts.because: The Cup was to stand at the centre of a maze filling the pitch, with the outer hedge at the pitch's edge. Harry saw it a hundred yards off from inside the maze, so centre to edge is at least that.

facts.text: Play uses the full height: Harry climbs to about fifty feet in practice, and Fred puts a fall at about fifty feet.
Keep the stadium at least about 300 yards (270 m) from the castle.
facts.because: Figures at the hoops cannot be told apart from the third floor, which needs a few hundred yards, and the front doors look distant from the pitch. Wood's fifteen minutes, dressing included, sets an upper limit of perhaps 600 yards of lawn.

facts.text: Wood allows Harry fifteen minutes to dress and get from the dormitory down to the pitch, which caps the walk from Gryffindor Tower.
It lies downhill of the castle: sloping lawns lead down from the front steps, and every return is uphill.
Walking down to it, the Forest is on the right and the Owlery tower stands in view.
The stadium is passed on the way from the front doors to the drive and gates.
Castle windows overlook it from far off: upstairs windows, McGonagall's office, the Headmaster's office and a corridor near the hospital wing.
From Umbridge's third-floor office the figures at the hoops are visible but cannot be told apart.
From the pitch the castle's front doors can be seen opening in the distance.
A tree stands about halfway to the castle, on the left going up.
Harry calls Hagrid's cabin the nearest refuge, and Hagrid can follow a match from it with binoculars. A walk from the stadium towards the Forest passes it.
From the air over the pitch, heavy rain on the lake is audible at a distance.
The pitch probably lies west or north-west of the castle.
facts.because: Inside the maze entrance Harry needed north-west for the centre, so champions coming from the castle entered on the south-east. From the broom shed the castle windows glow red at sunset, which needs a viewer on the sunset side.

facts.text: It is smooth flat grass when in normal order.
Its plan is not stated. The only Quidditch pitch given a shape, at the World Cup, is a long oval.
The way in is an opening between stands, and teams walk straight out from the changing rooms.
Use is by booking: captains reserve time, and in 1995 Snape books it repeatedly for Slytherin.
The surface changes with the weather: frost and hard ground in cold spells, deep mud at the centre in rain.
May to June 1995: it carries the third-task maze, first as low hedges, then twenty feet high. It is back in normal use by September 1995.
November 1993: at least a hundred Dementors stand on the ground during a match.

open: Plan shape and width. Only one long dimension can be inferred. A long oval fits the game, but Hogwarts is never described in plan.
Distance from the castle. It is always called distant, and no figure is given.

quidditch-stands.summary: The stands are the raised spectator seating around the Quidditch pitch, built up in banked benches with a front row, a top row and rows between. The text says hundreds of seats, yet the whole school sits here for matches, and the 1994 final implies a crowd of about 800, so model the seats at the very top of 'hundreds': at least 800 to 1,000. They rise high enough for a clear view, though many pupils still bring binoculars. A barrier separates seats from pitch, and stairs lead down to the lawn. The stands have edges and gaps, and one person crosses from stand to stand during a match, so they read as separate blocks rather than a closed ring. A wooden commentator's podium stands among them. Supporters gather at opposite ends. The text mentions no roofs or towers.

facts.text: Hundreds of seats stand raised round the pitch, and hundreds of footsteps are heard climbing the benches before a match.
The whole school turns out for matches in any weather, and the stadium is described as packed.
The crowd at the 1994 final was about 800.
facts.because: Three-quarters of the crowd wore scarlet, and 200 people behind the Slytherin goal wore green. If those 200 were the remaining quarter, the crowd was about 800.

facts.text: Seat at least 800 to 1,000 people, the whole school plus staff. That stays within 'hundreds', at the top end; do not build for two or three hundred.
facts.because: Crowd arithmetic gives about 800. Over a hundred pupils sat one O.W.L. exam, so seven years is 700 or more. About 100 coaches carrying four or five older pupils gives 400 to 500 at the least, plus first-years. Assumes one seat each.

facts.text: At 0.5 m a person, 800 to 1,000 people need 400 to 500 m of bench, for example ten rows of 40 to 50 m.
facts.because: Bench width is an assumption and no row count is given. This also shows that many rows in a closed ring round a 200-yard pitch would seat thousands, not hundreds.

facts.text: Many pupils carry binoculars, play can still be hard to follow from the seats, and Ron uses them to watch a teacher in the stand opposite.
Named tiers include the front row, a few rows up, halfway up, the second-highest row and the top row.
The stands surround the pitch close to its edge, with one stand directly across from another and supporters massed at the two ends.
The stadium is a landmark: the Headmaster's window shows it in the distance, the walk to the gates passes it, and it comes into view at the end of a ten-minute Forest path.
From the end of a stand the stretch of lawn to Hagrid's cabin can be checked.
Seating is banked benches raised high in the air, with people able to pass along behind a row.
The stands probably form separate blocks, not a closed ring.
facts.because: One pupil crosses to the stand where a teacher sits, there is a gap through to the pitch, and the stands have an edge to look round.

facts.text: A barrier runs between seats and pitch, low enough to vault and to pour over.
Sound carries: jeers from halfway up echo round the empty stadium, one camera's clicks sound loud, and commentary echoes over the grounds.
A wooden commentator's podium stands within sight of the play, used with a magical megaphone.
Banners, flags and rosettes are brought by supporters for a match, not fixed decoration.
Stairs lead from the rows down to the lawn, and rows are tight enough that people must stand to let others past.
June 1995: the stands stay in place around the maze, and hundreds of students file into them for the third task.
Autumn 1996: a collision reduces the podium to wooden wreckage. A podium is in use again by March 1997.

conflicts.text: Class-size clues point to a much smaller school: twenty brooms for a two-house first-year class and about twenty earmuffs for a two-house Herbology class suggest under 300 pupils, against a crowd of about 800 and over a hundred pupils in one exam year.

open: Layout of the stands: how many blocks and rows. Separate blocks fit hundreds of seats around so large a pitch; a closed ring does not.
Support structure and height. The text gives no towers, roofs or canopies, so do not add them on assumption.

quidditch-changing-rooms.summary: The changing rooms stand beside the Quidditch pitch, at the foot of the sloping lawns. They form a real building with a roof, a window and doors, and teams walk straight out of it on to the pitch. Inside are benches facing each other, cloak pegs, a cupboard for the balls and a separate Captain's office; showers are mentioned once. A room takes a team of seven with space for a captain to stand and brief them. The text names a Gryffindor changing room and has the opposing team coming from the far side of the pitch, so there are probably at least two rooms. A separate broom shed with a wooden door stands across the damp grass, with a view up to the castle's windows and front steps.

facts.text: They stand beside the pitch, at the foot of the sloping lawns.
Players file straight out of them on to the pitch.
There are probably at least two rooms, on opposite sides of the pitch.
facts.because: A room is named as Gryffindor's, and in a match the opposing team walks out from the other side.

facts.text: A room seats a team of seven on opposite sides, one side against a wall, with space for a captain and his boards.
It is a true building, warm and lit, with a roof that rain drums on, a door and a window; wind can be heard around it.
There are benches and pegs for cloaks.
A cupboard holds the balls, and a crate of them can be carried out to the pitch.
A Captain's office opens off the room.
Showers exist on Fred's word.
The broom shed stands apart, a walk across damp grass from the changing room, and has a wooden door.
From the shed the castle's windows and front steps can be seen up the slope.
From the Great Hall the route is through the Entrance Hall, out by the stone steps and on down the lawns.

open: Number of rooms, and whether each house has its own. The text uses room and rooms loosely.
Whether the building stands free or is built into the stands. The text does not say.

first-task-arena.summary: The first-task arena was the dragon enclosure of Book 4 as fitted out for 24 November 1994: a plank-fenced field at the Forest edge with conjured stands around it. It lay a long way round the Forest perimeter, behind a clump of trees, so that neither castle nor lake could be seen from it, about ten hurried minutes from the front doors. It had held four fully grown dragons and at least thirty keepers at once, so it was large, and the stands took hundreds and hundreds of spectators. Champions entered through a gap in the fence at one end. The nest lay at the far end, where five judges also sat in raised gold-draped seats. Before the gap stood the champions' tent, and outside the fence a first-aid tent divided into canvas cubicles. The seats were moved to the lake for the next task.

facts.text: It is the same spot as the dragon holding enclosure: the stands were conjured where Harry had stood on his earlier visit.
It lies so far round the Forest perimeter that neither castle nor lake is in view.
A clump of trees screens it. The champions' tent stands in front of those trees, facing the approach.
Going back, Harry had just under fifteen minutes in hand on leaving and under five at the front doors: about ten hurried minutes, with one stop.
The first-aid tent stands outside the enclosure.
It had held four fully grown dragons at once, each as big as a small hill, with at least thirty keepers.
Rearing dragons brought their mouths to fifty feet. Keepers warn of fire reaching twenty feet, and forty for the Horntail.
Many hundreds of faces looked down from the stands, and the crowd's feet were heard passing the tent on the way in.
Seat at least 800 to 1,000: the school, staff and guests.
facts.because: All pupils were released to attend, and the same seats were later crammed full by the lake. The 1994 stadium crowd was about 800. Assumes one seat each.

facts.text: Allow an enclosure about 100 yards long at the least.
facts.because: Four dragons taken as about 50 feet long, kept 40 feet out of each other's fire, need about 120 yards in a line, or a block about 60 yards square. Harry also has to squint up the field to read the judges' marks.

facts.text: From Harry's height the crowd's faces shrink to specks and the Horntail looks dog-sized.
The Horntail's spread wings match a small aeroplane, and her tail cuts yard-long gouges in hard ground.
The field is fenced with thick wooden planks, with a gap as the entrance.
Stands rise above the entrant and ringed the enclosure; the ground is hard and has at least one rock.
Five judges sit in gold-draped raised seats at the far end.
The champions' tent has low wooden stools and room to pace. The first-aid tent is split into cubicles by canvas.
From the castle the way is down the front steps and round the Forest edge. Lessons stop at midday so that everyone can get there.
The stands appeared between Harry's night visit and 24 November 1994. By February 1995 the same seats had been moved to the lake.
Ron reports that Krum's dragon crushed about half its real eggs during the task.

open: Bearing from the castle. The text gives only a long way round the Forest edge.

third-task-maze.summary: The third-task maze was a temporary hedge maze grown over the whole Quidditch pitch for 24 June 1995. A hedge twenty feet high ran round the pitch's edge with one entrance gap, and the hedges inside had been low growths a month before. The text calls it vast. The first fork lay about fifty yards in, and near the end a straight run of about a hundred yards led to the Triwizard Cup on a plinth at the centre, which makes the maze at least about 200 yards across. The centre lay north-west of the entrance. Paths were wide enough for a ten-foot Skrewt and a sphinx, and the thick hedges cut off the noise of the crowd in the stands around it. Four staff patrolled the outside. Creatures and spells blocked the way.

facts.text: The hedges are twenty feet high: planned in May and seen at that height in June.
The maze fills the pitch, with the outer hedge running right round its edge, and the text calls it vast.
The first fork is about fifty yards in from the entrance.
From the last fork the Cup is seen on its plinth a hundred yards away, down a straight path.
With the Cup at the centre, the maze is at least about 200 yards across on that line.
facts.because: Bagman says the Cup goes in the centre, and the outer hedge is at the pitch's edge, so the centre is at least the hundred yards of that last straight from the edge.

facts.text: Creatures show the clearance needed: a ten-foot Skrewt, a lion-bodied sphinx, a twelve-foot Dementor shape, and a spider visible above a hedge.
Allow paths at least 6 to 10 feet (2 to 3 m) wide.
facts.because: The sphinx paces from side to side of a path, a ten-foot Skrewt charges along one, and a spider's legs fill another. Widths assumed from those bodies.

facts.text: Harry spends ten minutes among dead ends in one stretch and a few minutes on another path; the total time is not given.
It fills the Quidditch pitch inside the spectator stands, and the return to the castle runs over the grass by the lake and the ship.
From just inside, the centre lies north-west, and later Harry finds he has strayed too far east.
Hedges are dense with brambles. Getting through one takes a blasted hole and hard kicking.
Grass paths include forks, dead ends, parallel runs, crossings and long straights.
Crowd noise vanishes on entry, whether from hedge or enchantment, though Bagman's whistle and a scream still carry.
One gap faces those arriving on the pitch. Champions go in at whistle blasts, in order of points.
Four staff marked with glowing red stars patrol the outside, and red sparks bring rescue.
The Cup stands on a plinth at the centre, and that day it has been made into a Portkey.
Set obstacles are a Boggart, golden mist that swaps ground and sky, Blast-Ended Skrewts, a sphinx and a giant spider.
May 1995: the hedges are low enough to climb over. A month later they stand twenty feet high.
Damage during the task: one hedge holed, and another flattened by the falling spider.
Bagman promises the pitch back afterwards, and it is in ordinary use by September 1995.
The impostor Moody says he cleared obstacles from the patrol line, so the route was emptier than designed.

conflicts.text: Narration returns Harry to the maze edge below the stands; Hermione later speaks of mid-lawn. Use the narrated position.

open: Full plan of the maze. The route fixes only local forks and turns.
Whether the goal hoops stayed up during the maze. The text does not mention them.

greenhouses.summary: The greenhouses are the school's glass teaching houses for Herbology, in the grounds behind the castle, beyond the vegetable patch. There are several, numbered: Greenhouse One for the first-years and Greenhouse Three for more dangerous plants. A Two is implied, the total is never given, and in mist pupils take longer to find the right one. Greenhouse Three holds a two-house class of about twenty at a central trestle bench, with deep trays of about a hundred seedlings, stored pots and compost, and flowers as big as umbrellas hanging from the ceiling, so these are large working halls and not garden sheds. They have glass walls and roofs, lockable doors and soil to grow in. From outside them the Whomping Willow can be seen in the distance, and pupils leaving them come within calling range of the castle's stone steps. A compost heap lies near by, and people can hide behind them.

facts.text: There are at least three: Greenhouse One and Greenhouse Three are named, which implies a Two.
facts.because: Numbers one and three are used as names. No other number appears anywhere in the books.

facts.text: The total is not given. They are enough alike and numerous enough that mist slows pupils in finding the right one.
facts.because: Mist delays the class in locating the right building.

facts.text: Greenhouse Three takes a two-house class of about twenty, working four to a tray.
Twenty pupils at four to a tray need at least five deep trays, together holding about a hundred Mandrake seedlings.
facts.because: Twenty divided by four, with the hundred or so seedlings shown in a row of trays.

facts.text: Allow Greenhouse Three at least about 15 m by 8 m.
facts.because: Twenty pupils at trays need about 3 square metres each with aisles, so 60, plus a central bench, stored pots and sacks, and dangerous plants kept out of reach. An assumption, to stop it reading as a garden shed.

facts.text: Flowers as big as umbrellas hang from the ceiling of Three, and cabbage-sized blooms open in late spring.
They stand behind the castle.
From the castle the walk crosses the vegetable patch, and so does the walk from Hagrid's lesson ground; in snow the way across can need clearing.
They probably stand near the castle wall, with the patch between them and the lawns.
facts.because: A car swerving away from the castle wall crossed greenhouses, then patch, then lawns, while a walker from the door crosses the patch first.

facts.text: The Whomping Willow is visible in the distance from outside them, and a route hidden from Hagrid's door runs from them past the Willow to the Forest.
On leaving a greenhouse, pupils can see the castle's stone steps and be hailed from them.
Harry gets from Moody's office to Greenhouse Three in about ten minutes at speed.
The castle's bell carries to them across the grounds.
They have glass walls that a thrown pod bounces off, a roof loud under rain, and panes that mist over in cold weather.
Doors lock, and they grow very hot under summer sun.
Inside, plants grow in soil and deep trays, and spilt beans flower at once on the floor.
Sprout carries a large key on her belt. Pupils use only Greenhouse One until their second year, when Three is opened to them.
First-years go three times a week, and classes queue and change over at the door.
A central trestle bench takes earmuffs, with pots under it, sacks of compost near by and gloves, goggles, secateurs and a watering can in use.
Dangerous plants include Venomous Tentacula, whose long feelers reach for people, and Snargaluff stumps with thorny vines.
Lesson plants named include Puffapods, Bubotubers, Flutterby Bush, Bouncing Bulbs, Screechsnaps and Abyssinian Shrivelfigs.
A compost heap lies near by, and the space behind them can hide people.
September 1992 to spring 1993: Mandrakes grow in Three, get socks and scarves in the winter blizzard, and turn rowdy by March.

conflicts.text: Book 1 puts them behind the castle, yet in Book 4 pupils leaving them climb the stone steps and are hailed from those steps. The two fit if they lie round a side of the castle, within reach of the steps.

open: Total number and arrangement: a row, a cluster, or a range. The text gives neither.

vegetable-patch.summary: The vegetable patch is the school's cultivated ground between the castle and the greenhouses, crossed on the usual walk to Herbology. The books also call it vegetable patches, vegetable gardens and a vegetable path, so it may be several beds with walkways. It is reached from the castle or from Hagrid's lesson ground. It lies a little off the direct line from the front steps to Hagrid's cabin, and a low stone wall stands there. From it the dark mass of the Forest and the far-off cabin lights can be seen. School cabbages suffer from slugs, and the ground floods in heavy rain. Its size is not given.

facts.text: It lies between the castle and the greenhouses, so pupils cross it on the way to Herbology.
It is also crossed on the way from Hagrid's lesson ground to the greenhouses.
A swerving car crossed greenhouses, then patch, then lawns, then reached the Willow.
It is a detour from the front steps to Hagrid's, not on the direct line.
From it the Forest and the far-off lights of Hagrid's cabin are in view.
It is probably several beds with walkways, as the text calls it patches, gardens and a path.
facts.because: The same ground is named as vegetable patches, vegetable gardens and a vegetable path in different books.

facts.text: A low stone wall stands at it.
Hagrid says slugs are ruining the school cabbages; the text does not say this bed grows them.
After a talk with Sprout here in spring 1997, Slughorn carries off an armful of leafy plants.
It floods in storms: sodden in September 1994, under water in October 1995.

open: Size and outline. The text says only that it is walked across.

flying-lawn.summary: The flying lawn is a smooth stretch of grass used for first-year flying lessons, on the far side of the grounds from the Forbidden Forest, reached down the sloping lawns from the front steps. An oak stands close by.

facts.text: It lies across the grounds from the Forest, which shows in the distance, reached down the sloping lawns from the front steps.
A lesson sets out twenty school brooms in lines for two houses of first-years.
The oak is tall: a hovering pupil is level with its top branches, and McGonagall speaks of a fifty-foot dive here.
The way back to the classrooms is up the front steps and the marble staircase.

front-lawns.summary: Front lawns and slopes is a group heading for the open grass that falls away from the castle front towards the lake, the Forest edge and the pitch; it is not one lawn. Known stretches are the forecourt lawn before the front steps, where the whole school can line up; the slope down to Hagrid's cabin; the slope to the Quidditch stadium; the slope to the lake; and the ground around the Whomping Willow. They share open grass and a steady fall away from the castle, so every return is uphill. Size comes from what they take: the school in rows with a house-sized carriage and a dozen elephant-sized horses landing beside it, and open ground where Death Eaters drew up opposite the doors in 1998. No stretch is measured from the castle.

facts.text: The forecourt takes the whole school in rows, with a house-sized carriage and twelve elephant-sized winged horses landing beside it.
The Beauxbatons carriage later stood on this open ground 200 yards from Hagrid's front door, with a paddock for the horses alongside.
A lesson table stood about 10 yards from Hagrid's door, with a class spread out on the grass.
Forecourt: the lawn directly before the front steps. The top of the lawns here overlooks the grounds and the lake.
Slope to Hagrid's: it runs from the front doors down to the cabin at the Forest edge, with a five-minute walk along the trees to a paddock.
Slope to the stadium: it leads down from the steps to the stadium and changing rooms, and a stretch of lawn links the stands to Hagrid's.
Slope to the lake: it leads from the doors down to the water, and the party coming up from the ship reaches the front doors this way.
Willow ground: a grassy slope climbs from the Willow towards the front steps, and from there the castle windows look distant at night.
Castle windows overlook the grounds: from Gryffindor, Hagrid's lit window can be seen, and a fallen teacher is watched from a dormitory.
The text marks only midpoints: halfway between cabin and castle, halfway to the Forest, halfway from stadium to castle.
All are open grass, springy and damp, sloping throughout.
Pupils cross freely with no surfaced path described. Routes from cabin and lake converge on the front doors, and fugitives cross them towards the gates.
Snow can lie two feet deep; walkers cut trenches in it and footprints record who has crossed.
Temporary uses include the Yule Ball grotto of Christmas 1994, Care of Magical Creatures tables in 1995 and sunbathing in June.
Battle of May 1998: about a hundred Dementors cross towards the castle, and bodies and a giant's clog as big as a small boat lie here afterwards.
At dawn Death Eaters draw up in a line opposite the open doors with Harry on the grass, and fighters come over the distant walls.

conflicts.text: Hermione recalls Harry returning mid-lawn, but narration puts him at the maze edge below the stands, inside the stadium.

open: Distances from the front steps to Hagrid's cabin, the lake and the stadium. The text gives none, only midpoints and sightlines.

yule-ball-gardens.summary: The Yule Ball gardens were a temporary rose garden and grotto conjured on the lawn directly in front of the castle for Christmas night 1994. Curving decorative paths ran among rose bushes, big stone figures and carved benches, lit by hundreds of real fairies, and led to a tall fountain with a bench facing it.

facts.text: It filled an area of lawn directly before the castle, visible through the open front doors and reached down the front steps.
Hundreds of real fairies served as lights in the bushes.
It was large enough to hide several groups from one another along winding paths with corners.
facts.because: Couples hide in bushes, two teachers come round a corner unseen, and people on a bench do not notice listeners behind a stone reindeer.

facts.text: Curving decorative paths ran among rose bushes, big stone figures of Father Christmas and reindeer, and carved benches.
A tall fountain stood beyond a large stone reindeer, with a stone bench facing the water.
Christmas 1994 only: the bushes were conjured, and Snape blasted some apart, while Madame Maxime sent swarms of fairies up as she pushed through.

open: Whether the fountain was conjured with the rest or stands there permanently. The text does not say.

hogsmeade-village.summary: Hogsmeade is a small all-wizard village outside the Hogwarts gates, at the foot of a mountain, and by report the only settlement of its kind in Britain. It is the weekend destination for pupils from third year. From the gates a road, hedged and twisting, runs downhill to the High Street, a curving main street of little thatched cottages and shops with side streets off it. Named premises are Honeydukes, Zonko’s, Dervish and Banges, Scrivenshaft’s, Gladrags, the post office, Madam Puddifoot’s, the Three Broomsticks and the Hog’s Head. The core is compact, a minute from one pub to the other’s corner, yet the post office alone holds hundreds of owls and the street can absorb the upper school on a visit day. Past Dervish and Banges the street becomes a winding lane with sparser cottages, ending at a stile below the mountain. The Shrieking Shack stands on a hill a little above the houses. The distance from the castle is never stated.

facts.text: Outside the Hogwarts gates: turn left between the winged-boar pillars on to the village road.
It lies downhill of the castle: the way back climbs a bending lane with a hedgerow, up to the gates.
It sits at the foot of a mountain that throws its shadow over it, with black mountains in view beyond the street.
It lies far enough north that the main street is still dark after sunrise at Shell Cottage.
The sky over Hogwarts can be seen from the High Street: in June 1997 the Dark Mark above the school is in plain view.
Flying to the castle means crossing the twisting lane, then the boundary wall, into the school grounds.
Reported to be Britain’s only entirely non-Muggle settlement.
