The core is tight: a minute from the Three Broomsticks to the Hog’s Head corner, and only minutes to the pub from Honeydukes or Madam Puddifoot’s.
From the shops to the stile at the far end is no more than a half-hour walk.
facts.because: The pupils set off at half past one for a meeting at the stile at two o’clock.

facts.text: The post office holds at least three hundred owls on shelves, from Great Greys to palm-sized Scops owls kept for local post.
Modelling minimum: 90 m of perch shelving in the post office, at 0.3 m an owl. On five tiers that is about 18 m of wall.
facts.because: Three hundred owls and shelves are stated; the spacing per owl and the five tiers are assumptions.

facts.text: Visit days fill the place: pupils crowd the road and the High Street, and Zonko’s is so packed that moving is hard.
Little thatched cottages and shops, with trees along the street that carry enchanted candles at Christmas.
The High Street is the spine. It curves towards the Hogwarts road, and side streets leave it, some narrow.
A few streetlamps light it at night, and shops have rooms above them with windows over the street.
Past Dervish and Banges the street becomes a winding lane: cottages thin out, gardens grow, and it stops at a stile below the mountain.

At least nine named premises: Honeydukes, the post office, two pubs, Dervish and Banges (magical instruments), Zonko’s (jokes), Scrivenshaft’s (quills), Gladrags (clothes) and Madam Puddifoot’s teashop, cramped and up a side road.
Ron and Hermione report the post office’s owls colour-coded by delivery speed.
Pupils from third year may go on set weekends with a signed permission form; younger years are barred.
Filch checks names at the front doors before anyone leaves, and from 1996 passes a Secrecy Sensor over them too.
Pupils normally walk the road. The Knight Bus has also driven through to the gates, and extra Apparition practice was held here in spring 1997.
1993–94: by Ministry notice, Dementors patrol the streets every night after sundown.
1996: Death Eater wanted posters fill shop windows, Zonko’s is boarded up by October, and Aurors are stationed in the village.
February 1997: the next visit is cancelled. June 1997: funeral visitors take the lodgings. Autumn 1997: Ginny is barred from the village.
May 1998: curfew and a Caterwauling Charm cover the whole village, Disapparating from the street fails, and ten or more Dementors roam it. Aberforth points to the mountains as a way out.

conflicts.text: Ron and Hermione report about two hundred owls in the post office in 1993; Harry sees at least three hundred a few months later.
Up and down are used both ways along the High Street: up leads towards Hogwarts in one scene and towards the far end and the mountain in another.

open: The length of road between the gates and the High Street. No figure or walking time is given.
The exact order of shops along the High Street. Only partial sequences are narrated.

three-broomsticks.summary: A pub and inn on Hogsmeade’s High Street, the usual meeting place for visiting pupils and staff. It has a bar with a mirror behind it, tables packed into its corners, a fireplace and a window at the back, and at least one interior pillar. Madam Rosmerta sleeps upstairs, with a window over the street. The text calls it both tiny and large, so model a modest building whose bar is still big by village standards and is nearly always crowded.

facts.text: On the High Street, close to Honeydukes, and on the way to the slope that climbs to the Shrieking Shack.
Within minutes of Madam Puddifoot’s side road, and a minute from the corner of the Hog’s Head street.
Almost always packed: pupils, warlocks and others such as hags crowd it, and crossing the room means squeezing between tables.
It seats dozens at once: on one 1994 visit at least five separate parties sit in it, including a large group of Ravenclaws, in a room called packed.
facts.because: Harry, Hermione, Ron’s group, Ernie and Hannah, Cho’s group and Hagrid with Moody are all placed there together.

facts.text: The bar is long enough for a private word at the end away from Rosmerta, and a mirror behind it shows the shadowy corner tables.
A window and a fireplace stand towards the rear of the room, with small tables nearby.
An interior pillar stands among the tables.
A ladies’ bathroom opens somewhere off the pub; its position is not given.
Rosmerta’s bedroom is upstairs, with curtains and a view of the High Street.
The front door opens straight on to the street.
Rosmerta keeps two brooms behind the bar; Summoned in 1997, they burst out through the front door.
December 1993: a large Christmas tree stands beside the fireplace, and Rosmerta says Dementors have searched the pub twice.
May 1998: a dozen hooded Death Eaters rush out of its door when the alarm sounds; it is lit while the rest of the street is dark.

conflicts.text: The narration calls it a tiny inn in 1993, but Harry contrasts its large bar with the Hog’s Head in 1995.

hogs-head.summary: A small, dirty inn at the top of a side street off Hogsmeade’s main road, much quieter than the Three Broomsticks. Downstairs is a single small bar room with grimy bay windows, rough tables, a stone floor under years of dirt, a counter and a back room. A doorway behind the counter leads to a rickety wooden stair and the upper floor, with rooms for guests and Aberforth Dumbledore’s sitting room, where in 1998 the portrait of Ariana hides a tunnel to Hogwarts. Small as it is, the bar seated 28 pupils and its regulars in 1995, and hundreds of evacuees poured through the building in May 1998.

facts.text: At the top of a side street, reached past Zonko’s and the post office; Hermione notes it is not on the main road.
A minute’s walk from the Three Broomsticks, round a corner; its sign can be glimpsed down the side street from the main road.
A small inn. Its battered sign hangs from a rusty bracket above the door, showing a severed boar’s head bleeding on to white cloth; it creaks in the wind.
The bar is one small, dingy room that smells of goats.
In 1995 that room seats 28 pupils on pulled-up chairs, 25 of them arriving at once, while other customers stay.
Modelling minimum: about 40 m² of bar, say 6.5 m square. Twenty-eight pupils, four other customers and the barman need at least 1.2 m² each, seated, with tables.
facts.because: The head count comes from the 1995 scene; the area per person is an assumption. It stops a room called small being modelled too small for that crowd.

facts.text: Bay windows so crusted with grime that little daylight enters; a table stands in at least one of them.
The floor is stone under so much old dirt it looks like packed earth; in 1998 it has sawdust on it.
Rough wooden tables lit by candle stubs, and a fireplace with a shadowy corner beside it. One flickering candle is all that lights it in 1998.
A counter with dusty bottles stored beneath it, an old wooden till with a self-opening drawer, and a back room behind.
A second doorway behind the counter leads to a rickety wooden stair that comes out directly in an upstairs sitting room.

That sitting room has a threadbare carpet, a small fireplace, a table and a wobbly chair. Ariana’s large portrait hangs over the mantelpiece as the only picture, with a small rectangular mirror below it.
A grimy upstairs window looks down on the side street.
It has guest rooms: sixteen years before 1996 Trelawney stayed upstairs over the bar, and Snape, caught outside, claimed to have climbed the wrong stairs.
A bolted street door on the narrow side street leads directly into the bar.
Flitwick confirms that pupils are allowed in, by Hermione’s account.
In 1998 allies Apparate straight into the bar, whatever the outdoor charms do.
May 1998: hundreds of evacuated pupils pour down through the building from the tunnel, by Aberforth’s complaint.
Hagrid names it as one of the village pubs, where he met a hooded stranger in 1992.

open: How many rooms the upper floor holds, and how the guest stairs relate to the stair behind the counter.

honeydukes.summary: A sweetshop on Hogsmeade’s High Street, with a stock cellar below that hides the village end of the secret passage from the one-eyed witch on Hogwarts’ third floor. The shop holds a crush of pupils among walls of shelves and barrels, with Unusual Tastes in its furthest corner. A door behind the counter leads down wooden stairs to the crate-filled cellar. The owners are said to live above.

facts.text: On the High Street, near enough to the Three Broomsticks that people leaving the pub walk past its wall.
The cellar trapdoor is the Hogsmeade end of the one-eyed witch passage.
Packed on visit days: the crush of pupils is dense enough for Harry to go unnoticed, and he has to squeeze through it.
Shelf after shelf of sweets, including hundreds of kinds of chocolate set out in rows.
Large barrels stand on the floor, one wall carries novelty sweets, and a sign reading Unusual Tastes hangs in the furthest corner.
Mullioned windows look on to the street; in 1993 a Ministry notice is stuck inside the door.
A door behind the counter opens on a wooden staircase down to the cellar. A shop bell and street door can be heard from below.
The cellar has a stone floor under dust and is stacked with wooden crates and boxes, one crate big enough to hide a boy.
Closed, the trapdoor cannot be told from the dusty floor.
Ron says the owners live over the shop.

shrieking-shack.summary: A crumbling house of at least two storeys on a hill just above Hogsmeade, reputedly the most haunted building in Britain and in fact built for Remus Lupin’s monthly transformations. Its windows are boarded, its garden overgrown and fenced, and every outside entrance is said to be sealed. The only known way in is the tunnel from the Whomping Willow, which comes up through a small opening into a wrecked ground-floor room. From there a door leads to a hall, a crumbling staircase and a dark landing, where one door opens on a bedroom with a grand four-poster. It seems an ordinary-sized house. In May 1998 one ground-floor window is unboarded and looks towards the castle.

facts.text: Stands slightly higher than the other houses, on a hill reached by a slope past the Three Broomsticks.
A second path climbs from the opposite side of the hill, muddy and puddled.
It looks out towards Hogwarts: in May 1998 an unboarded window shows distant flashes where the castle stands.
At least two storeys: a ground-floor room and hall, a staircase, a landing with several doors, and an upper room.
An ordinary house, not a mansion: Harry gets across the upstairs bedroom to the door in three strides.
facts.because: The strides start from his position at the time, so they show a modest room rather than an exact width.

facts.text: Outside it is a crumbling house with boarded windows, a dank overgrown garden and a fence pupils can lean on.
The twins are said to have tried and failed: all entrances are reported sealed.
The tunnel enters a ground-floor room through a small opening: entrants pull themselves up out of it, and three chained people had to turn sideways to get back in.
The ground-floor room has peeling wallpaper, a stained floor, boarded windows and smashed furniture, including a chair with chunks torn out and one leg gone.
An open door to the right of the arrival point leads to a shadowy hall and a crumbling staircase, thick with dust.
On the dark landing only one door stood open in 1994. Do not infer the number of closed rooms.
The upstairs bedroom holds a grand four-poster with dust-laden curtains, and has floor enough to pace and fight in.
That bedroom’s windows are boarded and it has only one door.
Reputedly Britain’s most haunted building. In fact it was built with the tunnel for Lupin; the shrieks were his transformations, and Dumbledore let the story spread. Villagers still keep away.
Lupin says he and his friends left it at night to roam the grounds and the village.
June 1994: a broad polished track shows where something was dragged through the dust to the upper floor.
In 1995 Sirius proposes it for lessons; Hermione objects that one Cloak cannot hide 28 pupils getting there. No capacity is established.
By 1997 Hermione notes that Snape can get in, though nobody else goes there.
May 1998: the tunnel room has one oil lamp and a table; an old crate blocks the tunnel mouth, leaving a sliver of view.
May 1998: Voldemort uses the room as his base, with Nagini in a floating starry sphere that he moves through the air.

open: Which outside door or window still works. Entrances are reported sealed, yet in 1998 people come and go while a crate blocks the tunnel mouth.

whomping-willow.summary: A violent, thick-trunked willow standing by itself near the centre of the Hogwarts grounds, below the front doors and in view from the greenhouses and Gryffindor Tower. It was planted the year Remus Lupin came to school, over the mouth of the tunnel to the Shrieking Shack, to keep people away. Its boughs, some as thick as a python or a battering ram, strike anything within reach, and its trunk can bend almost double. A large gap among the roots at the foot of the trunk leads underground. A single knot low on the trunk freezes the whole tree when touched, whether by a paw, a long stick or a levitated twig. Its height is never stated.

facts.text: Stands by itself near the centre of the grounds.
It is lower than the entrance: from near it a grassy slope climbs up to the front steps.
Flying out from the castle wall the order is greenhouses, vegetable patch, lawns, then the tree.
It can be seen in the distance from outside the greenhouses, and from a boys’ dormitory window in Gryffindor Tower.
It is well out from the castle: at night the windows look distant from it, and their lights grow only slowly as one walks back.
A short chase off the walk from Hagrid’s cabin to the castle ends in its shadow, and a clump of trees at the Forest edge commands a view of it.
A hidden way from the Entrance Hall to the Forest edge goes by the vegetable gardens and greenhouses, then skirts the Willow.
Branches run as thick as a python and as a battering ram on a trunk described as thick.
Its blows dent and cave in a car and smash a broomstick into a dozen splinters.
The trunk can bend almost double, and the roots creak as it strains after a target.
Modelling minimum: a danger radius of about 8 m. Its boughs reach every part of a car, and the pupils need seconds to run to the trunk once it stops.
facts.because: A two-second dash at an assumed 4–5 m/s is about 8–10 m. The text states no reach or height.

facts.text: It looks ancient and gnarled, with twisted boughs and twigs that clench like knuckles.
A large gap among the roots at the trunk’s foot leads underground; a huge dog can drag a boy into it.
A single knot in the bark, low on the trunk near the roots, freezes the whole tree.
Any touch on the knot works: a cat’s paws, a rat by report, a long stick or broken branch, or a levitated twig.
The stillness does not last: the tree began moving again as soon as the children had gone down.
Lupin says Madam Pomfrey led him across the grounds towards it at evening, on the way to his transformation.
Pupils once dared each other to touch the trunk until one nearly lost an eye, after which it was forbidden to go near.
Planted the year Lupin started, because he had come, to guard the tunnel mouth; that was after Mrs Weasley left school.
September 1992: the crashing car damages this valuable tree, and several branches end up in slings.
Autumn 1993: the wind carries Harry’s Nimbus into it and the tree destroys the broom.
May 1998: the trio run to it through the battle; Ron stills it with a levitated twig, and the tunnel beneath still works.

conflicts.text: The narration calls the tree ancient, yet Lupin says it was planted the year he started school, within living memory. Model an old-looking tree.
In 1993 the Weasley twins think nobody has ever used the passage under it, but Lupin’s friends used it regularly in their schooldays.

willow-tunnel.summary: A low, narrow earth tunnel from the roots of the Whomping Willow, in the middle of the Hogwarts grounds, to a ground-floor room of the Shrieking Shack above Hogsmeade. It was built, with the Shack, so that Remus Lupin could be taken out of the castle for his transformations. It runs under the school boundary for a long way: to Harry in 1994 it seemed no shorter than the Honeydukes tunnel, itself a walk of over an hour. The ceiling is so low that a thirteen-year-old goes bent almost double, and by 1998 the trio have to crawl. No length is given.

facts.text: Runs from the gap in the Willow’s roots to a ground-floor room of the Shrieking Shack.
It must pass under the edge of the grounds and on to the hill above Hogsmeade.
facts.because: The Willow is inside the grounds and the Shack is beyond the boundary wall, so the tunnel crosses that line.

facts.text: To Harry it seems no shorter than the Honeydukes tunnel. That is an impression formed while running, not a measure.
Modelling minimum: 1 km. Half the Honeydukes minimum, allowing for how long a tunnel feels when run at a crouch.
facts.because: The Honeydukes estimate is at least 2 km; halving it is a deliberately cautious assumption. The tunnel must span from mid-grounds to the village hill.

facts.text: Very low: bent almost double in June 1994, and a crawl by May 1998 when the same three people are grown.
The ceiling is roughly waist to chest height on a teenager.
facts.because: A thirteen-year-old walking bent almost double, and crawling at seventeen, cannot have much more headroom than that.

facts.text: Narrow: a group goes single file, and three chained people turn sideways at the Shack end.
Earth-sided, with rock jutting from the ceiling in places; Harry cracks his head on one piece.
At the Willow end the entrant crawls in headfirst and slides down an earth slope to the tunnel floor; leaving means climbing up through the hole.
Near the Shack the floor rises, twists, and ends at a small opening into the room.
No lighting and no fittings are mentioned; users rely on wands.
Reported history: built with the Shack for Lupin’s use, and the scene of Snape’s near-disaster as a pupil.
It is drawn on the Marauder’s Map but runs off the sheet’s edge. Snape reads Lupin’s dot along it and out of sight.
May 1998: no barrier stops the trio, but a crate sits against the Shack opening. They crawl back the same way.

conflicts.text: Neville says all seven old passages were sealed by autumn 1997, with Death Eaters at their exits, yet the trio meet no barrier here in May 1998.

one-eyed-witch-passage.summary: A secret passage from Hogwarts to the cellar of Honeydukes in Hogsmeade, entered through the hump of a stone one-eyed witch about halfway along a third-floor corridor. A stone chute slides a long way down through the castle to cold earth; then a very low, narrow, twisting tunnel runs on for what feels like an hour, begins to rise, and after ten more minutes reaches worn stone steps. Two hundred steps and more climb to a trapdoor in the cellar floor. The whole route falls from the third floor to well below the village and climbs back, over a length of kilometres rather than metres. The Weasley twins used it often; it went unguarded in 1994 and was sealed by 1997.

facts.text: The statue stands about halfway along a third-floor corridor, on a route from the marble staircase up towards Gryffindor Tower.
An empty classroom lies to its left, and doorways stand on either side nearby.
A stone one-eyed witch with a hump, standing clear enough of the wall for boys to hide behind.
Tapped with a wand and told Dissendium, the hump opens just wide enough for a fairly thin person, who goes in headfirst.
It also works from within: a tap on the inside of the hump opens it, and it closes after the user climbs out.
A stone chute slides a considerable way down, ending on cold, damp earth.
The chute must drop at least three storeys inside the castle, since it starts on the third floor and ends on earth.
facts.because: Bare earth cannot lie above ground level, so the chute clears the second, first and ground floors, inside walls or a hidden shaft.

facts.text: It is a sloping chute rather than a sheer drop: Harry climbs back up it, hands slipping on its sides.
A shadowy corner at its foot is deep enough to leave a Cloak in.
The earth passage is very narrow and low, unlit, with an uneven floor.
It twists and turns like an animal burrow.
Walking fast, Harry goes for what feels like an hour before the floor begins to rise. That is his impression, not a timed figure.
Ten minutes after the rise begins he reaches the foot of the stairs.
Worn stone steps then climb out of sight: he passes two hundred before losing count, and his head hits the trapdoor.
Modelling minimum: about 2 km of passage, and about 3.5 km if the hour is taken at face value.
facts.because: Seventy minutes at an assumed 3 km/h in a low tunnel is 3.5 km. Halving the felt hour gives 40 minutes, or about 2 km.

facts.text: Modelling minimum: 36 m of stair rise, at 0.18 m a step, before counting any further steps. That is about the height of the castle from ground to seventh floor.
facts.because: Two hundred steps is the stated minimum; the riser height and the assumed 4–5 m a storey are not from the text.

facts.text: The tunnel at the stair foot lies far below the village street, and far below the castle’s ground floor too.
facts.because: At least two hundred steps and a ten-minute rise lead up to a cellar in the village, and the village is downhill of the castle.

facts.text: Tunnel and road are comparable journeys: Harry sprinting back from Honeydukes emerges just as Snape arrives, sent by Malfoy who ran from the Shack.
facts.because: Malfoy ran by road to the dungeons and Snape then climbed to the third floor in about the time Harry took, so the tunnel is not many times longer than the road.

facts.text: The far end is a trapdoor in the cellar floor of Honeydukes.
It works in both directions, and pupils can run the whole way; the return felt almost instant to a distracted Harry.
The twins say they have used it often and that Filch does not know it. In early 1994 it stays unboarded and unguarded.
Sealed by the start of 1997–98, with curses and guards, as part of the seven old passages.

open: Where the corridor with this statue lies relative to the forbidden corridor of 1991–92.
How the chute is hidden as it passes the lower floors.

hogs-head-passage.summary: A lamplit tunnel between the upstairs sitting room of the Hog’s Head and the Room of Requirement, created by the Room in spring 1998 and absent from the Marauder’s Map. Its village end is the portrait of Ariana above the fireplace, which swings out as a door, so users climb on to the mantelpiece. Stone steps lie just inside, then a worn earth floor where people walk upright. After a long stretch the passage climbs steeply, turns a corner and ends at a short flight of steps and a small matching door into the refuge. No length is given. Hundreds of pupils were evacuated through it on the night of the battle, before Mrs Longbottom sealed it.

facts.text: One end is in the upstairs sitting room of the Hog’s Head, behind Ariana’s portrait over the fireplace.
The whole picture swings out on the wall as a small door, and users climb on to the mantelpiece to get through.
Smooth stone steps lie just inside, then a worn, smooth earth floor, with brass lamps hanging on the walls.
People walk upright and talk freely, and Neville walks backwards to face the others, so it is roomier than the older tunnels. Voices echo along it.
facts.because: No width or height is given, but nobody stoops or crawls, in contrast with the Willow and Honeydukes tunnels.

facts.text: Seen in the portrait it is a long tunnel: Ariana’s figure shrinks into the dark and comes back as a tiny white dot.
Modelling minimum: 400 m. About 1,100 words of talk pass as they walk, some seven minutes of speech, at an assumed 4 km/h.
facts.because: Word count of the walking conversation at 150 words a minute. It sets only a floor; the span from village to castle should be longer.

facts.text: The far stretch slopes upward and then climbs so steeply that Neville pants while talking.
It ends round a corner at a short flight of steps and a small door like the portrait, opening into the Room of Requirement’s refuge.
The Room end is a hole in the wall, apparently above floor level.
facts.because: People climb through it, and Percy overbalances and falls on arriving.

facts.text: It carried hundreds of pupils on the night of the evacuation, and Aberforth complains of them thundering through his pub.
Reported origin: the Room made it once Neville had hidden there some thirty-six hours and wanted food, nearly two weeks before May 1998.
Mrs Longbottom says she was the last through and sealed it during the battle, after Aberforth left. How is not stated.

conflicts.text: It looks as if it has been there for years, yet Neville says the Room opened it only about two weeks earlier.
Ron recalls seven passages, and this one is not on the Map. It is an eighth route, not one of the seven.
The Room’s door is on the seventh floor, but that night the refuge’s stair climbs a long way up to a fifth-floor corridor, so the tunnel’s end cannot be fixed to one floor.

open: How far it really runs. Crossing from the village to the castle should take far longer than the conversation narrated, as the Honeydukes tunnel does. It may not obey ordinary geometry.

secret-passages.summary: The secret passages out of Hogwarts as a set, not one place. The Marauder’s Map shows seven, and many of them run into Hogsmeade. Filch knew four, whose routes the text does not give. The other three are the one behind a large mirror on the fourth floor, roomy but caved in from the winter of 1992–93; the Willow tunnel; and the one-eyed witch passage to Honeydukes. Those with known entrances start at a disguised opening: a statue, a mirror or a tree’s roots. Gregory the Smarmy’s statue and an unnamed statue of 1998 also hide passages, which may or may not be among the seven. The set was watched from 1996 and sealed, with guards at the far ends, in 1997–98. The Hog’s Head passage of 1998 is an eighth route.

facts.text: Seven passages in all are drawn on the Marauder’s Map.
Many of the seven run into Hogsmeade; the text does not say that all of them do.
Filch is said to know four of them; the twins think they alone know the other three.
They differ in form and in where they start: a statue’s hump, the back of a big mirror and a tree’s roots are all confirmed entrances.
facts.because: Three of the seven have named entrances, each hidden differently, so no standard door or tunnel type should be assumed.

facts.text: Named instances: the one-eyed witch passage to Honeydukes, the passage under the Whomping Willow, and the fourth-floor mirror passage.
The mirror passage stood behind a large fourth-floor mirror, and Sirius remembers it as roomy enough to practise jinxes in.
The mirror passage is reported completely blocked by a cave-in since the winter of 1992–93.
The twins believe a passage out of school lies at the statue of Gregory the Smarmy, found in their first week.
In May 1998 a statue that has left its plinth reveals a concealed hole into a secret passage, guarded by Fred and others.
The Hog’s Head passage is a separate, later route, not among the seven.
1994: Filch boards up cracks and mouseholes along the corridors, but the one-eyed witch stays open.
1996: Umbridge says Filch is watching every passage in and out. June 1997: McGonagall says all are covered.
1997–98: Aberforth says both ends are watched; Neville says all seven were sealed before term, cursed at their mouths, with Dementors and Death Eaters posted at their far ends.
May 1998: groups are posted to defend the passage entrances during the battle.

conflicts.text: Hermione assumes Filch knows every passage; the twins say he knows four of seven.
All seven are said to be sealed in 1997–98, yet the Willow tunnel is open and unbarred in May 1998.

open: The routes and castle ends of the four passages Filch knew, and whether the two statue passages are among them.

trophy-room.summary: A display room on an upper floor, the third or the sixth as the text disagrees, with a door at each end, another room beyond one door and a long gallery of armour beyond the other. Its crystal cases hold silver and gold cups, shields, plates and statues, about a hundred cups by one pupil's guess, including the Quidditch Cup, special awards, medals and a list of past Head Boys. Malfoy claims it is always unlocked. A 1991 night journey goes to the third floor, while a 1995 reading of the Marauder's Map puts it one floor above the fifth. The walked journey supports the third floor, but this is not settled.

facts.text: It has a door at either end, so people can pass straight through.
It has windows, since moonlight reaches the cases.
facts.because: At night the cases shine where moonlight catches them (B01-048); no window is mentioned directly.

facts.text: Another room lies beyond one door, and a long gallery of armour beyond the other.
Pupils think of it as a very long way from the Charms classroom.
Its crystal cases display silver and gold cups, shields, plates and statues.
Ron guesses about a hundred cups, and a detention polishing them runs until late at night.
Awards include the Quidditch Cup and a Special Award for Services to the School.
A burnished gold shield sits in a corner cabinet; the room also holds a Medal for Magical Merit and a list of past Head Boys.
Its shields carry names: Riddle searched them for his father.
Malfoy claims it is always unlocked, and the pupils do enter at midnight.

conflicts.text: Third floor against sixth. In 1991 the pupils go up a staircase to the third floor and on towards the trophy room (B01-047). In January 1995 Harry, in the corridor outside the fifth-floor Prefects' bathroom, reads Peeves on the Map one floor up, in the trophy room, which makes the sixth floor (B04-139, B04-131).
The third-floor claim has a flaw of its own: the pupils set out from the seventh-floor Gryffindor entrance (B01-053), yet they go up a staircase to reach the third floor (B01-047).

Weight of the journeys, not a settled answer: the only walked route supports the third floor. The escape runs through the armour gallery, corridors and a tapestry passage to the Charms corridor, whose end door opens on the forbidden third-floor corridor, with no stairs mentioned (B01-049, B01-050). The sixth floor rests on one glance at the Map.

open: The room's size is never given.

marauders-map.summary: A magical parchment, not a place: a map of the castle and grounds with a detailed plan of every floor, showing people as moving labelled dots. It matters here as evidence for the castle's layout. It shows many shortcuts and secret passages, and the twins count seven passages to Hogsmeade on it. It shows Gryffindor and Ravenclaw in separate towers, Slytherin in the dungeons and Hufflepuff in a basement near the kitchens. It reaches only to the school boundaries, reveals people under invisibility, and never shows the Room of Requirement. Positions on the sheet are not compass bearings.

facts.text: It shows the castle and grounds in detail, with a plan of every floor.
It reaches only to the school boundaries.
It is a sheet of parchment that folds into a square and looks blank until woken.
People, the caretaker's cat and Peeves appear as tiny moving dots with names.
It shows many shortcuts and secret passages.
The twins count seven passages to Hogsmeade on it.
It shows Gryffindor in one tower, Ravenclaw in another on the west side, Slytherin in the dungeons and Hufflepuff in a basement near the kitchens.
Dumbledore's study lies in its top left corner and Snape's office in its bottom left corner.
Sheet positions are not compass bearings.
facts.because: The text never says which way up the sheet lies or how the floors are arranged on it.

facts.text: A wand touch and a spoken pledge bring it up; a touch and Mischief managed blank it.
It reveals people under an Invisibility Cloak and Animagi under their real names.
The Room of Requirement never appears on it, and a person inside drops off the Map.
It keeps working far from the castle.

portraits.summary: Paintings hang throughout the castle, along corridors, up staircases and on landings. This is a subject, not a place. Their subjects move, talk, whisper at passers-by and visit neighbouring frames, so a frame can stand empty or crowded. Whole staircases are picture-lined. Known examples include Sir Cadogan's large landscape on a seventh-floor landing, women in crinolines and monks on the North Tower stair, a landscape with trees on the fourth floor, a map of Argyllshire on the second floor, drunken monks near Charms, and bewigged witches on a marble-stair landing. Former heads have other frames elsewhere and can travel between them. Pictures were scrubbed in 1994, damaged in 1996 and 1997, and packed with shouting figures during the 1998 battle.

facts.text: Pictures line whole staircases: Violet is reckoned to have run through every one on seven of them.
Corridors above the marble staircase are portrait-lined, and the subjects whisper, point and mutter at passers-by.
A flight just below the Gryffindor entrance is lined with old witches and wizards.
Sir Cadogan's large landscape hangs on a seventh-floor landing, beside a picture holding a big wolfhound.
Women in crinolines hang on the narrow North Tower spiral, with sinister monks near its top.
On the fourth floor hangs a landscape with trees, and on the second a map of Argyllshire; the fleeing Fat Lady used both.
A picture of drunken monks hangs somewhere near the Charms corridor.
A witch in a meadow hangs next to card-playing wizards, one floor below the Defence office.
Violet's frame is in the chamber off the Great Hall, next to a walrus-moustached wizard.
Bewigged witches hang on a landing of the marble staircase.
Subjects leave their frames and enter neighbouring pictures, leaving a frame showing only its background.
Former heads travel between their own portraits, including ones at St Mungo's and Grimmauld Place.
Subjects can leave the castle only to visit another painting of themselves.
October 1994: grimy portraits were scrubbed before the foreign guests came.
A 1996 rocket blasted a hole in one painting, and a 1997 curse struck the bewigged witches' picture.
May 1998: painted figures in old dress ran alongside Harry, crammed into each other's frames and shouted news and advice.

armour-and-statues.summary: Suits of armour and statues stand throughout the castle, usually on plinths in corridors. This is a group, not a place. A long gallery near the trophy room is full of armour. Statues range from smaller to larger than life and include animals; several are big enough to hide a person. Named or located examples are Boris the Bewildered on the fifth floor, Lachlan the Lanky on the seventh, the humpbacked one-eyed witch halfway along a third-floor corridor, Gregory the Smarmy, Wilfred the Wistful, a bust of Paracelsus, a large stone griffin and a muttering stone head in a recess. Suits creak, turn their helmets and laugh, and in December they glow or sing. In May 1998 all were animated and sent to the boundaries, leaving empty plinths.

facts.text: A long gallery next to the trophy room is full of suits of armour.
They are found on floor after floor: in 1998 they stepped off plinths along one corridor, with crashes from above and below.
facts.because: Armour is a general corridor fitting (B01-027), and the crashes elsewhere imply the same on other floors, as Harry himself judges (B07-063).

facts.text: Statues range from smaller to larger than life and include animals.
Many are big enough to hide behind: a griffin, a large suit, an unnamed statue, and a stone head with its recess.
Boris the Bewildered, shown as a puzzled wizard whose gloves are on the wrong hands, stands on the fifth floor.
Lachlan the Lanky stands on the seventh floor near the top of a staircase.
A humpbacked one-eyed witch stands halfway along a third-floor corridor, beside an empty classroom.
Gregory the Smarmy hides a passage, and his corridor is apparently on the fifth floor of the east wing.
facts.because: The passage is the twins' report (B01-044). They name his corridor for a diversion set in the east wing (B05-226), and the swamp is on that wing's fifth floor (B05-235).

facts.text: A statue of Wilfred the Wistful and a bust of Paracelsus stand on routes from Gryffindor up to the Owlery.
A large stone griffin stands in a side corridor near the toilets of Book 1.
A muttering stone bust of a medieval wizard stands on a column in a recess of the Defence office corridor.
A tall suit stands near the classroom of the Mirror of Erised, and another near the kitchens.
A suit stands at the top of the trick-stair shortcut.
Suits stand on plinths and are hollow enough to hold Peeves.
Suits creak, turn their helmets to watch, and one laughs at a trapped pupil.
At Christmas lights shine inside them (1993) and they sing carols (1994).
October 1994: suits were polished until they gleamed and stopped squeaking.
May 1998: McGonagall sent statues and armour, carrying swords and chained spiked balls, out to the boundaries.
Statues left empty plinths, and one exposed a hole to a secret passage.
Suits were destroyed in the fights of 1997 and 1998.

open: How far suits can move before 1998 is unclear: they creak, turn helmets and are said to move without squeaking (B04-038), and Harry believes they walk (B01-026), but none is seen crossing a floor.

ghosts.summary: The castle's ghosts: translucent pearly-white figures that move through walls, doors and tables. They are a subject, not a place. About twenty crossed a chamber together in 1991, and hundreds gathered at a dungeon party in 1992. For a modeller the point is that ghost routes need no openings, and that ghosts drift a few inches off the floor and all but vanish in bright sun. Myrtle also travels by plumbing.

facts.text: About twenty ghosts crossed the antechamber together in 1991.
Hundreds crowded a dungeon dance floor at the 1992 party.
They are translucent and pearly white, and barely visible in strong sun.
The Grey Lady is tall, with long hair and a floor-length cloak, and glides a few inches above the floor.
They pass through walls, tables and blackboards, so their routes need no openings.
Myrtle travels by plumbing: she dives into her toilet and surfaces elsewhere in the castle's bathrooms.
Nick says the Bloody Baron likes to go up the Astronomy Tower and make a noise there.
A petrified Nick turned black and smoky, hung six inches above the floor and had to be fanned upstairs.

unnamed-rooms.summary: One-off rooms the text mentions without naming or placing. They are listed together only for convenience, and they are not one room. Known instances are an empty room with a closing door, a school laundry, a student store-cupboard for potion ingredients, a lockable broom cupboard between Defence and the staff room, a dungeon cupboard where the young Aragog lived, a quiet room used during exams, a vanishing room of chamberpots, and a Vanishing Cabinet on the first floor.

facts.text: A Vanishing Cabinet stood on the first floor in 1996.
A lockable broom cupboard lies round a corner from the Defence classroom, on the way to the staff room.
A cupboard door stands round a corner, about five minutes beyond the Potions room, in a memory from fifty years earlier.
That cupboard, or another at the school, housed the young Aragog on table scraps.
A store-cupboard holds common potion ingredients that pupils may take.
A school laundry holds spare robes.
An unnamed empty room has a door that closes for private talk.
A quiet room took a pupil recovering from an exam in 1994.
Dumbledore reports a finely proportioned room full of chamberpots, found on a wrong turn and gone when he came back.
Under the Carrows a first-year was chained up somewhere in the school.
